Therefore, one who is endowed with knowledge and joined with that [practice] is the eldest. || 30 ||
One should not, under any circumstances, salute a person who is inferior in caste or inferior in relationship. || 31 ||
If he were such [a person], some say that he should also offer salutation to one who is junior to his own relative.
Some say that there is a mutual attainment [of results] between those of the same caste and those in the same stage of life. || 33 ||
If both are equal in every respect, there is mutual embracing. || 34 ||
All those who offer salutations should be joined with blessings by all. || 35 ||
Brahmā says: "Even those of lower caste or stage of life who have been initiated first must be saluted by those of higher caste or stage of life who have been initiated later."
Some say that there should be mutual salutation among persons who possess lordly power. 37.
Viṣṇu says that for powerful men, mutual embracing [is the appropriate form of greeting]. || 38 ||
"Those who possess lordship may perform salutations, embraces, and blessings as they please," said Unmattabhairava. (39)

Having recited his own caste (*varṇa*), his own *pravara*, his own *gotra*, his own Veda, his own thread of initiation (*saṃskāra-sūtra*), his own stage of life (*āśrama*), his own name, the knowledge he has studied himself, and the sacrifices he has performed, he should utter the name of the person to be saluted,
preceded by the word "sir" (*bhoḥ*) and ending with the vocative particle, and then loudly proclaim, "I salute you" (*abhivādaye*).
One should touch the ground with the toes of the feet, the two knees, the two hands, and the forehead; this is the procedure for salutation. || 40 ||
"One's own knowledge and one's own austerity should not be proclaimed," so says the Sun. || 41 ||
The Kṣatriya, having recited his own caste, his own family priest, his lineage, his purificatory rites, his ritual manuals, and the Vedas;
having declared his own stage of life and his own name; having recounted the knowledge studied by himself;
the sword-strokes dealt by his enemies in battles, as well as those he himself dealt; and the victories he achieved upon the field of battle.
Having recited [the name] in that same manner and having proclaimed it, one should offer salutation. || 42 ||

A Vaiśya, having recited his own caste, his own family priest’s *gotra* and *pravara*, his sacramental rites, his *sūtra*, and the Vedas; having recited his own stage of life (*āśrama*), his own name, the sciences studied by himself, the number of persons to be supported by him, and the annual yield of the livestock to be supported by him; [should perform the offering].
In that very same way, having announced his name, he should offer salutation. || 43 ||

A Śūdra, having pronounced his own caste, his own stage of life, his own age, his own name, and likewise the caste of his master, should prostrate himself after having made such a proclamation. || 44 ||
Those worthy of salutation should return the greeting with a blessing to those who salute them. (45)
A Brahmin,

having been addressed by another Brahmin— who was himself authorized for the stages of life (āśrama) as a student, householder, forest-dweller, or renunciant— as "Long-lived one," "Most disciplined," "Most firm," "Most strong," and "Wise through learning and austerity," [should respond] by loudly proclaiming this with the gesture of the boon (varamudrā) and a blessing.
It should be applied. || 46 ||

Thus, O venerable one presiding over the stages of life as a student, householder, or forest-dweller, may you be most disciplined, most firm, and most strong; may you be endowed with learning, austerity, wisdom, and intelligence, and be joined with the supreme seal of blessing that is irreproachable.
Thus, O venerable one presiding over the stages of life as a student, householder, or forest-dweller, may you be most disciplined.
Having loudly proclaimed himself most firm and most strong through his learning and valor, he should join the Kṣatriyas with a blessing by means of the excellent seal. || 48 ||

Thus, having loudly proclaimed, "May the venerable Āśiṣṭha, who holds authority over the stages of life as a student and a householder, be most firm, most strong, and most powerful through both knowledge and wealth," the Vaiśya should be joined with a blessing by means of the *vara-mudrā*.
Thus, having loudly proclaimed, "O householder, may you, the master of the stage of life, prosper in long life and health," the Śūdra should be joined with the blessing by means of the *vara-mudrā*.

Because the Śūdra lacks the entitlement to the Vedas—and because the rules for the student (*brahmacārin*) are based upon the Vedas—this [student] lacks that [entitlement]. This is the rule regarding salutation and the return of the blessing: in the case of one not previously seen, [one should say]; but in the case of one previously seen, having taken up one's own name ending in "Śarman," and having taken up the name of the person being saluted in the vocative case, one should salute him.
Thus he should offer salutation; the one being saluted should respond with the blessing, "O long-lived one, may you prosper.
For all those belonging to the [student] orders, [the name] ends in *varman*; for a Kṣatriya, it ends in *pālita*; for a Vaiśya, in *gupta*; and for a Śūdra, in *dāsa*—so say some.
If both were equal in every respect, then they would embrace one another. || 53 ||
Placing heart against heart and neck against neck, and having joined them together, one should support the back with both hands; this indeed is the sequence for embracing. || 54 ||
Having loudly proclaimed, "I anoint you with affection," he should embrace her equally. || 55 ||
Some say it is "tṛṣṇīm" (silently). 56.
A woman who is senior in age should be saluted; if she is younger, she should be joined with a blessing. If she is of equal age, she should be joined with a blessing by men.
A man possesses limbs more exalted than those of women; therefore, the man is superior to women. The man is the enjoyer, while women are the objects of enjoyment.
Women should be employed as servants for the sake of the great feet of the enjoyer. Thus are women described. 58.
Among women, seniority by marriage alone is the cause for being saluted; other qualities are not causes for being saluted. (59)
Now, one who is to be saluted should behave toward a wealthy person in such a way that he becomes inclined to offer a greeting. 60.

Having recited according to the sequence of one's own conduct, one's own deity-connection, one's own doctrine, and one's own name and conduct— whether in the right, left, or northern [traditions]— one who is initiated should likewise offer [the oblation].
Some say that one should salute another with the intention of honoring their seniority by birth.

One should salute those who have undergone consecration according to the sequence of their consecrations; one should salute those initiated according to the sequence of their initiation. Likewise applies this to embracing and the bestowing of blessings.
When one's mother, father, teacher, and lord meet together, whom should one salute first?

Among mother, father, teacher, and sovereign, each subsequent one is more venerable than the preceding; therefore, when both mother and father are present, one should salute the father; when both father and teacher are present, the teacher; and when both teacher and deity are present, the deity.
Some maintain that one should first bow to whichever of these was encountered earlier, with the permission of the other. 66.
When there is a conjunction of the Guru and the Arghya-guru, Kālabhairava says that one should address the Guru with the words "O Guru," having been authorized by the Arghya-guru. || 67 ||
In that conjunction, the Guru, authorized by his own Guru, [offers] the arghya to the Guru; thus says Unmattabhairava. (68)

(36) According to the sequence of salutation, to whatever extent one recognizes the worthiness of the person who offers salutation, to that same extent the person being saluted should speak, act, and honor that saluter. || 69 ||
Having bowed to the Guru or the Deity, he should remain with his gaze fixed upon their lotus feet; he should perform their service, recite what they command, and sit only when permitted by them.
Once permitted by them, he may laugh, speak, look about, and move about according to his own will.
One should enjoy those remnants as one's sustenance. || 71 ||
"One should not eat the leavings of another, nor that which belongs to others, nor that which is common [to all]," so says Kālabhairava. (72)
"One should eat with his permission"—thus says Ākāśabhairava. (73)
Nor should one salute someone who is on a terrace, or who is marked with a sign of office. || 74 ||
Having saluted his own teacher at the tip of his branch, he should not salute others who are worthy of salutation. || 75 ||
Some say that one should prostrate to the Guru before the deity. || 76 ||
If he should bow there, the teacher should strike him; that which the teacher strikes constitutes his atonement. || 77 ||

If the Guru does not strike him, then he should ask that Lord for forgiveness by means of His mantra or His Gāyatrī, and offer six handfuls of flowers upon His head; this is the alternative expiation. || 78 ||

Alternatively, one should bow to the Guru while mentally meditating on the deity as concealed behind a cloth or similar object; thus says Digbhairava: "One who has undertaken the practice of deity worship should not offer salutations [to others]. || 80 ||
"One should salute with a mere verbal greeting"—this refers to the Gārhapatya fire. || 81 ||
One should not bow to one who is not composed in meditation. || 82 ||
One who is not composed should not prostrate. || 83 ||
In the absence of his mother and others, having prostrated before the teacher— who is like a deity— as well as guests and the virtuous, he should likewise prostrate before his mother and father.

If one who has been initiated by the Lord (aiśvara-dīkṣita) desires to salute someone who is merely [initiated] through the sacramental process (sāṃskārika), he should not salute him according to the order of initiation; rather, considering his status as one to be saluted according to the order of the sacraments, he should salute him according to the order of the sacraments and not according to the order of initiation— thus says Dakṣiṇāgni.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Pārānandasūtra. || 7 ||
The preceding chapter is completed.
Oṃ. Now we shall explain the sequence of worship. || 86 ||
A devotee should always meditate thus upon Him as being twenty-one years of age.
He is certainly elephant-faced, four-armed, and has a human body.
The Lord is red in color, endowed with the power of nourishment (puṣṭi-śakti), and clad in red garments;
in his two right hands, he holds an axe and a goad.
Holding a lotus and a noose in his two left hands, riding upon a rat, adorned with various ornaments, and smeared with red sandalwood—such is the visualization of the Elephant-faced One (Gaṇeśa). 87.
The weapons are placed in order on the right upper and lower hands and the left upper and lower hands; the *śakti* is always on the left.
A devotee should always meditate upon Sadāśiva as white, five or six years of age,
having one face, four arms, and two eyes, appearing certainly human.
One should visualize [the deity] as a bull, or as one endowed with power, naked, or clad in white garments; and in his two right hands, he holds an axe and a trident (or,
according to the Āhavanīya fire ritual, an axe and a trident).
Holding a hand-drum and a lotus in his two left hands, riding upon a bull, adorned with various ornaments, and smeared with white sandalwood—this is the visualization of Śiva. (89)
A devotee should always meditate upon Viṣṇu, who is sixteen years of age, the eternal Hari,
with a dark-complexioned body, four arms, and a human form.
The Lord, joined with his consort Lakṣmī and his Śakti, is worthy of praise and clad in yellow garments;
in his two right hands, he holds the discus and the mace Kaumodakī.

In his two left hands he holds a lotus and a conch; he has the eater of serpents (Garuḍa) as his vehicle, is adorned with various ornaments, and is smeared with yellow sandalwood—such is the visualization of Viṣṇu. (90)
The devotee should always meditate upon Kauśikī, who is nine years of age,
whose body is like well-refined gold, and whose form possesses a human appearance.
She is joined with the brindled Caṇḍikā, wears red garments, and has four arms;
in her two right hands, she holds a sword and a trident.
Holding a lotus and a bell in her two left hands, riding upon a lion, adorned with various ornaments, and anointed with saffron and aloe-wood—such is the meditation on Śakti. (91)
A devotee should thus constantly meditate upon the Sun for twelve years— [visualizing him] as having a body of light, with arms like those of a youth, possessing a human form, and eternal.
The divine Lord, endowed with the power of consciousness, is clad in red garments;
he holds a discus in his right hand and an auspicious lotus in his left.
"Mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven horses, praised at all times by sages, adorned with various ornaments, and anointed with red sandalwood"—this is the meditation on the Sun. (92)

She who is dark like a water-laden cloud, ten years of age, with four arms holding a sword, a severed head, and the gestures of fearlessness and boon-giving; adorned with serpents; she who wears a garment of tiger-skin smeared with vermilion and sprinkled with red sandalwood paste; she who is naked, wearing an elephant’s hide as a lower garment and a girdle made from the hands of corpses; she who is mounted upon a lion.

Or she may be seated upon a corpse, her head adorned with curly locks of hair, delighted by the fragrance of wine, longing for the consumption of ritual offerings, satisfied and bestowing satisfaction,
bringing joy through the sight of her playful pastimes for the sake of her devotees, and wearing all the sciences as a garland of speech.

A devotee should meditate upon Kālikā, who is fond of battle, whose mouth is stained with the blood from the circle of the battlefield, who is joined with the spear of Kurukullā, and who possesses a human form; this is the meditation on Kālikā. (93)
The great vidyās beginning with Tārā, Siṃhanī, and Ṣaṣṭhī. || 94 ||
They maintain that the great vidyās each have their own distinct forms and mounts. || 95 ||
The staff (*daṇḍa*) is three *vitasti* long and as thick as a big toe; below it is a hilt (*tsaru*) six *aṅgula* long;
above the staff is a space of four *aṅgula* shaped like the sky, surrounded by a crescent shape—such is its form.
The axe. || 96 ||
The sword-hilt is the weapon-handle. || 97 ||
In all cases, the handle is six finger-breadths long. || 98 ||
The handle of the staff has the characteristics already described; upon it, the goad is shaped like a thumb of the hand, being low and long at the base and high at the tip. || 99 ||
The serpent is the noose. || 100 || 900 ||
The lotus stalk is two vitastis long. || 1 ||
Rising by means of his own measure, the mouse became seven spans in height and one span in length. || 2 ||
Vighneśa is raised to the height of one’s own span, seven spans in height, and extended accordingly to suit that [proportion].
Their attendants likewise have human forms, with corresponding garlands, ointments, and weapons; such are the Bhairavas of the Directions. 4.
All these lords are seven spans in height, and their lengths vary accordingly to suit that proportion.
His attendants were likewise shaped like humans, adorned with similar garlands and unguents.

All these lords, in their respective worlds, are unarmed, without vehicles, and two-armed; beyond that [world], Kālabhairava is present for all of them, with hands in the *padma* and *abhaya* mudrās, possessing forms corresponding to theirs, bearing their respective ages, having their respective vehicles, and wearing their respective unguents and garments.
The powers. || 8 ||
Since Vighneśa is twenty-one years old, therefore everything pertaining to him is numbered as twenty-one.

Bathing, libation, unbroken rice grains, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, fruit, betel leaf, the waving of lights (ārārtika), the waving of a thousand lamps, the waving of camphor, the water for the feet offered to a courtesan, circumambulation,
the offering of handfuls of flowers, prostration, the seeking of forgiveness for transgressions, fire sacrifice, flowers, and hymns of praise.

Regarding the animal sacrifice, Kālabhairava states that for the specific worship [of a deity], the number of years corresponds to the age of the Lord; however, in the daily worship, this [animal] becomes the libation (tarpaṇa) and the flower. || 10 ||

A staff (*daṇḍa*) as thick as a big toe and eight *vitasti* long, with three sharp-pointed tridents (*śūla*) above it, each twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long and as thick as a ring finger— this is the form of the trident (*triśūla*) belonging to Tatpuruṣa.

This is the form of Mahādeva’s *ḍamaru* drum: it has a mouth that is broad and rounded at both ends and narrow in the middle; its two mouths are bound with leather, and it is connected by a cord with a knotted tip; when whirled by the movement of the hand and struck at its two mouths with the end of the cord, it produces sound. || 12 ||
One span in width at the center, circular all around, with sharp edges on the perimeter, hollow in the middle and solid within— this is the form of Nārāyaṇa’s discus.
39) Above the aforementioned axe-handle, there is a circular mass six finger-breadths in height;
upon that mass are four sharp-edged [blades] extending as far as the middle joint of the middle finger.
Then, lines measuring only the breadth of a thumb appear; this is the form of Vāsudeva’s mace.
The conch of Viṣṇu is one span in width and one cubit in length. || 15 ||
The power of Kurukullā has a sword and the gesture of fearlessness, and the power of Caṇḍikā likewise. || 16 ||

It should be three or two vitastis in length; it is extended with the middle fingers, ring fingers, and index fingers held upwards with their tips uncut; it is like the middle petal of a bilva fruit, having two edges, a single groove in the middle, sloping downwards on both sides, and possessing sharp edges on both sides. || 17 ||
A sword with a hilt six finger-breadths long is of this form. || 18 ||

A bell of this form is one span long, as wide as a hollowed palm, low and rounded at the base, with a single high handle and a swinging clapper inside; it produces sound through the movement of the hand. || 19 ||
All the great vidyās beginning with Kā are ten years of age. || 20 ||
Their ages are the years, their powers are those [energies], and their colors are likewise.

Some maintain that these great vidyās are distinct from one another; because they possess their own respective origins, they are counted as powers (śakti), and their spheres of influence are different. || 22 ||

Those who consider themselves learned, yet whose intellects contradict the scriptures, ask: "Even if Īśvara and the others are limited by space and even if they are limited by the ether, how can they be beginningless and endless? How can they be omniscient? (23)

How is it that by worshipping through the empowerment of a deity one becomes worshipped by the deity? How does one conquer the heavenly world through well-performed action? How does one arise with a perfected, infinite, and divine body?
And how is this the empowerment of a deity? Thus do those who rely on fallacious reasoning remain faithless.
Those whose intellects contradict the scriptures suffer a great ruin. || 24 ||
If asked how it is that there can be many presiding agents for a single [object], we shall explain. || 25 ||
It is like a village or a house belonging to another person. || 26 ||

The well-spoken words of those who govern districts and villages, whose intellects contradict the scriptures, though they may be pleasant to hear when one has entered the interior of a house, are not to be accepted, like the talk of a parrot. 28.
For the Lords, whose bodies are beginningless and endless, the assumption of a second body during descents is like [the manifestation of] armor, finger-guards, and so forth. (29)
The Lord's body is eternally situated and unmanifest because of His inconceivable sovereignty. || 30 ||
[One should meditate on] him who is copper-red like a young sprout, two-armed and four-faced, holding a rosary in his right hand and a water-pot in his left;

appearing seven years of age, clothed in garments as copper-red as a young sprout, seated upon a swan-vehicle, anointed with fragrances as copper-red as a young sprout, accompanied by Sarasvatī, and possessing the form of a human being.
"One should meditate [on Him] as the devotee"—this is the meditation on Brahman. || 31 ||
The power Sarasvatī is seven years of age, clad in white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents, and has a swan as her vehicle in her celestial chariot. || 32 ||
The state of being worthy of service through skillful conduct belongs to Brahman. || 33 ||
"Like Vighneśa and others," says Nārāyaṇa. (34)
The fact that the Vidyās beginning with Kā and others are to be practiced through the left-hand path (vāmācāra) constitutes the Tatpuruṣa [aspect]. || 35 ||

(40) Dhyānayoga consists of being engaged in the restraints (yama), observances (niyama), postures (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), and meditation (dhyāna). || 36 ||
He clarifies them. || 37 ||
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the restraints (yamāḥ). || 38 ||
Purity, contentment, austerity, and self-study are the observances (niyamas). || 39 ||
The posture with a steady face. || 40 ||
Prāṇāyāma is the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation. || 41 ||
Pratyāhāra is the non-appropriation by the mind of sense objects, even when those objects are present before the senses. || 42 ||
Concentration (dhāraṇā) is the binding of the mind to a particular place. 43.
In that [state], meditation is the stabilization of the mind. || 44 ||
Karmayoga is the performance of the obligatory rites prescribed in the treatises on ritual, carried out by an eligible person who has abandoned violence and emulates those [ancient sages]. || 45 ||
The knowledge of the Śruti, Tantra, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, as accomplished in accordance with them by the qualified practitioner, is the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga). || 46 ||
Self-restraint, austerity, study of the Vedas, meditation, and devotion constitute the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga). || 47 ||
Non-violence, purity, austerity, celibacy, and truthfulness are the observances (niyamas). || 48 ||
Violence is indeed the complete separation of the vital breath from the body. (49)
Because that which is severed from a living being does not grow back there, that severing is indeed violence (hiṃsā). || 50 ||
Some maintain that the appropriation of another's property, even with their permission, is in fact theft. (51)
Except for the purpose of the daily worship of the deities, the unauthorized appropriation of another's property—that is, the taking of what belongs to another—is, according to some, theft. (52)
Falsehood is the verbal activity of living beings that obstructs the gods. || 53 ||
Some say that false speech is untruth. 54.
The remainder is clear. || 55 ||
From one sunrise until the next sunrise, during that interval, among gods, animals, and humans, [the Bodhisattva] makes a request—or according to some, a non-request—to any one of them. 56.
"Except for a human being, [giving] to another is begging, not non-begging"—thus says Unmattabhairava. (57)
Austerity is the performance of prescribed duties. || 58 ||
Some say that austerity consists in eating sparingly. 59.
"Fasting is austerity," says Kālabhairava. (60)
"Austerity consists of eating only leaves from the tops of trees," says Ākāśabhairava.
This recitation of the sacred texts is a continuous flow of retention, situated within the stream of the river of one's own desired and ordained duties. || 62 ||
"Having performed this, [it is] 'svādhyāyana' or 'svādhyāya'; thus says Digbhairava. (63)
(41) Meditation is the contemplation of the Lord, thinking: "There is no other protector for me but you. || 64 ||
"May I see him at some time"—this contemplation of the Lord is meditation; thus says Ākāśabhairava. || 65 ||

"He is the one to be served; I am the servant. He is the one to be propitiated; I am the propitiator. There is no other than him who performs what is desired by me"—this contemplation of the Lord is meditation (dhyāna), according to Kālabhairava. (66)
Devotion is attachment. || 67 ||
In this yoga of devotion, there are three modes of conduct; these have been explained previously. || 68 ||
One whose sole resolve is the dharma of non-violence,
devoted to self-study, and who practices even a single limb of the fourfold path through long-term, uninterrupted, and respectful cultivation, attains the satisfaction of the Lord.
Some maintain that even an act preceded by violence brings satisfaction to the Lord.

From one sunrise until the next sunrise, he who constantly and with self-restraint practices even a single limb [of yoga] preceded by the observance of non-violence attains that supreme devotion; thus say Digbhairava and Unmattabhairava. 71.

For those who, relying on violence, perform rituals while thinking, "We are practicing the duties of the lords," do not attain those [results]; they do not reach the worlds of the lords, but are subject to downfall.
For violence destroys longevity, and violence annihilates the multitude of merits. || 73 ||
Even if one were to perform thousands of floods of meritorious deeds by resorting to violence,
they would not be able to grant us happiness in any way whatsoever.

One should not desire treatments that bring about pleasure by relying on diseases such as consumption (yakṣman) and the like; otherwise, the dull-witted person will find that they do not grant him happiness. || 74 ||
Just as water mixed with poison can never quench thirst, so too merit joined with violence does not deserve to bring happiness to the giver. (75)
For any violence toward the innocent, whether prescribed or prohibited, results in suffering in every way; therefore, one should utterly avoid it. (76)
If a man were to create mountains of sin by relying on even a single instance of non-violence,
he makes all those mountains of sin pure through that very non-violence.
"He makes all things like his own self, just as fire [consumes] wood and mountains. || 77 ||
For those men who, at any time, perform the cutting, slaughter, buying, or selling of this very body which is not to be harmed by others;

Furthermore, those who are experts in non-violence (ahiṃsā) should indeed perform services, ritual refinements, and the granting of permission for the cessation of enjoyments regarding the body's constituent parts. || 78 ||
The cutting, slaughter, or purchase of the limbs of innocent creatures killed by humans— limbs whose moisture has not yet been shed and which have not previously been offered [as sacrifice].

Sale, processing, or enjoyment— whichever of these actions is performed, or even the approval of such an action— anyone who does any one of these also partakes in the suffering resulting from violence and the like.

Slaughter, purchase, sale, assistance, processing, enjoyment, and approval—these seven types of violence are secondary and equal to actual injury. Therefore, one who seeks the welfare of the Lord should avoid these eight forms of violence. (80)
One who has been directly initiated becomes authorized in all four yogas. || 81 ||
Some maintain that initiation consists of the cultivation of the state of supreme bliss within the yogas of action, knowledge, and meditation, which are themselves states of supreme bliss.

Some maintain that when violence is practiced preceded by the cultivation of the four [means] or any one of them, through the service of even a single limb, supreme devotion arises; and by means of that, the attainment of the primordial and infinite body occurs. || 83 ||
The worshipper is of two kinds. || 84 ||
The superior and the middling. || 85 ||

He who is a believer and, knowing the injunctions from the scriptures, feels extreme devotion toward the symbol of the Lord as an insentient object and performs its worship, he is the most excellent. || 86 ||

One should worship the Lord upon any one of these: a pedestal, a mechanical device, a sacrificial mound, naturally pure water, fire, wind, the directions, or space— each having the form of the weapon of its respective presiding deity, and made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or stone.
O Pārānanda, if one worships the Lord elsewhere than in these [places], he falls from the state of Pārānanda. || 88 ||
Therefore, Pārānanda should not worship another temple. || 89 ||
There is no purification of the elements, nor the web of ritual placements (nyāsa), nor violence toward moving or stationary beings;
nor indeed is there worship of deities or gods within the bodies of living creatures, whether mobile or immobile.

According to the instruction "of those who delight in the Supreme" (pārānandānām), Pārānanda should not worship the Lord within his own heart-lotus, nor in the Guru, nor in a worthy living being, nor in the solar orb; he should worship no other Lord. 90.
Some say that only flowing water is pure water. || 91 ||
Worship is threefold. || 92 ||
Worship through honoring, worship through giving, and worship through the application and employment [of offerings]. || 93 ||

Having invoked the deity and offered her a seat, one should perform prostration, meditation, the forgiveness of offenses, the declaration "I am your servant," the offering of one's good deeds, and the prayer for direct vision; then one should dismiss her—this is the worship of honoring (arhaṇārcana). || 94 ||
In this regard, some say there is the casting of a handful of flowers. 95.

Having invoked the deity and offered a seat to her, having arranged the various ritual offerings, and having placed all the articles of worship in one large vessel, one should offer the *tāmbūla* (betel) to her; then, having praised her with hymns, performed a circumambulation, and offered a handful of flowers, one should fix the mind in meditation.
(44) Having crossed over [the water] and put on another garment, he should sip water for purification. || 16 ||
A loincloth, a waist-string, two large white garments,
earrings, and a finger-ring are prescribed for the householder.
Some say that this excludes the Śūdra. || 17 ||
Whether a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic, those who are devoid of the loincloth and the waist-thread are Śūdras; of this there is no doubt.
The loincloth shall be twelve finger-breadths wide and five spans long; likewise, the waistband shall be six finger-breadths wide and [the same] length. || 18 ||
Garments made of hemp, grass, cotton, linen, deerskin, reeds, or bark should be worn as far as possible.
"Even the twice-born (dvijas) should wear these very [marks]," says Unmattabhairava. (20)
A Brahmin [should wear] white, a Kshatriya red, a Vaishya yellow, and a Shudra householder black.
"If these [marks] are worn by twice-born men belonging to the householder stage of life, they should be cast out like Śūdras; there is no doubt about this."
"If a Śūdra should be righteous, he may wear a loincloth," so says Bṛhaspati. || 22 ||
A Brahmin householder should not wear anything other than cotton cloth.
Bṛhaspati says that one becomes purified by wearing [the garment], bathing, performing three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and consuming clarified butter. || 23 ||

If the Śākta, Saura, and Vākratuṇḍa householders are present, [the thread] should be red; likewise, if the Śaiva is present, it should be white; and likewise, if the Vaiṣṇava is present, it should be yellow—so says someone.
Now we shall explain the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). || 25 ||

Having sipped water three times and wiped [the mouth] twice, one should wash the hands and touch the mouth, the right nostril, the left nostril, the right eye, the left eye, the right ear, the left ear, and the head; such is the rite of *ācamana*, according to Yājñavalkya. (26)

One should drink from, wipe with, or touch [the water] using the divine names of one's own chosen deity (iṣṭeśa), accompanied by vocative case endings, dative case endings, or the word "namaḥ"; this is called *ācamana* according to Unmattabhairava. || 27 ||

Having sipped water with the portion ending in *suvidmahe* from the Gāyatrī of one’s chosen deity (iṣṭeśa), having sipped water with the portion ending in *dhīmahi*, and having sipped water with the portion ending in *pracodayāt*, one should wipe the mouth silently; this touching [of the body] is called *ācamana*.
Thus says Digbhairava. || 28 ||
"O Vāmācārya, one should perform this sipping of water (ācamana)," so said Janārdana.
Having sipped water three times, one should wipe the lower lip twice with the base of the thumb in reverse order,
wash the hand, and then wipe the upper lip twice with the index, middle, and ring fingers in reverse order;
having washed the hand again, [one should touch] the right nostril with the thumb and middle finger.
One should touch the left nostril with the thumb and ring finger; the right eye and the left eye;
the right ear and the left ear; the heart with the palm; the upper part [of the head] with all five fingers;
and the root of the right arm and the root of the left arm with the right hand—this is called *ācamana*.
Devānanda || 30 ||
Having washed both hands, having sipped water three times, having wiped [the mouth] twice, and having touched the mouth once,
one should sprinkle the left hand, the feet, the head, the eyes, the ears, and the heart.
"One should touch [the water]"—this refers to the sipping of water (ācamana) for Brāhmaṇas.
"Of us Brahmins, not of others," said the Four-faced One.
Ānanda says that one should perform this sipping of water (ācamana) only after the [recitation of] the Uttara, and not otherwise.
When he sips water, he thereby makes himself pure and fit for all ritual acts. || 34 ||
In that he sips water twice, he thereby makes himself bathed; this is a secondary rule for bathing.

In rites pertaining to the lords (Aiśvara) and the gods (Daiva), one becomes worthy when having the topknot tied, wearing the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), and clad in garments; therefore, in all rites pertaining to the lords and the gods, one must have the topknot tied and wear the sacred thread,
because at the outset of [rites] involving worn garments, such attire is prohibited.
The marking has been explained. || 37 ||
Now we shall describe its constituent substances. || 38 ||
By means of vermilion, one becomes a leader of the Gaṇas. || 39 ||
One who is devoted to Śakti [should worship] with red sandalwood. || 40 ||
By that very [means], it is solar. || 41 ||
A follower of Śiva [should worship] with a bilva fruit. || 42 ||
The Vaiṣṇava [should mark himself] with yellow pigment (hāridra). || 43 ||
Some say that the Gāṇapatyas, Śāktas, and Sauras [should be worshipped] with non-alcoholic liquor and blood. || 44 ||
Some say that by means of the white, non-decaying [seed], one becomes a Śaiva. 45.
Some say that by drinking the non-decaying [soma], one becomes a Vaiṣṇava. || 46 ||
Since pure clay is the material for all the lords, they should therefore make all their marks with pure earth. || 47 ||
Having performed the twilight worship, one should attend upon one's chosen deity.
When he is marked, he casts out that evil. || 49 ||
If she is a woman, having performed the Tantric twilight ritual (sandhyā), she should worship her own chosen deity. || 50 ||
By performing the twilight worship (sandhyā), one thereby renders oneself qualified for the act of adoration. || 51 ||

If one performs the morning twilight ritual (*sandhyā*) or the bath (*snāna*) pertaining to that [Smārta] system, one becomes qualified for that Tantric [practice]; if one performs the second twilight ritual belonging to that Tantric system, one becomes qualified for its worship. Therefore, O Vāmī, having performed the Smārta bath, one should then perform the Tantric twilight ritual itself.

Desiring to worship according to the rite of daily worship, being pure, in a clean, level, and pleasing place, wearing the sacred thread and having sipped water (ācamana), he should leave his own seat for a space two cubits away and, in front of the lion-throne of the deity,
in a consecrated area, prepare a six-cornered, circular, sixteen-petalled mandala to his right.
Having arranged the vessels for the water-offering (vācana) and other purposes to the left of himself, he should likewise place a pure vessel made of gold,
conch-shell, metal, clay, or lotus, and perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
Some say that one should place the food offering (naivedya) to one's left.
Some say that the lion-throne of the deity is two spans high. (55)

Having placed upon that throne— whether it be made of gold, or of radiant metal, or of clay, or of grass, or of leaves, or of wood, or of stone— a representation of the deity, one should seat it upon a soft-to-the-touch skin or upon a heap of rice shaped like the vehicle of that deity. || 56 ||

First comes the bath; thereafter, the Tantrika performs the Tantric bath. Therefore, the Smārta performs the first *saṃdhyā*, and then the Tantrika performs the second *saṃdhyā*. Likewise, having performed the Smārta worship, one does not perform the Tantric worship. In this regard, it is resolved thus: for one who is about to bathe according to the Smārta rite...
The deities of bathing are distinct from those of the *saṃdhyā* and likewise from those of worship;

therefore, worship does not belong to both [categories], nor is it obligatory (*nitya*). If one enters the Southern Tantric path, only then does one abandon the Smārta obligatory worship of that deity.
Therefore, a second [husband] should not perform the daily worship prescribed by the Smṛtis.

If this Parānanda, without first worshipping his own chosen deity, should tend to the single domestic fire (*ekāgni*), or the sacrificial fires (*vaitānikāgni*), or should tend to any other divine, ancestral, or obligatory rite,
then the fires, being enraged, and the gods and sages, will curse this Parānanda and bring him under the power of death.
The gods and sages lead [the soul] away; therefore, a wise man should not act in this manner. Others say that Pārānanda may worship him as he pleases—either before or after—so some maintain.
To the south of the fire, he should prepare either a pit or a sacrificial mound. || 59 ||

The vessels for the articles of worship may be made of gold, silver, stone, clay, grass, leaves, sacrificial wood, metal, leather, or lotus-fiber; they may also be made of a combination of these materials. || 60 ||
Since those stones exist as distinct entities, they are not the bodies of living beings; and since the bodies of living beings are not stones, one should worship the Supreme Bliss within them.
The Śāligrāma is the representative symbol of all the lords; therefore, one should worship all of them within the Śāligrāma.
The Śālis are their lords; this stone has become the village of those Śālis.
Therefore, for that reason, one should worship all of them within them.
Śālayas, suyās, and kaṇās— those which are thus broken are stones that are worshipped in every village by gods, humans, and sages; therefore, these stones are called Śāligrāmas.
Because delight arises for those who are virtuous, endowed with devotion, and devoted to their own village in these stones, therefore these stones are called Śāligrāmas. || 65 ||
On a sacrificial mound, in natural pure waters, in fires, in winds, in the cardinal directions, or in any portion of space— whichever deity one may invoke, that very deity one should worship there.
If one worships on a sacrificial mound, one becomes possessed of firm devotion to the feet of those two deities. || 67 ||
If one worships in water, one becomes truly devoted to the deities. || 68 ||
If one worships in the fire, he becomes radiant in body, health, longevity, fame, splendor, and devotion. || 69 ||
Or if one worships in the air, the power of devotion alone is accomplished for the deity. || 70 ||
If one worships in this direction with unceasing devotion to the deity, then Mā, who is the object of comparison for devotees, becomes the subject of comparison to be designated. || 71 ||
If one worships in space, that form of a Siddha is attained without delay. || 72 ||

For the sake of attaining the grace of one's chosen Lord through the worship of that which is dear to oneself, one should resolve: "I shall worship my chosen Lord with daily ritual," and contemplate thus. (73)

For the sake of attaining the grace of one's own chosen Lord through the mediation of pleasing another Lord—preceded by the attainment of extreme devotion toward that other Lord during the worship of someone else—one should form this resolve: "I shall indeed worship with special offerings. || 74 ||
Or one may gather whatever other desired object one wishes for. || 75 ||
They say that the action which one performs without forming a resolve yields diminished fruit; therefore, one should perform every action after having formed a resolve.
"Without forming a mental resolve for a great fruit," says Unmattabhairava. (77)
In a circular, six-cornered, or sixteen-petaled diagram that has been sprinkled with water, one should place a pure vessel for drinking, such as a conch-shell, to one's left;
having filled it with pure water and added flowers and perfumes, one should decorate its exterior, invoke the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) into it, and establish oneself [within it] with "Oṃ bhūḥ."

One should sprinkle the ritual materials with "Oṃ Bhuvaḥ," the representative form of the deity with "Oṃ Svaḥ," and the intermediate directions with "Oṃ Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ. When one sprinkles oneself, one makes oneself pure, removes [impurities] resulting from errors, and— regarding transgressions committed of one's own accord— renders oneself a fit object for the diversion of the deities.

When he sprinkles the sacrificial materials, he thereby makes them pure, pleasing to the deities, and fit to be presided over by the deities; when he sprinkles the intermediate directions, he thereby makes the animals, humans, and gods coming from those quarters pure and worthy of conversation, and transforms those who are hostile into those who are favorable. Therefore, it is thus.
One should sprinkle it with water. || 78 ||
Some say that one should sprinkle everything with this very mantra: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. (79)

Some say that one should sprinkle oneself with the first quarter of the Gāyatrī of one's chosen deity, the ritual materials with the second, and the representative image of the deity along with all intermediate directions with the third.
"In this manner, one should sprinkle the left [side]," so said Unmattabhairava. (81)
A Śūdra should employ as many Vedic mantras as are required in whatever rite he performs, using his own desired name in the dative case followed by the word "namaḥ. || 82 ||
Anointed with that ointment and adorned with ornaments, the wise man, following the Smṛti tradition, should recite the armor-mantra (kavaca).
One should recite the Vāmī-tantra armor-mantra (kavaca). || 84 ||

The root mantra of all deities consists of the name ending in the dative case, preceded by "aut" (oṃ), followed by "ubhayaṃ," "dvayoḥ," or "anyataraṃ," and ending with "praṇaya" or similar terms. || 85 ||
This same [mantra], excluding the syllable *praṇava*, is for the Śūdras. || 86 ||
In this very homa, it ends with svāhā. || 87 ||
One should worship the lamp, which illuminates from afar all the provisions [of merit], with incense, unbroken grains, and flowers.
One should perform the service with the Gāyatrī of that respective Īśvara, with the mantra for the praise of that respective Īśvara, or with the root-mantra (mūlamantra). || 89 ||
From the world beyond, from this world, from oneself, from those who are more devoted, from those nearby, or from the outside, one should attend to them; then, one should dismiss them. || 90 ||
One should invoke [the deity] together with his weapons, ornaments, personal powers (*sva-śakti*), vehicle (*vāhana*), and attendants (*bhakta*);
having invoked him and offered a seat, one arranges the positions. On the seat, one arranges Vighneśvara; to its upper right, an axe; and below that, a spear.
I fashion an elephant goad from my upper left hand; I fashion a lotus from the hand below it;

I fashion a noose from that hand; I fashion earrings for my ears; I fashion a garland hanging from my neck down to my navel; and I fashion bracelets on my wrists, as well as garments and other ornaments.

"One should visualize: 'I fashion beautiful limbs according to their respective parts; I fashion nourishment and power on the left; I fashion the rat as the vehicle on the right; and all around that, I fashion the gods, sages, and Siddhas who are devoted to him. (91)

Having invoked [the deity] together with his weapons, ornaments, own powers (*sva-śakti*), own vehicle (*sva-vāhana*), and own attendants (*sva-bhakta*), and having offered a seat, he arranges the positions on the seat: "I arrange Rudra on the seat; I arrange an axe in the right upper hand; I arrange a trident in the right lower hand; I arrange a garland hanging from the neck down to the navel."

"I fashion bracelets upon my hands; I fashion beautiful ornaments such as garments and the like for each limb; I fashion Gaurī, the Śakti, to my left; I fashion the bull, the vehicle, to my right; and I fashion the gods, sages, and Siddhas who are her devotees all around"—thus one should visualize.

Having invoked [the deity] together with his weapons, ornaments, own powers (*sva-śakti*), own vehicle (*sva-vāhana*), and own attendants (*sva-bhakta*), and having offered a seat, he prepares the positions; on the seat he prepares Viṣṇu, on the upper right hand he prepares the discus (*cakra*), on the lower right hand he prepares the mace *Kaumodakī*, and on the upper left hand...
I fashion a lotus from his lower hand, I fashion a conch from his upper hand,
and I fashion garments and ornaments according to their respective limbs; I fashion Śakti and Lakṣmī on his left, and I fashion Garuḍa on his right.
One should visualize: "I shall arrange the gods, sages, and perfected beings who are devoted to him all around. || 93 ||

Having invoked her—equipped with weapons, ornaments, her own power (*śakti*), her own vehicle, and her own attendants—and having offered a seat, he arranges the positions: "Upon the seat, I arrange the *Śakti*;
upon the upper right hand, I arrange a sword; upon the hand below that, I arrange a trident."
I visualize a lotus in my left upper hand; I visualize an unfading garland of lotuses hanging from my neck down to my navel; I visualize earrings for my ears;
I visualize garments and other ornaments upon the respective limbs; and I visualize the Śakti Caṇḍikā to my left.
"I visualize the lion as the vehicle from the right;
I visualize the gods, sages, and perfected beings who are devoted to him all around"—thus one should visualize.

Having invoked Him along with His weapons, ornaments, own powers (*sva-śakti*), own vehicle, and own attendants, and having offered a seat, he prepares the locations on that seat: "I prepare the Sun; from the right hand I prepare the Discus (*cakra*);
from the left hand I prepare the Conch (*śaṅkha*); in the two ears I prepare the two earrings."
I fashion garments and ornaments for you according to their respective places; on the left, I fashion Saṃjñā as your Śakti;
on the right, I fashion the golden chariot with seven horses as your vehicle—[the chariot] moving through the dark space, establishing both the immortal and the mortal, [fashioned] with gold.
"May the divine Savitṛ travel on his chariot, beholding all beings"—from this [mantra] regarding seeing, one should visualize: "I surround those devotees of his with gods, ṛṣis, and siddhas. || 95 ||

Having invoked her—equipped with weapons, ornaments, power, vehicles, and her own devotees—and having offered a seat, one arranges the positions: "I arrange Kālī upon the seat; I arrange a sword in the right upper hand; I arrange [a skull-cup] in the hand below that."

I visualize him with a crest reaching to his neck, having the form of a human with a shaven head; from his upper left hand I visualize the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), from his lower left hand I visualize the gesture of boon-granting (*vara*), and from his right [hand] I visualize him mounted upon a lion.
One should visualize: "I shall provide for the gods, sages, and perfected beings who are devoted to him on all sides. || 96 ||
In this manner, one should infer and apply [this principle] elsewhere as well. || 97 ||

The preparation of the image, the preparation of the ritual requisites, the placement of those [requisites] for their purpose, the visualization of oneself as pure and pleasing, the invocation of the deity, the conceptualization of providing a seat for her,
the bringing of the image to another vessel, the pouring of waters into it, the installation of the image upon the lion-throne, and the offering of garments.
Adorning with ornaments, anointing with perfumes, scattering unbroken grains, strewing flowers, showing a mirror,

having [the deity] smell fragrant oil, burning incense, lighting lamps, offering food, offering drinks, causing [him] to hear stories, causing [him] to hear prayers, or pouring water from another vessel for the purpose of washing the face.

Aside from washing the hands, washing the feet, pouring out water to the north of what has been offered, sweeping the ground, offering betel-leaf in front, showing a mirror, having [the deity] smell fragrant oil, fanning with a beautiful fan, and cooling measures,
there may be the offering of camphor-lamp light in front, circumambulation, prostration, prayer, or hymn of praise.

At the end, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and the oblation (*havir*). Then follows the worship of the fires or the fire itself, after which one should worship the weapons, ornaments, the spear (*śakti*), the vehicle, and its attendants with perfumes, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and flowers.
Thus indeed is the worship of the mandala; the sequence for the worship of the mandala is as follows: prostration to the deities and dismissal (*visarjana*) to the north.
The removal of the floral offerings and the dismissal of the sacred waters. || 98 ||
The preparation of the Pratīka [mantras]. || 99 ||
If the limbs of that [deity] are manifest, one should worship the feet and so forth with ritual offerings (upacāras) according to their respective places.
(100) One should also cultivate the meditative realizations (bhāvanās) of all these ritual offerings. (1)
And with these three names, ending in the accusative or nominative case, one should satisfy them along with Gāyatrī. || 2 ||
In the libation, the contemplation is that "this [goddess] is pleased. || 3 ||
If she possesses two garments, he should wrap one garment around her navel, fasten it at the sides, and then secure a portion of it as a back-knot;
likewise, he should do so from the front over the shoulder.
If one wishes to have him clothe himself in a loincloth (*kaupīna*), one should tie the knot of the waist-string (*kaṭisūtra*) on the right side of the hips;
for that purpose, having brought the cloth from behind, one should arrange the fold (*kacchā*) in front and above with one part, and then arrange the fold behind.
If one wishes to have him clothe himself in an ornamented garment outside the navel, he should do so himself.
If one wishes to hold it, one should indeed hand it over. || 5 ||
Having brought that [substance] onto the throne-seat, if one so desires, one should apply a drop of fragrant paste along with its ingredients to the forehead using the ring finger;
or else, one may apply it with drops to the hollow of the throat, the heart, the base of the arms, and the head.
Thus, one should perform self-pride (*svamāna*) either in this manner or in whatever way is desired. || 7 ||
The offerings consumed by them should be placed at a distance to one's own left. || 8 ||
Some say that for those who have eaten it, there is a ritual with water containing sesame seeds, but for those who have not eaten it, it need not be performed.

Just as there is impurity below one's own navel and purity above it, so it is with the Lord; He has *saccidānanda* (existence-consciousness-bliss) for His head and *saccidānanda* for His feet. Therefore, others maintain that there is no prohibition against offering the water used for washing His feet and other such items upon the head, even in cases involving impure substances. || 10 ||
Some say that one should place unbroken grains on the forehead and on the head. (11)
Flowers on the head. || 12 ||
A mirror in front [of him]. || 13 ||
Having taken fragrant oil with a flower, one should cause it to be smelled; some say that one should place it in front of him. 14.
The incense offering is placed in a vessel to the left of the deity. || 15 ||
The illumination [is performed] with unbroken rice grains (akṣata) for the deity. || 16 ||
The food to be eaten and the drink, having been sprinkled with water, should be placed in a vessel—either within a square mandala or simply before [the deity] to the right;
likewise, the drink for the left-hand [deities] should be placed in a vessel before [the deity] to the left.
One should not offer [it] only before the deity. || 19 ||
Some say that one should purify wine with [mantras] dedicated to Soma, Varuṇa, Agni, and Rudra, and that once sprinkled with these, it becomes pure. || 20 ||
Some say that because it is purified by the sprinkling of the ritual materials, it becomes pure through that very act; therefore, no further purification of it is required.
The liquor is on the left side of the deity. || 22 ||
One should praise the deity with hymns or entertainments; one may cause the deity to laugh, sing the glory of the deity, or perform a dance for the delight of the deity. || 23 ||
Then, for the purpose of drinking, water is placed in the middle and to the right of the deity.
Then, having placed the vessel before the deity, he should pour water into it for the washing of the hands, the washing of the face, and the washing of the feet. || 25 ||
Betel-leaf is in front. || 26 ||

Having uttered the mantra, one should offer it during the ritual application and worship in this manner: "I apply [this] for the sake of such-and-such a purpose, for such-and-such a deity, at such-and-such a place, for such-and-such a practice. || 27 ||
Likewise, during the offering of gifts and worship, one should say "dada" and give. || 28 ||
One should perform the ritual arrangement with the thought, "I arrange [this] for the worship of the Arhat. || 29 ||
One should offer all ritual services, honored with perfumes and flowers, except for the perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and flowers. || 30 ||
Some say that one should give [the offerings] as worshipped with flowers alone.
If none of these are available, one should offer water or fragrant oil for the purpose of scenting the deities' garments or ornaments placed before them. || 32 ||
One should show him a mirror. || 33 ||

Then, having gone behind the fire-pit, wherever one intends to offer oblations, one should prepare a square area measuring at least one arrow's length on all sides; it should be smeared with the dung of a yellow cow, sprinkled with her urine, swept with a broom of *kuśa* grass, wiped clean, and sprinkled with water using a vessel made of gold or silver.
With a ritual vessel (dharmapātra) made of copper, iron, or sacrificial wood,
having its tip and middle carved into the shape of a bilva leaf with a six-finger-long handle,
and adorned with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and fragrant oil, he should draw six lines. || 34 ||
(51) "O Dharmapāla, by my own fist I grasp the hilt for the sake of strength and freedom from obstacles"— with these words, one should grasp Dharmapāla. || 35 ||
These are indeed many fires: the Sāra, Gāṇapa, Śākta, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Kāpāla, Brāhma, Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇa, Āhavanīya, Sabhya, Āvasathya, Māṇḍala, Pārthiva, Audaka, Vāyavya, Vediyuta, Sumaṅgala,
Valavardhana, Aindra, Saumya, and Vaiśvadeva.
Therefore, one who desires that fire which devours raw flesh should not utter its name.

"O such-and-such fire, I draw for you the first line extending toward the north; likewise, one extending toward the east; its second [line] likewise; its third [line] extending toward the east; and between those two lines extending toward the east, three more lines extending toward the east in that same manner—one should thus draw six lines with the tip of the *dharmapāla* on this sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or in the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*). || 37 ||
Then, having sprinkled [the site] for such-and-such fire— whether it be the *samāṇḍala* fire or the *vaiśvadeva* fire—
one should invoke it with the words, "I invoke; may you be seated here," and covering the fire with both hands,
one should establish it upon the lines, in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), or on the leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
If one should desire, "May I be a performer of sacrifices," he should establish a fire produced from friction;

if he should desire, "May I be radiant and handsome," he should establish a fire produced from a sun-crystal; if he should desire, "May I be more powerful than all those who are prosperous," he should establish a fire produced from stone. || 39 ||
In the light of the lamp, there are these three colors: white, copper-colored, and black. That which is white is the bright;
that which is copper-colored is the ruddy; and that which is black is the darkness. Therefore, that face of the sun which rises in the morning is the ruddy;
that which shines at midday is the white; and that which sets in the evening is the darkness. Thus, it is the sun alone—

He establishes [the fire] because the sun takes half of the oblation from Agni; therefore, if one should desire, "May I be peaceful, possessed of ritual power, and successful in all things," he should bring fire from a white [horse] and establish it. Because the sun is in the middle of the white [horse], and because he establishes [the fire] in the middle of the sun.

In the same way, this [sacrificer] becomes what he strives for: if he should desire, "May I be radiant," then having taken fire from the red [cow], he should establish it; if he should desire, "May I be covered with hair," then having taken fire from the black [cow], he should establish it. || 40 ||
This sword is indeed of the nature of fire; therefore, one who does not possess a sword should not perform any rite pertaining to Agni. || 41 ||

Having kindled the fire and taken two or three pieces of fuel, he should offer oblations of clarified butter into this consecrated fire for Jātavedas; [he should worship] the aforementioned deity once or twice,
and with the remainder, [he should offer] the weapons individually or [the] ornaments— three, four, five, six, or as many as there are of that [deity's] attendants.

Having offered oblations to Sviṣṭakṛt and to the Maṇḍala, and having placed two fuel-sticks with the words "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," and having swept around [the fire] with water, he should strew Kuśa grass three times— eastward, southward, westward, and northward— and perform the sprinkling with water three times.
One should heat the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in the fire.
Among milk, curd, and ghee, one or another is the oblation for [the sacrifice] beginning with the cow and the goat.
In the daily worship, we desire that ghee be the sacrificial oblation. || 45 ||
Some say it should be according to the prescribed rule. 46.
Two blades of kuśa grass, with uncut tips, without internal nodes, and measuring one span (prādeśa) in length, are the two purifiers (pavitra).
"Some say [it should be offered] into the fire of the chinā plant. || 48 ||
(52) The purification of liquid offerings by means of two blades of *kuśa* grass is *utpavana*. || 49 ||
Or, by means of a golden probe, the sacrificial oblation is made clearly pure by Dharmapāla. || 50 ||
This is the purification for all sacrificial offerings. || 51 ||
Wherever this [mantra] has been recited, one should offer oblations into the fire of the Āgneya rite for Jātavedas, that is, the fire within the maṇḍala.
Having offered [the oblation] into that fire, he should silently add pieces of fuel for its increase. || 53 ||

These many winds are indeed these: the solar, the Gāṇapa, the Śaiva, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śākta, the Kāpāla, the Brāhma, the Aindra, the Saumya, the Āgneya, the Meghya, the Vaidyuta, the Varṣya, the Vaiśvadeva, the Māṇḍala, the prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna; therefore, these and whatever others there may be.

"O Vāyu, you are the friends of Agni; therefore, whenever there is fire, one should always fan that Vāyu with a fan, saying, 'For the sake of the kindling of such-and-such fire, I fan such-and-such Vāyu with a fan,' and thus he shall kindle it. || 54 ||

The Viśvedevas are its deities; therefore, this [day] belongs to the Viśvedevas. It is the circle of the gods, the circle of the ṛṣis, the circle of human beings, and the circle of the Siddhas. This [day] belongs to the circle (maṇḍala); therefore, it is called Māṇḍala. Consequently, the Vaiśvadeva and the Māṇḍala [days] should be observed together. || 55 ||
Or, wherever the fire might be dimmed, one should rekindle it with this [mantra]. || 56 ||
"Only once, not repeatedly"—thus [is the teaching of] Digbhairava. || 57 ||
Therefore, he offers to Agni. || 58 ||
These indeed are many earths: that of Sūrya, Gaṇapati, Śakti, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Bhairava, Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Yama, Agni, Vāyu, Pṛthivī, Vaiśvadeva, Maṇḍalī, Jīvī, and Ūkharī.
All these indeed serve as supports; therefore, [it is] Vāyu.

Thinking, "May that [earth] be possessed of its deity; I shall sweep the earth named so-and-so, which has become the support for the fire and which occupies this sacrificial mound," he should sweep the sacrificial mound three times or once.
One should strew the sacrificial ground with kuśa grass.

These waters indeed are the depths: those belonging to Sūrya, Śiva, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śakti, Gaṇeśa, the clouds, Agni, Vāyu, the Earth, Jālinī, the Viśvedevas, the Maṇḍalī, those with sand as their upper layer, those with stones as their upper layer,
those filled with swarms of harmful aquatic creatures, those filled with swarms of harmless aquatic creatures, those remaining in their natural state, and those that are pure.

All [the earths] are indeed above the mud and are peaceful; the sprinkling is performed with peaceful waters. Therefore, whatever fire it may be, one should pour out those waters together with their respective deities and sprinkle [it], saying: "With these waters, I sprinkle such-and-such a fire, or such-and-such an earth. || 61 ||
He should offer either four portions taken with the *sruc* ladle, or, having filled that *sruc* as large as it may be with as many *sruva* spoons as are required, he should sacrifice.

Therefore, having cleared away as much ground as would suffice for a large man lying down to the east, one should bring fire onto a consecrated altar strewn with grass. This fire may be half the size of that [main] pit, or according to the available space;
since it has been brought from the east, it shall have two names: "the Fire of the Deity" (*devatāgni*) and "the Fire of Time" (*kālāgni*).
For whichever deity he brings the oblation, having established the fire for that deity, having added fuel, and having swept around it, he should sprinkle water around it. 63.
One should offer oblation to the deity of one's chosen *gāyatrī* into that fire, using either the root mantra with a *sruva* ladle or a *sruc* spoon. || 64 ||
One oblation for the deity, two or three for the weapons of the deity, four for the ornaments of the deity, and [one] for the power of the deity. (p. 53)
For the invocation of the deity, he offers oblations with the *sruva* or *sruc* ladle—either six for the devotees of the deity or six for the deity herself; five for the ornaments of the deity;
four for the weapons of the deity; three for the *śakti*;
one for the invocation of the deity; and one for the devotees of the deity, according to those respective numbers.

Having filled it with the *sruva* ladles, one should offer a single oblation from the *sruc* vessel; one should take the sacrificial portion (*havis*) for all [deities], taking it while saying, "I take the sacrificial portion for [Name], I take it by truth. Having offered it into the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) while standing before the deity, one should then take half of that from the Fire of Time.
When Kālāgni seizes half [of it], this fire, being led away, should indeed be established upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) as previously described.

It has two names: Digagni and Paricchinnābhāsa Agni. One offers oblations into this fire for the sake of ornaments, weapons, power, and vehicles; while proceeding, one offers to these deities at this southern fire (dākṣiṇa-agni).

The exponents of Brahman say that because this fire of the direction stands to the south of the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), having circumambulated the Fire of Time and facing east, he offers oblations to his ornaments; again, facing west, he offers oblations to his weapons; and again, facing north, he offers oblations to his spear (śakti).

Furthermore, facing south, he offers oblations for the purpose of setting out; when he thus offers repeatedly, having circumambulated this divine mandala around this fire, that becomes offered even as he is traveling. || 66 ||
Since the fire of time (Kālāgni) is led forth from this, it has two names:
Ākāśāgni and Māṇḍalāgni; one offers oblations into this while seated for the sake of devotees. || 67 ||
Or they do not carry forward the fire; they offer oblations into a single fire alone—thus say those who discourse on Brahman.
Some, having taken the remnants of the offering to the deities, offer them into this fire of space. 69.

Having entered the chamber for the disposal of the oblation, he takes the vessels of the remnants of the deities in due order; having drunk the water for the feet, the water for the hands, the water for sipping, and the water for bathing,
he anoints his brow-center, the hollow of the throat, the heart, the roots of the arms, and the head with the fragrant substance, provided it is of the female variety.
"I take this purifying nectar, the medicine for existence, which severs the bonds of the individual soul and is the cause proclaimed by Bhairava"—with these words, one should consume the wine. (70)
Having recited, "I anoint myself with sovereign splendor," one should smear the aforementioned locations with fragrant substance.
The marking has been explained. || 72 ||
"Some say that one should take up all the remnants with the formula: 'The remnant of such-and-such deity; for the sake of the lord of such-and-such [lineage], for luster, I apply it to myself. (73)

After accepting it with the words, "By this being taken up by Īśvara, may I become capable, free from disease, stainless, and one who rejoices in immortality," there follows the recitation of the mantra. || 74 ||

"I offer nectar into nectar, svāhā!"—this is the mantra of acceptance (*svīkāra*). Some say that after the acceptance, one should recite "May I become immortal through the nectar offered everywhere," and this [mantra] applies everywhere.
One who has been initiated should eat the remnants of all the deities, but he should not offer back to that same deity what has already been eaten by her.

One should consume seats, garments, water, food, perfumes, mirrors, edibles, drinks, objects for enjoyment, things to be worn, ointments, and auspicious items that have been used by a deity; having sprinkled them with water, one may use them again, provided they were not touched by the feet. || 77 ||
Some say that at the conclusion of the ritual action, there is the disposal of the oblation.
(54) For all mantras, the alternative practice is either silence or meditation upon their meaning. || 79 ||
For all substances, the secondary substitute (anukalpa) is water or the visualization of the object.
The secondary alternative for everyone who has permanently desisted [from formal practice] is the recitation of the mantra of one's own chosen Lord. || 81 ||
For all mantras, the secondary alternative is the Gāyatrī, or else their respective root-mantra (mūlamantra).
The secondary alternative for the investigation of the doctrine is one's own investigation of the four categories as intended by one's own scripture. || 83 ||
The secondary rule for saluting the guru is humility toward him for his sake.

If a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has been given to a deity, one should not take it for oneself; rather, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to that deity, for in this way one’s own ownership of it ceases. This applies everywhere through such a transfer of ownership. Or, just as there is the offering of unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) to the spirits (*bhūta*) and the casting of flowers into water for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), so it is in other cases as well. || 85 ||
Having accepted the grace of the deity, having washed his face,
and having sipped water twice, he takes half of the fire from the eastern fire and casts it into the fire of time; then, having offered oblations in two external pits,
he takes half of the fire from the bodily fire and casts it into two external pits of the sacrificial fire.

One becomes worldly when one offers oblations to these deities into this fire: having offered to earth, water, fire, wind, the quarters, time, space, Agni-Soma, the meters, and the sages, and having offered into the external space-fire of this [internal] space-fire, one becomes worldly, just as those two [became].
Some say that one should take the remaining portion and offer it as the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation into this fire.
Some say that one should not offer the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to one's own deity during daily worship, nor during special worship. 88.

As a secondary alternative for the expiation of all offenses, one should perform the recitation (japa) of the Gāyatrī mantra ten times, or that of the specific root-mantra (mūlamantra) pertaining to each offense.
"Surānanda maintains that for those who have been initiated and are guilty of great offenses, this very same expiation applies even when the offenses are repeated. (90)
Or, just as for one who has been touched by mud, the purification in a lake is the expiation; therefore, by means of that washing it becomes clear,
and even when there is a recurrence of contact with mud, this expiation indeed makes it clear again.
"Even in the case of its repetition," says Surānanda. (91)
"Upon the recurrence of evil, there is the recurrence of atonement"—thus says Unmādānanda. || 92 ||
Muktānanda says: "If a sin is committed once, the expiation is one-fold; if twice, it is two-fold; if thrice, three-fold; and if four times, it is indeed four-fold."
If it falls once, it has one quality; if twice, two qualities; if three times, it becomes fallen and there is no atonement for that—thus says Jñānānanda. 94.
Amṛtānanda states that there is no expiation for an act committed once, whether it was done through ignorance or even with knowledge.
The fire-ritual (agnikārya) is performed or not performed [accordingly]. (96)

Having circumambulated the deity clockwise, one should offer a handful of flowers upon the head of the deity; or, having circumambulated as much as desired, one may perform either the circumambulation or the prostration from the north.
"At the two feet" refers to the abode of Īśāna. || 98 ||
One should bow to the right-hand [deity] from the right and to the left-hand [deity] from the left. || 99 ||
The connection to meditation and the plea for forgiveness, saying "forgive my transgressions," constitute the act of atonement. || 100 || 1200 ||

"Whatever I sacrifice, whatever I do for my desired goal, whatever I give, and whatever severe penance I perform—that I offer unto You. Having said this, one should pour water into the right hand of the Lord, or onto the ground to His right. || 1 ||
The declaration, "I am a slave. || 2 ||

"Oṃ, [Name], [Name], appear, appear for me, svāhā!"—with this prayer for manifestation, one should worship [the deity] with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and flowers, or with any one of these. || 3 ||

Having worshipped in that very same manner according to the prescribed sequence, one should offer three handfuls of flowers upon the heads of the deities of the maṇḍala, or a number equal to the years of their age. || 4 ||

I perform the ritual dismissal for the goddess Amukā— who is adorned with ornaments, equipped with weapons, endowed with power, together with her own vehicle, accompanied by her own devotees, and established in her own world—
for the sake of her returning again and for her appearing once more; or one may dismiss her using forms ending in the accusative case.
And one should apply the word denoting the action corresponding to that.
Then one should mutter the mantra of the deity.
Rinsing the mouth, silence, and the posture should be maintained everywhere according to the prescribed rules.
The garland is threefold. || 8 ||
It consists of the fingers and joints, it consists of the sense organs, and it consists of the objects of perception.

The ring finger, the little finger, the middle finger, and the index finger—these four have three joints each, and all their joints are to be stepped upon. The two joints that are between the middle and ring fingers constitute the Meru; from the middle of this [Meru], the thumb has two joints, and it is to be stepped upon.
Therefore, one should step upon them in this manner: first from the base of the thumb; second from the base of the little finger; third from the middle of that [little finger]; fourth from its tip;
fifth from the joint at the tip of the ring finger; sixth from the joint at the tip of the middle finger; and seventh [from the joint at the tip of the index finger].

The eighth joint from the tip of the index finger, the ninth from its middle, the tenth from its base, and likewise from the base of the middle finger—one who counts this group of ten on the left hand reaches the number one hundred. He who makes this rosary leads himself to the state of the Avadhūta. || 10 ||

He who makes a rosary composed of any one of these—rudrākṣa, bhad-rākṣa, coral, pearl, gold, or silver beads—and adorns it with a *sumeru* bead, conquers the heavenly world accessible to householders. || 11 ||
Making the unformulated [text] consist of the meanings of words, he brings order through the enumerated [substances] such as sugar and so forth;
he dwells in the heavenly world, which is accessible by forest-dwellers. || 12 ||
In the daily rite, the recitation (japa) is desired to be tenfold, hundredfold, or thousandfold; it is not intended to exceed the number of one thousand.

Or one should recite [the mantra] a number of times equal to the years of one's age, or twice or thrice that number; or one should recite while intending, "I shall recite for two ghaṭīs or three ghaṭīs," but one should not recite with a mind fixed on the physical form of Mount Meru.
One should perform the recitation using any one of these. || 15 ||
Now we shall explain the procedure for the recitation within the mandala. || 16 ||

If one recites the mantra of one's chosen deity one hundred times, one should then recite "Obeisance to the weapons of [Name]" (amukāyudhebhyaḥ namaḥ) for the circle of weapons ten times each; or, having recited [the main mantra] one hundred times, one should recite "Obeisance to the ornaments of [Name]" (amukābharaṇebhyaḥ namaḥ) for the circle of ornaments ten times each. In the same manner, one should recite "Obeisance to the vehicle of [Name]" (amukavāhanāya amukāya namaḥ) for the vehicle.

One should recite ten [times] for each respective name, or one should recite ten everywhere as follows: "Obeisance to such-and-such Śakti" (*amuka-śaktaye namaḥ*), or "Obeisance to such-and-such [deity], to the devotees, to the Siddhas, to the Sages, to the Devas" (*amukāya bhaktebhyaḥ siddhebhyaḥ ṛṣibhyo devebhyo namaḥ*), or "to such-and-such and the others" (*amukādibhyaḥ*). In this manner, the procedure for the recitation of the entire maṇḍala is the same. || 17 ||
If one recites that mantra ten times even once, it is as if the entire mandala were recited; this method of reciting the entire mandala is indeed swift. || 18 ||
Today, there is either one maṇḍala or even a single maṇḍala; likewise, this is the procedure for recitation using separate maṇḍalas.
"The worship of the mandala is not joined with the recitation [of mantras] within the mandala at any time," says Unmattabhairava. (20)

One should praise the southern [deity] with the thousand divine names according to the Smṛti tradition, and the northern [deity] according to the Tantra; in the absence of those, one may use either the Śruti or Smṛti for the southern, and either the Śruti or Tantra for the northern. In the first daily worship, one should use whichever method was employed, and continue with that same method perpetually.
Or he worships with incense, flowers, unhusked grain, or any other such offering. || 22 ||
Having worshipped the deity one, two, three, or twice that number of times according to the count of years,
one should worship the mandala. Having worshipped the mandalas either collectively or individually according to the ritual injunctions,
one should again scatter flowers over them for [the deity] such-and-such, who is equipped with weapons and ornaments.

"I appoint you for dismissal—whether equipped with weapons, with vehicles, with powers, and with your own devotees; for the establishment of your own world, or for abiding according to your own will, or for returning again, or for being seen again"—thus one should dismiss her, employing the words in the accusative case, or saying: "I appoint you for dismissal so that you may roam as you wish."
The floral remains (nirmālya) led to one's left become all worldly prosperity;
having dug a pit in some clean place, one should cast all of that—measuring two armspans in length and one man’s height in width—into it. || 24 ||
Therefore, one should dig as long as water is not reached from the ground; this is the rule for the Bhairavas of the directions. || 25 ||
The sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) is that which he pours out to the north; therefore, when he sprinkles himself and when he pours it out, he thereby dismisses the *tīrtha*.
When he sprinkles himself, he makes himself bathed in the Ganges; this is the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). || 26 ||

Because it is led away from the left of the practitioner, because of its abundance, because of contact with impurity, and because of its transformation into another form, the *nirmālya* becomes unworthy of worship; it also becomes worldly in nature. Whoever should worship that which has become unworthy of worship becomes a sinner.
