Therefore, having placed it upon his head, he should lead it away to the left. || 27 ||

57) Some say that because it is poured out to the left, it becomes discarded as *nirmālya*; others [say so] because of its abundance; others because of contact with something pure; others because of its transformation into another form; and others because of the act of worship—some hold that it becomes *nirmālya* by any one of these factors.
Those living beings who, in whatever manner, become utilized in this [sacrifice], they desire heaven; yet they are indeed characterized by passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa). || 29 ||
Only a human being, acting in this way, is capable of accumulating unseen karma (adṛṣṭa); no one else is capable—thus says Kālabhairava. (30)

Or rather, those courtesans who are employed here win the heavenly world; for just as the officiating priests cause the sacrificer to sacrifice, they themselves do not win the heavenly world. This [heaven] is indeed high, and these heavy sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are the means to it; if the sacrificer abandons them among the officiating priests, he becomes light.
Those officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) by whom sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) have been received conquer the high heavenly world;
therefore they are called "heavy" (*guru*). Therefore, those who are "heavy" do not go to the high heavenly world; such indeed are those [fees].
If one does not perform the fire-rite, then after dismissing the deity, one should perform the disposal of the oblation. || 32 ||

Or one should offer what has been prepared into the fire of space itself, for there is no separate preparation; thus says Ākāśabhairava. (33) Whatever services might be undesirable to oneself, one should not offer those to her; thus says Unmattabhairava. (34)
Some say that, except for the fire-ritual and all mantras, one should give everything else to her. || 35 ||
The application, the employment, and the worship constitute the threefold [classification]. || 36 ||
Among these, one has already been explained. || 37 ||
That which employs a single application is the second. || 38 ||
That which was turned back then is the third. || 39 ||

This deity is to be served by means of the four Vedas; therefore, one should invite her with a *ṛc*, offer oblations with a *yajus*, praise her with a *sāman*, and dismiss her with an *atharvāṅgirasa*. Indeed, this *praṇava* belongs to all four Vedas; therefore, one should seek everything from it, or rather, the *Bṛhat* [Sāman]. Of that, "bhūḥ" is the *ṛc*-portion, and "bhuvaḥ" is the [yajus-portion].
"From the Yajus it is *svāhā*, from the Sāman it is *svar*, and all these are the *vyāhṛtis* of the Atharvāṅgirasas; some say *mahas* [is the fifth];
therefore one should perform that first [rite]. Some say that this rite, which is not performed anywhere else, is a light procedure for those who desire supreme bliss. (40)
And when the remaining [portion] has been explained. || 41 ||
Pārānanda never, at any time, performs a worship that is devoid of both invocation (āvāhana) and dismissal (visarjana).
That which one performs as the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha-arcana) without invocation and dismissal does not constitute the worship of the deity; it does not become that which delights the deity.
In every case, whatever is incomplete, one should mentally bring that to completion. || 44 ||
"Unmattabhairava says that one should not perform the worship of the maṇḍala during the worship of giving or the worship of honoring. (45)
A seat, a mirror, a fan, anything else made of metal or clay intended for shade,
a drinking vessel, and a food vessel— even if already used— he may employ them again and again for the deity after sprinkling them with water, provided they cannot be obtained otherwise. || 46 ||

58) There is a relationship of total identity between the deity and the devotee; therefore, having become the father, the devotee serves the deity as "this is my son. Or, just as one does not provide excessive food to a virtuous son, so too [does the deity].
One protects oneself from all sufferings; for that purpose, one exerts oneself and does not serve [the body] in such a way.
Therefore, service should be like that between a father and a son; it is for this reason that some serve in this manner. || 47 ||

Just as a son, being devoted, serves his father thinking, "He is a deity," or just as he does not transgress his father's command even when it is difficult to fulfill, so too does he serve; that is the service of a son to a father, and therefore they perform this service.

Being devoted, one serves the deity as a son serves his mother, thinking, "She is my mother"; or, just as a son who has committed an offense does not fear his mother, so too one who has committed an offense does not fear the deity;
or, being devoted, one serves as a disciple, thinking of the deity as a teacher, just as one serves a teacher.

Even when struck, he desires the welfare of the teacher through the actions of his mind, speech, and body; he eats what remains after the teacher has eaten, and whatever he acquires, he offers that to the teacher. Or, he serves him in this way as a devoted subject, serving him with the thought, "This king is a deity," or just as a king might show compassion toward me.
One might act with the thought, "I shall practice in such a way," or out of fear, thinking, "He might make me powerful, or else he might command me otherwise.

Out of this fear, one strives for his favor; thus one serves, having become a devotee and a worshiper, thinking, "I am worshipping the deity. Or, it is like [the fear] that "this tiger's blood is tasteless."
These sacrificial fuels (*samidh*) are indeed this prepared flour without condiment; because it has been prescribed, it should be given, thinking "it is prescribed.

Having given it, he touches that remnant with devotion, thinking "it is prescribed," and thus becomes pleased. By means of what is prescribed, she (the deity) is to be satisfied; for just as these sages (*kavayaḥ*) are worthy of worship, when they have been honored, he [is satisfied] by them.
He becomes gracious, just as these passionate women who are devoted to him become gracious when they are cherished by those who cherish them; or just as these wicked thieves,
tigers, beasts, and other humans— who are to be slain— are rendered gracious by those very ones who have been slain.

He becomes pleased, thinking, "It has been performed. Thus sacrifices proceed, thinking, "It has been prescribed"; gifts proceed, thinking, "It has been prescribed"; punishments proceed, thinking, "It has been prescribed"; executions proceed, thinking, "It has been prescribed. Therefore, his satisfaction comes only through what is prescribed.
Thus, one who performs what is prescribed serves him; or rather, becoming a devoted friend, he serves the deity.

He serves [the deity] thinking, "She is my friend. Or, just as those who provide intoxicants [think], "These are pleasant to eat" or "They have a good taste," yet they find neither [of these things] for themselves; nevertheless, having eaten it and knowing it to be pleasant, they offer it to her—so too does he serve.
In all relationships between the deity and the devotee, the deity is the one to be propitiated and this person is the propitiator.

The deity is the one to be worshipped and this devotee is the worshipper; he is the teacher and this one is the disciple; he is the giver of fruit and this one is the enjoyer of the fruit; he is the lover and this one is the beloved. Therefore, the relationships between the devotee and the deity are inexpressible.
Or rather, as each desires, so does he serve that [deity], and through that service with devotion, he pleases them.
Therefore, this yoga of devotion is weightier than all other yogas; the wise one who knows this is fit for immortality. 49.

Having offered oblations into the Vaitānika fires, or having offered the Vaivāhika fire, the householder—remaining celibate—shall place a fuel-stick on the fire and give [the gift] to the students (brahmacārins) and female disciples (antevāsinyaḥ) for the purpose of recollecting the Veda; or he may give it to those who follow the rules of studentship after they have performed their ceremonial bath (snāta). They, belonging to the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes, shall also recite that which has been taught by them.

If one recites [the Veda], it becomes accompanied by mindfulness; if one gives to them and does not accept a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), then by that gift of the Brahmin, one conquers the heavenly world or gratifies one's own chosen deity. || 50 ||
(59) Or how could they accept [the gift] without having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), since these two— the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya— are not recipients?
Therefore, the question as to why these two should not accept it without having given is resolved here.

Since a Brāhmaṇa may accept these—food, water, clothing, security, and a maiden—from both a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, while the other two (the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya) may accept [these] from a Brāhmaṇa as their sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), except for the maiden; some say that one may accept a maiden along with a sacrificial fee.
Therefore, they may accept them. 51.
Or if he should accept [gifts] from them, this mode of livelihood indeed leads both to heaven and to liberation. || 52 ||
It is known that when a Brāhmaṇa subsists on the sacrificial fees from teaching and officiating at sacrifices, he anoints himself solely with splendor. || 53 ||
Whatever a student (brahmacārī) or one following the student’s discipline (brahmacārikalpa) recites, by that recitation he conquers the heavenly world or gratifies his own deities. || 54 ||
It is known that when a religious student lives on what is obtained by begging as the remains of his teacher's meal, he anoints himself solely with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). || 55 ||
In that the student lives by means other than forest-gathering, and the kṣatriya lives by protection and battle, he anoints himself with splendor alone. || 56 ||

If a Vaiśya, having passed beyond the stage of a religious student (brahmacārī), lives by means of interest and profits from other stages of life, he also [should be treated] in this same manner. || 57 ||
Even a Śūdra who lives by service or crafts should likewise regard himself in this manner. (58)

The Brāhmaṇa is characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva) and splendor; the Kṣatriya by passion (rajas); the Vaiśya by both passion and darkness (rajas and tamas); and the Śūdra by darkness (tamas).

Some say that he who lives on withered leaves, flowers, fruits, or water— all wild and not domestic, or obtained whether wild or domestic— establishes himself in the assembly of Brahman; for he who lives on wild things, or even on water and air, anoints himself with pure, passionless, and radiant splendor.
A student who has completed his studies, one afflicted by lust, or one unable to maintain the vow, may perform the ceremonial bath.
A householder who has become dispassionate, yet remains devoted to his duties, should retire to the forest.
One who is forest-dwelling, weary of ritual action, and whose mind is solely intent on meditation should enter into renunciation.
Then the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya should bestow wealth, grain, clothing, medicine, and utensils upon the Brāhmaṇas. || 65 ||
A Brahmin who is such by virtue of knowledge, austerity, refinement, and birth is the worthy recipient for all gifts, with the exception of forest-dwelling and renunciation.
He who gives to the *apāna* leads himself downward; he who accepts from the *apāna* destroys himself. Therefore, one should not give to the *apāna*, nor should one accept from the *apāna*. || 67 ||

If, while reflecting and searching, one does not find [a suitable recipient], then one who is endowed with noble birth, refinement, learning, health, great luster, beauty, and austerity— being thus endowed with birth, refinement, learning, and health— should bestow it upon someone who likewise possesses that same [noble] birth.

One should give it to him who is endowed with refinement; one should give it to him who is likewise endowed with birth in the Brāhmaṇa caste. Therefore, one should bestow a gift for the sake of dharma upon a Brāhmaṇa. || 68 ||

60) Or rather, these are the gifts of Dharma and wealth: namely, the gift of water, the gift of medicine, the gift of food, the gift of ointment, the gift of clothing, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of a bed—these are the gifts.
All things should be accepted by all; everyone should give whatever brings happiness to living beings, giving each creature what they desire.

Of these gifts, one should give to each person exactly what they most intensely desire. By giving this, one enjoys the supreme state; therefore, there is no rule against giving to one who is not a Brahmin.
One should give [to him], because he does not become negligent. || 69 ||
One should not give a gift according to the prescribed rule to those who are not Brahmins, nor should one give more than the prescribed amount.
One should give food and water to anyone at all, until they are fully satisfied.
Then one should go to the teacher's residence and pay homage to the teacher; if the teacher is not there, one should bow toward that place where the teacher was previously seen.
If the teacher is affectionate toward his disciple, he may give him jeweled earrings, clothing, an umbrella, sandals made of wood, leather, or cloth, a staff, a golden garland,
a collyrium stick, a water vessel, a horse, or the skin of an antelope or a tiger.
He should give one of these, which has been long enjoyed by himself, to that disciple; the disciple, bearing it upon his head, should place it inside the house and worship it. || 73 ||
Whatever the guru gives is the very image of the guru; therefore, one should honor that gift and not personally enjoy it for oneself. || 74 ||
One should worship that very [deity] with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and flowers, as well as with prostration. || 75 ||
He is to be worshipped with offerings of horses and other things, just as one would worship the Buddha. || 76 ||
The northern direction is the symbol of the non-existence of all things; therefore, one should pay homage to it. || 77 ||

This northern direction is indeed the representative symbol (pratīka) of all the gods, sages, teachers, the individual souls (īśvarātman), the living souls (jīvātman), and the supreme soul (paramātman); therefore, one should worship it. In its absence, one should worship in that direction whichever deity one wishes to sacrifice to. || 78 ||
Or a Kṣatriya, such as Pārānanda, accompanied by a fourfold army, might set out for a hunt mounted on a horse and enter a forest— one frequented by ascetics, or where,
despite the asceticism of those practitioners, creatures and beasts have not abandoned their predatory nature; in that forest, those who...
If there are predatory creatures, one should deprive them of their lives with weapons, not with missiles (astras). || 79 ||

For those who harm human beings are themselves the harmful ones; they alone are the doers of evil, since man is superior to all other births. This person born as a human shall be the sovereign of all births, and he has been, and he remains, the sovereign of all beings, both those already born and those yet to be born.

He presides over these births; this human birth is [the essence of] manhood. "Man indeed is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be"—he presides even over this of the immortal god, and he is the lord of immortality itself.

From the statement, "That which grows by means of food," it is known that the person (*puruṣa*) alone is superior to all these [castes], because in former times the exponents of Brahman (*brahmavādinaḥ*) ordained this very human birth—
that is, they divided it— into the fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*), and this very Brahman remains encompassed within it. What [is it]?

How many times did they fashion that fourfold caste-system separately for each person? How many times did they arrange it? What is said to be his mouth, what his two arms, what his thighs, and what his feet? He is the highest...

"The Brāhmaṇa is the highest caste; lower than him is the Kṣatriya, lower than him the Vaiśya, and lower than him the Śūdra. The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya (Kṣatriya) was made from his arms; that which is the Vaiśya was his thighs; from his feet the Śūdra was born.
From this scriptural statement, it follows that the human being alone excels all others. 80.
Violence has been explained previously. || 81 ||

If a beast of prey runs to kill an innocent animal such as a deer that is fleeing, then until it has killed it, the [protector] should deprive that predator of its life; by this act, he conquers both worlds. Furthermore, in that he liberates living beings from death, he conquers this world; and in that he [protects them from] cruelty...
By that [act], he destroys [his merit] and conquers heaven. || 82 ||

Pārānanda should not eat the meat of even a beast that is edible, if it is cruel or killed during a hunt; if Pārānanda were to eat such meat, he would become cruel himself. Therefore, Pārānanda should not eat it. 83.

"One may eat the flesh of a predatory creature that has been killed during a hunt and offered to one of the lords; however, the village pig (*grāmyasūkara*) is inedible, whereas the wild [pig] is understood to be edible"—thus says Unmattabhairava. (84)

For this violence of the violent leads either to heaven or to liberation; or rather, one should offer those very victims as an oblation before Kālī according to the rite of offering oblations. By whatever living being one slays before Kālī, through that act one conquers the heavenly world, but not liberation. || 85 ||
Some say that when one strikes back at an offender, he is not purified by that act; rather, it is through the joy of the enemy that he is purified. 86.

Indeed, even he who is killed by a *kālyagra* goes to the heavenly world; for as many hairs as there are on his body, for that many years does one killed by a *kālyagra* remain established in heaven. O Pārānandarya, if another is killed by a *kālyagra* even without the prescribed rite, [the result lasts] for that many... cycles (*ayana*).
In the Agniṣṭoma as well, [one should perform] the seasons for that many [days]. || 87 ||
O Pārānanda, for as many finger-breadths as one strikes with a sword at the tip of Kālī’s head, for that many years one is established in the heavenly world. || 88 ||
For when he kills predatory creatures in the hunt, he frees himself from sins;
when he protects the forest-dwelling Brahmins and domestic animals with these [acts of protection], he conquers the three worlds.
When he protects himself, he conquers this world; when he protects the forest-dwelling Brahmins, he conquers the world beyond.
In that he protects domestic animals, he conquers the Bhuvarloka; therefore, one should desire to protect them. || 89 ||
Whatever living being is killed during the hunt becomes a human being. || 90 ||
Having bathed at midday and put on a garment, being consecrated with the marks, he should perform the Brahmayajña, except for those who are seated together and for Śūdras.

Wearing the sacrificial thread as an upavīta, nivīta, and prācīnāvīta respectively, one who possesses the sacrificial cord should offer libations to the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors using the devatīrtha, the ṛṣitīrtha, and the pitṛtīrtha.
The Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvāngirasa, the Brāhmaṇas, the Tadyāmas (?), the Kalpas (?), the Ārṣeyakalpas (?), the Nārāśaṃsīs, and the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.

When one studies the Ṛg verses together with their ancient commentaries, one thereby satiates the deities with offerings of milk; when one studies the Yajus formulas, with offerings of ghee; when one studies the Sāman chants, with offerings of honey; and when one studies the Atharva-Aṅgirasas, with offerings of Soma. In this very way, one satiates both the seers and the ancestors. Therefore, one should perform the Brahma-sacrifice in this manner.
This very thing is the sacrifice of recollection; this is the sacrifice of sound; this is the sacrifice of the seers;

this is the sacrifice of muttering; this is the sacrifice of self-study. Among these sacrifices—the Agniṣṭoma and the rest—this shines as their head, even like a sovereign king over them, whether it be a Ṛg-verse, a Yajus-formula, or a Sāman-chant.
From this [study] sacrifices proceed, from this gifts proceed, and from this alone punishments proceed;
therefore, the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña) is the most venerable of all. || 93 ||

Then, having offered libations and returned home, whatever he gives to a Brāhmaṇa becomes his sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); or rather, that which he offers as libations to the Ṛṣis becomes his sacrificial fee.
Having prepared pure, fragrant food that is sweet when cooked, that which he offers as an oblation into the fire is the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*);
that which he offers into the fire or into a non-Brāhmaṇa is the *bali*, the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*);
and that which he offers as an oblation into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa, into the fire, into water, or upon the earth, intending it for the ancestors, is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*).

Whatever one gives to humans with the words, "O Fire, to humans, svāhā! or whatever food one sets down for them, that constitutes the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣya-yajña*). Then, having gone out from the house, [one should give] food and water to the *caṇḍālas*, the fallen (*patita*), the atheists (*nāstika*), the diseased, those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), and to dogs.

Having given on the ground, one should give in such a way that they obtain what is well-flavored, and it should not be strewn with dust; one should give in a place where heat, rain, wind, or cold will not distress the recipients. Having come to the house, one should wash one's feet, hands, and face with pure water.

Having fed those who have gathered—the sick, Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, along with their kinsmen, relatives, friends, and Shudras—and having satisfied those who are hungry, he himself should eat. || 95 ||
In the same way, one who belongs to the forest should be honored by those who belong to the forest. || 96 ||

A celibate student (brahmacārī) and a renunciant (saṃnyāsī), or a householder and a forest-dweller, or a graduate (snātaka) and one whose wife has died, may eat after having brought food from various castes (varṇins). || 97 ||
For the Snātaka, there are indeed three sacrifices: the one for Brahman, the one for the ancestors, and the one for men.
Having eaten [the meat], some who have been initiated into the Kālī-mantra worship Kālī. || 99 ||
In that very way, they recite a verse: || 100 ||
Īśa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others are fond of fasting;
yet Caṇḍikā becomes angry with her devotees because of their fasting.
Therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship Kālikāmbikā. || 1 ||
Likewise, they also cite this verse: || 2 ||

Having completed the ritual preparations ending with the meal, the youth who has performed the ceremonial bath (snātaka), or the initiated one, should worship Kālī; this is the eternal worship, a treasure-house of merit.
Thus they recite this verse: || 4 ||
The maiden should be worshipped by those from Daurga who are endowed with devotion to Lalitā;
the married woman should be worshipped, while others should worship the prostitute as the Kārikā. (5)
(p. 63) Some recite this verse differently: || 6 ||
Brahmins are to be worshipped by the devotees of the four Īśvaras;
those of the Śākta tradition [should worship] Suvāsinyas, and those of the Āyudheya tradition [should worship] the Khādira tree.
Flowers of those specific colors should be praised with ornaments;
bulls should be worshipped with vehicles, or else [those] belonging to that same species.
The Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) in the form of a maiden is worshipped by those possessed of devotion;
she may be a virgin, Kālikā, or even a courtesan. (7)
Having performed worship together with learned and beloved ones— whether those of their own mind or of other minds— they wander about, [reciting] the Purāṇas and the concluding sections of the epics.
Having performed the evening twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), having tended the sacred fires or the common fire, and having eaten, they should go to sleep without being over-satiated.
Then they practice what is to be practiced according to its extent. || 10 ||

Having removed the sacrificial thread, they may remain either unclothed or clothed as they please; for the sake of progeny, they sport with women on couches provided with cushions and coverlets, or they sleep with women while remaining unclothed.
This sequence of purificatory rites for the Pārānandas has been explained.

If these rites— the morning remembrance (*prātaḥsmaraṇa*), bathing (*snāna*), branding (*aṅkana*), the *vāmī*, the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), hymns of praise (*stuti*), the recitation of the armor-rite (*kavaca*), worship (*arcana*), muttering of mantras (*japa*), the recitation of the Thousand Names (*sahasranāma-pāṭha*), and salutation to the Guru—
are not performed by those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*), they result in sin for those initiates.
Death, or profound ignorance, constitutes a suspension of study (anadhyāya); there is no other suspension.
According to Caturmukha, the period from the initiation for a sacrificial session (satra) until its conclusion, or a severe illness, also constitutes such a suspension.
Unmattabhairava states that for these [students], any mental unease caused by disease, poverty, or any other such cause constitutes a suspension of study (anadhyāya).

Mahādeva says that the failure to perform these five—namely, the armor (*kavaca*) and the others—results in transgression; the investigation regarding the periods when study is prohibited (*anadhyāya*) for these is as previously stated. || 15 ||

Worship, the recitation of mantras, and salutation to the Guru—these are the daily rites; the deliberation regarding the days of suspension for these is as previously stated; such is the capacity. || 16 ||
For those initiated into the Pārānanda [tradition], Janārdana has declared that their daily rites grant prosperity if performed, and there is no transgression if they are not.
"According to the Parānandamata, for initiated men, the two daily rites—japa and salutation to the guru—result in the arising of meritorious fruit; so says Bhāskara. (18)

Ekadanta maintains that for those initiated into the Pārānanda tradition, there is a constant avoidance of practices such as the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the contemplation of the Lord as one's own object of worship, and the contemplation of oneself as supreme bliss. || 19 ||

Being himself healthy, pure, and with an undistracted mind, [he should perform the rite] in a clean place at his own preferred time, facing his own preferred direction, while free from any illness or other affliction. (p. 64)

One endowed with faith should accomplish the rite somehow or other—whether having eaten or not having eaten, whether standing on the ground, seated, in water, in a vehicle, in air, or in fire—from sunrise until the next sunrise; the wise one should perform it at least once. Thus says Unmattabhairava.
"In times of calamities"—this is the direction [given] by Bhairava. || 21 ||
Ākāśabhairava is [the deity] of the two subsequent [sections] beginning with "vā". || 22 ||
Thus, Kālabhairava [taught] the recitation of the armor (kavaca) and the thousand names (sahasranāma). || 23 ||

The capable one should worship them according to the Smārta rite, or the follower of Tantra according to the Tantric rite; the superior one [should worship] by either of these two, while all [others] should worship according to the Śrauta rite.

He who constantly worships with either the Smārta, Tāntric, Śrauta, or self-contrived rite beholds the Deity in no time at all; among the Śrauta, Tāntric, Smārta, and self-contrived rites, each subsequent one is inferior to the preceding.
In whatever manner the living being brings about its end, in that very same manner it attains peace. || 26 ||
The Pratīka is of two kinds: divine and non-divine. || 27 ||
Those who know the cries of all beings are perfected; those other than them are unperfected.
That which is consecrated by the Siddhas is divine; that which is consecrated by others is non-divine.
Some say that Pārānanda should also worship the deities upon the stones and wood.

Whether the icon be divine or non-divine, one should not perform worship devoid of invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarjana*). Even if one were to do so, it becomes deficient, and one falls from *pārānanda*.
Therefore, one should not perform worship devoid of invocation and dismissal; for such worship is [merely] *pārānanda*.
One should perform [it]. || 31 ||
Where many worshippers of supreme bliss are present in one place, they should perform the invocation and the dismissal separately for each. || 32 ||
"Where there are many worshippers, O Pārānanda, there that which is invoked by one is invoked by all, and that which is dismissed by one is dismissed by all; thus says Unmattabhairava. (33)
Some icons become objects of worship once those deities have been invoked, but become unworthy of veneration once they have been dismissed;
some icons, however, remain worthy of veneration and worship both before the invocation of the deities and after their dismissal—thus there are many such varieties of icons. || 34 ||
The informant is of two kinds. || 35 ||
The practitioner and the perfected one. || 36 ||
He desires various offerings of sweet food and other articles with the thought, "By these I shall serve the deity";
therefore, he eats the remains (ucchiṣṭa) consumed by the deity, and thus he becomes perfected (siddha). || 37 ||
With the mind, one desires to eat sweet food and the like for oneself; with speech, one speaks for the sake of the deity;
or one goes to a temple to see a social gathering or festival, and by chance beholds the deity; or one speaks for the sake of the deity with speech and with the body.

65) He offers prostrations; with his speech he says, "May I act with my body just as I speak," and with his mind he desires, "When shall I come to have devotion for the deity? [The deity responds: "May devotion for you be established in me."
The practitioner by whom the deity is entreated with speech attains perfection in no time at all. || 38 ||
When a single deity has been invoked upon a single Śāligrāma stone, until its formal dismissal (visarjana), no other deity may be invoked or worshipped [upon that same stone]. || 39 ||
One should worship constantly with any one of the arcane mantras. || 40 ||

We shall now describe the improper times for special worship. It is true that there is the daily dissolution (*dainaṃdina-pralaya*), the partial dissolution (*khaṇḍa-pralaya*), and the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). Among these, first occurs in the world of *Tapoloka*; second, in the world of *Īśvara*; and third, somewhere else. Truly, [the cycles] are Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali;
likewise the *saṃvatsara*, *idvatsara*, *ilāvatsara*, *parivatsara*, and *anuvatsara*.

From the beginning of the northern solstice to the end of the northern solstice; from the end of the northern solstice to the end of the southern solstice; from the beginning of spring to the end of summer; from the beginning of the rainy season to the end of autumn;

from the beginning of winter to the end of the cool season; from the end of Caitra to the beginning of Vaiśākha; from the beginning of Jyeṣṭha to the end of Āṣāḍha; from the beginning of Śrāvaṇa to the end of Bhādrapada; from the beginning of Āśvina to the end of Kārttika; and from the beginning of Mārgaśīrṣa [to its end].

The period beginning with Pauṣa and ending with Māgha, or beginning with Phālguna and ending with the end of the bright fortnight, or beginning with the dark fortnight— some maintain that in the dark fortnight, the sixth day is for Skanda, the fourth for Vighneśa, the ninth for Śakti, the tenth for Viṣṇu, the eleventh for Śiva, the twelfth for Sūrya, and the seventh for Brahmā.
On all festival days, on the tenth day of the month of Kārtika for Kālikā,

or by worshipping her on any one of these occasions, one becomes distinguished by all desired things: the destruction of disease, victory in battle, the acquisition of clothing, food, drink, gold, and wealth, the attainment of health, and [the gain] of beautiful women who are healthy and capable of crossing over [difficulties].
The perfection of love is for the sake of sexual union; this is the time for special worship of the northern [and southern] [directions].
It is the perfection of provisions, the attainment of the image of all deities, the attainment of the supreme sacred ford, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.

The attainment of a good field, the pacification of calamities, and the establishment of affectionate association through the specific worship of fellow students, equals, those on the same path, those of the same caste, those of the same lineage, those possessing the sacred rites and the Sūtras, those possessing the Vedas, those possessing the means of livelihood, and even the deities themselves, according to the prescribed rules; this is "grasping."

Between the moon and the sun, the lunar eclipse is superior to the solar eclipse. Regarding special worship, when a desire arises [to perform it], Sunday is for Āditya, Monday is for Śiva, Tuesday is for Śakti, Wednesday is for Viṣṇu, Thursday is for Brahmā, Friday is for Gaṇeśa, and Saturday is for Kapālin.

Saturday is the time for Mahākālī; the great night (mahārātra) for Upakauśikī; sunrise for Brahmā; midday with the sun accompanied by cows for Sūrya; afternoon for Śiva; evening for Vighneśa and Mahākālī;
and for Viṣṇu, the time after sunrise but before the great night. Some say this applies to all [deities]. This constitutes the perfection of the materials for special worship.
A single specific time for the worship of all [deities] has been explained as the occasion for the festival. || 41 ||
We shall now describe the special worship.

Some say that the daily rite of worship is indeed the general worship; whereas worship performed at a specific time is "special worship" (viśeṣārcana), because it is both performed and not performed [at other times], and therefore it is called special worship. || 43 ||
Some say that special worship is not distinct from daily worship.
Then, being pure and having performed the preliminary rites, facing north or facing whichever direction he desires, at one of the aforementioned times—

In a level and pure place for the special worship, the elder [initiate], having sipped water (ācamana) together with the initiates according to the sequence of initiation and knowing the ritual procedure, should apply the garland and ointment accordingly. || 45 ||
Some maintain that he would also be superior by virtue of his own caste and stage of life. 46.
Having invoked the deity and offered a seat, having prepared and presented the services beginning with water for the feet (pādya), and having served them with other charming offerings,

they should perform the ritual consumption of the sacrificial oblation (havis-pratipatti) and, having sipped water (ācānta), offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali). Then, having performed the service as previously described, he— or they— should worship and prostrate before the son [of the deity] together with his maṇḍala.
One should dismiss [the deities]. || 47 ||

Therefore, one who desires to worship with a more elaborate rite during a special adoration should offer an oblation for each individual name into the Kālāgni fire; or, he should offer a thousand oblations using those names preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava), ending in "svāhā," and having the dative case in the middle. || 48 ||

The Brāhmaṇīs should perform the special worship; they themselves should perform the offering of the oblation by means of the initiated Brāhmaṇa, as well as the handful of flowers, the hymn of praise, the prostration, the contemplation of [the deity] as one’s own object of worship, and the declaration, "I am your servant. This status of being a primary member of the assembly is possible only for a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, it must not be experienced by anyone else.

By means of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra, one should first worship Brahmā and Viṣṇu as the deity according to the specific rules of special worship; and by means of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, gods, and even animals, one should conceive of all these as Viṣṇu through the conventional method. Thus, all are Viṣṇu.
They were invoking a deity, and that deity arrived. They said to her, "Take this!

Take this! Viṣṇu became angry with them, saying, "Why is he worshipped by all? In a special worship, there must be one principal deity (mukhya) for this worship; therefore, this is not a special worship."
Because you have not made even one primary conventional agreement in this manner,
having thus accepted those words of Viṣṇu, all those devotees, detached from worldly existence, became attached to the lotus feet of Viṣṇu;
perspiring from their ears, they praised him, saying, "What can we do, whose ritual procedures remain unknown?"

To them, while they were still present, he said: "In the special worship (*viśeṣārcana*), having performed the convention of the Murus, one must perform a single special worship according to the rules with things conducive to it; by that which is worshipped by him, He becomes worshipped by all.
Therefore, [this applies to one] endowed with caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), through the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣā*), and by means of knowledge (*vidyā*) and austerity (*tapas*)."

One should perform the primary conventional [initiation] according to the sequence of birth, learning, austerity, stage of life, and consecration. Some say that one becomes superior by each subsequent factor and inferior by each preceding one. This is the nature of the primary conventional [initiation].
Whatever worship one performs other than the daily worship constitutes "special worship" (viśeṣārcana), according to Vighneśa;

that which is performed at a specific time is so called, according to Sūrya; that which is performed with special ritual materials is so called, according to Bhairava; and all agree that whatever is performed by the principal initiates (sāmayika) is indeed such. Or rather, [it is] thus.

"One should cause that [obstacle] to cease"—this is the power [of the rite]. That which has been performed by many at a specific time with specific provisions, distinct from both the particular daily worship (*nityārcana*) and the special worship (*viśeṣārcanā*), is what is called "general worship" (*sāmānyārcana*).
Regarding this special worship, Caturmukha maintains that the principal members of the assembly (*samayika*) should perform the worship; thus all agree.
Having thus declared to them that this was the preeminence of Viṣṇu as the primary member of the assembly, Viṣṇu desisted;

and having appointed Brahmā as the primary member of the assembly, they were to worship Viṣṇu. Therefore, those who are not primary members of the assembly should not worship any other lord by means of a special act of worship.
The adept performs the worship of the object through invocation, offering of a seat, water for the feet, the *arghya* offering, garlands, ornaments, and so forth;

if he is otherwise occupied, [he may perform] the offering of wine, the display of mudrās, the recitation of hymns, the acceptance of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), and sexual union in secret with the Śaktis. Together with his peers who observe the same rules, he performs the special worship during the ritual proceedings.
(p. 67) Upon satisfaction and bliss, there is the contemplation of the Manu, the dismissal of the fires of the fires, circumambulation,
the offering of a handful of flowers, and the dedication of all meritorious deeds.

The connection of meditation, the forgiveness of offenses, the declaration "I am your servant," the petition for the direct vision of the Lord’s desired form, the worship of the mandala by all, and the dismissal must be performed by the principal initiate.
Or, just as he may desire, if he is skillful, he should perform extensive special worship with many conventional offerings, including intoxicants and sexual union. (51)
Desiring to perform worship with a grand ritual application, one should consecrate [the deity] with the Thousand Names, using water that is cold according to the season, or lukewarm, or warm.

Then, if he should desire another great ritual application, having consecrated the deity and anointed him with fragrance, he should worship him with flowers or with unbroken grains (akṣata), so say some.
If he should desire another great [deity], he should worship him with flowers and praise him in this manner. || 54 ||

Then, if he should desire another great deity, having worshipped and praised him in this manner and offered oblations into the fire of time (kālāgni) as follows: he should offer into the fire of the directions using the root mantra (mūlamantra), starting from the weapons, ornaments, powers, and the lords of the vehicles of those powers and ornaments, up to the lord of the vehicles and their ornaments.
Having offered ten oblations with the root mantra into the fire of the sky for a hundred devotees of Īśvara, one should offer them either combined or separately;
if one offers them combined, some say that one should offer one oblation each into the two subsequent fires, or else one should take them in the ladle in that same manner.

If he should desire, "May I sacrifice with an animal," he should offer a mouse to Gaṇeśa, a horse to Sūrya, a peacock to Viṣṇu, a bull to Śiva, a lion to Śakti, a tiger or a predatory beast to Bhairava, a swan to Brahmā, or a beautiful bird. || 56 ||
"Women are not to be sacrificed for these [deities]," so say some who are exponents of Brahman; others who are not exponents of Brahman say that women may also be sacrificed.

Having placed the broth to the north of the fire of the sky and having offered oblations with special worship, one consecrates the sacrificial animal— Vaiṣṇava by means of a large or small application— with yellow [liquid], Śaiva with white, Saura, Gāṇapa, and Śākta with red,
and Kāpāla with either white or black water, [saying]: "I offer you to such-and-such a deity."

Having bathed it with the formula, "I bathe thee, acceptable [to the deity]," and having bound it fast with the same cord with the formula, "I bind thee fast, acceptable to such-and-such a deity," and having sprinkled it thoroughly with that same water with the formula, "I sprinkle thee,
acceptable to such-and-such a deity," he should likewise cause it to drink from those waters with the formula, "I cause thee to drink, acceptable to such-and-such a deity."
Having caused [the sacrificer] to drink, they place the vessels outside to the south of the fire of the sky (ākāśāgni):
a vessel of curd and clarified butter, a vessel of milk, and a vessel of clarified butter; having sprinkled and purified these placed cups, and having taken up a firebrand (ulmuka).

Therefore, having performed the circumambulation with the formula, "From this fire, for the sake of the deity [named] Triramukā, I perform the circumambulation for you as one who is pleasing," he casts the firebrand toward the southwest (nirṛti) with the words, "To those who are his obstructors, who run after him for the sake of his destruction,
and who harass him while he is seated in the ultimate truth— to them [he casts] this firebrand."
Thinking "I shall cast it away," the principal officiant casts it; he thus becomes free from affliction. Therefore, one should cast it away in this manner.
That which he casts away as a firebrand becomes [the deity] Hriyam.
Therefore, having cast it away, one should touch water and make a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) with that same color for the sake of the animal's mother, [named] Amukā.

Saying, "I make thee agreeable to the deity, together with sesame," the principal officiant, stepping toward the north according to the established rule, should offer the oblation and take [the portion] with the *sruva* ladle into the *sruc* (p.

Having taken the oblation from the first vessel, saying, "I take what is pleasing to [Name]," and having offered it with the ladle, saying, "To [Name] the deity, this animal has been bathed; svāhā!", he takes [the portion] from that same vessel in the same manner, saying, "To [Name] the deity, this animal has been bound."

Having offered with "svāhā," and having likewise taken from the second vessel, he offers with "This animal is sprinkled for such-and-such a deity, svāhā"; having likewise taken from that [second vessel], he offers with "This animal is strengthened for such-and-such a deity, svāhā"; and having likewise taken from the third vessel for such-and-such...
Having offered with "To this deity, this animal, for which the fire has been carried around— Svāhā!", and having taken [the portion] from that very vessel in the same manner,
he offers again with "To such-and-such deity, this animal, marked with sesame— Svāhā!". Then, having touched the remaining oblations—
one ordinary [oblation] with the *sruva* ladle and three ordinary [oblations] with other vessels— he [proceeds].
With the primary conventional formula, "To all the gods, the Sviṣṭakṛts, svāhā!
they release that animal to the north; indeed, by releasing that animal, or by giving food and water, or by granting fearlessness, they all go to the highest state.
Even King Sāhasra, by providing food and water to the animals released, attained fearlessness and the supreme goal. Those who release the animal shake off their own sins;
those who are their assistants do the same; and those who eat the sacrificial offerings also attain the supreme goal.

Having thus caused oneself to go [to the fire], one should release either the animal or the animals, whether collectively or individually; having offered the remaining oblations with all [the fires], one should complete the remainder. || 58 ||
Thus, the wise Pārānanda should not perform the animal sacrifice.
Some say that one should perform [the rites] all at once.
The virtuous king, having thus performed animal sacrifices, spoke to that deity: "I desire to sacrifice;
do not sacrifice with insentient objects alone, but sacrifice with those that are sentient and permeated by consciousness.

For the meditator is of the nature of consciousness, the object of meditation is of the nature of consciousness, and meditation itself is [permeated by] consciousness; likewise, the act of sacrificing is insentient, while the sacrificer is of the nature of consciousness."
The objects of sacrifice are indeed of the nature of consciousness; likewise, the ascetic is the one who performs austerity, and austerity is that which is to be performed by the ascetic.
Therefore, those who violate this sequence become joined with sins. For this reason, do not perform sacrifice with insentient things.
Therefore, the exponents of Brahman, whose bliss is supreme, having severed the violent offering for me, [offered] blood and the insentient.
"From that they offer [oblations], and I am pleased; I rejoice at the smoke produced from the hair of their heads.

Therefore, sacrifice in this manner. Having been told this, King Pārānanda, by means of the slaughter of those bound for death, sacrificed to Kālī and attained liberation while living (jīvanmukti). Therefore, a wise man should not perform such an act as Pārānanda did.

Now, if she should desire to sacrifice with the Mahāyāga, [the procedure is as follows]: excluding the animal sacrifice (*pāśuka*), she offers six oblations to the deity Gāyatrī according to the *sruva*-ladle rite. Having cast out the firebrand (*unmuka*), she sets down the vessels: first, she fills a vessel with semen and blood; second, with fermented liquors (*āsava*); third, with a seal (*mudrā*) or with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*).
We shall now describe its production: having brought a woman who is beautiful, healthy, charming, skilled, and exuberant in her youth,

and having bathed her with lukewarm or hot water after massaging her with fragrant oil, and having sprinkled her with a mantra dedicated to the Water-deity (Varuṇa), one should place two embryos that have not yet been separated into her womb while she is adorned with ornaments.
Taking two *kuśa* blades the size of a span (*prādeśa*) and covering them with his hand over the fire, he should recite the *kāmabīja* one hundred and eight times while positioned near it.

The *candrabīja*, the *sveṣṭeśabīja*, or whichever *kāmayīna-bīja* belongs to that particular deity—namely, the first letter of her name joined with the *anusvāra*—becomes her seed-syllable (*bīja*). This is the method.
This single-syllable seed-mantra (*bīja*) of mine is "Yadāka. Because this deity is joined with it,
one should therefore arouse that seed-mantra and, having united with her in secret,
perform sexual intercourse in such a way that her blood flows out first and only then does one discharge the semen into the womb.
In that very womb, another who is firm and of the same age as you should perform [the act]; therefore, take him who has engaged in sexual intercourse.

He should say "Take it" three times. When this has been said, the principal officiant—or another who is acting according to convention—being prepared to take [the offering] with the *sruva* spoon, should say "I am taking, I am taking" three times; if there is another officiant acting by convention, the principal officiant should say "Take it" three times. Having set down the *sruva* on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he should again [proceed] with that same [spoon].

Having taken clarified butter into the vessel with the *sruva* ladle and set the *sruva* aside, one should draw out the semen with the middle finger and likewise pour the blood into the cup. If the man is weak and unable to discharge the blood through sexual intercourse, one should instead place red sandalwood paste within that very vaginal circle.

One should pour it over that [fire]; or, if she should be overwhelmed by her menses, one should take that menstrual blood with a cloth, pour it into the cup, and then pour [milk] over it; or, if it is on a cloth, having soaked that cloth with water, one should pour over that blood-stained water.
Of these two, either one is the rule for the descendant of Uttara.

"Oṃ svāhā to such-and-such a deity," with this he offers the first oblation; likewise the second, third, fourth, and fifth. He offers the sixth with "Oṃ svāhā to such-and-such a powerful deity. [He offers] "Oṃ svāhā to such-and-such a vehicle. There are thus six oblations; the remainder is as before.

In whatever manner one considers worship to be appropriate, in that manner should the devoted one perform it correctly according to the procedure prepared for oneself, since the yoga of devotion is the cause for the delight of the deity.
Therefore, even if one is unwell due to mental or physical ailments and trembling, one should not cease the daily performance [of worship]. 64–65.
As is appropriate, with as many powers as he desires, and with as many ritual preparations and offerings as are customary, he should worship. || 66 ||

When they strive to perform the *sattra* sacrifice at midnight or when the dawn has risen, they worship each individual image (*pratīka*) with all the ritual materials brought by themselves; and among those *sattra*-performers who have chosen one another, one becomes the principal officiant (*mukhya*) by convention, and he alone performs the invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarjana*), while all the others perform the *sattra* rites separately.

Some say that they should not perform all other [rites] separately; those who are *upasāmāyika* (subsidiary) to the *sattras* perform what is customary for them in a special worship, and the *upasāmāyikas* practice that here in the *sattra*.
Some say that a *sattra* does not exist without the *upasāmāyikas*; they elect everyone for all [the roles]. Whatever... [the text continues].

"Whomever you worship, he is my object of worship; whoever you are the worshippers of, I am his worshipper. Therefore, I choose you as my companions in the ritual (sāmayika) and as my sacrificial partners (sātrika). Having chosen them as the primary ritual companions, they recite: "Whomever is worshipped there, that is our object of worship."

"Since you are a worshipper of that deity, we too are worshippers of that deity; therefore, we choose you as a participant in the sacrificial session (*satrin*), both in accordance with the agreement and according to the primary agreement. Having thus chosen him according to the primary agreement, the one chosen by the primary agreement recites: "Because you have commenced the sacrificial session (*satra*), therefore I..."
The primary, the occasional, and the secondary-occasional [rites] are for you; I am your primary-occasional human [officiant].
Thus, having been chosen as the performers of the sacrificial session (*satrin*), they mutter: "Since you have commenced the sacrificial session, therefore we are your performers of the session;
we are your secondary-occasional humans. Having so chosen, they begin.

For as many years, half-years, seasons, months, fortnights, days, or morning and other times as one may desire, one should perform that sacrificial session (*satra*) with worship during those periods;
it is such a session where one priest performs the invocation and the dismissal, while the others act as worshippers according to their respective directions.

The *sāmayika*, *upasāmayika*, *arcana*, and *satrin* priests, as well as the *muraya-sāmayika* and the *satrin*, shall not perform the constant ritual cessation of the divine consecration (*saṃskārika-aiśvara*); they shall not discharge urine, nor feces, nor sleep, nor engage in sexual intercourse; they shall not be overcome by the three [impurities], nor shall they consume food.
Having performed one of these offerings along with the fire-puja for the sake of seeking forgiveness from the deity, they should drink water;
then, having washed their feet, hands, and face, they should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice.
One should scatter eight handfuls of flowers upon the head of the deity, or even a single flower;
with both hands, anus, eyes, ears, mind, hunger, thirst, sleep, tongue, and teeth, whatever sin has been committed— all that I cast away.

"Therefore, through the scattering of flowers, forgive all that; forgive, forgive! Salutations, salutations!"—this is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). When the sacrificial session (*satra*) has commenced, others who are deficient in their senses, deformed, or aged do not enter; however, some who are devoted may enter once they have joined within the session.

While departing, except in the event of mental anguish, physical illness, or ill health, one should offer this oblation into the *ākāśāgni* until the completion of the *satra*, saying: "My *satra* has been completed; my desire has been fulfilled.
Salutations again and again to the one who brought it to completion! May he make all well-sacrificed, well-offered, and well-performed; may he [who is] in the center..."
"May those obstacles depart far from them; svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt! Having said this, the performer of the sacrifice (sattrin) should exit.

When he has gone out, the other participants, holding onto him by the hem of his garment, offer oblations. Whether it be the principal sacrificer or a temporary participant who offers, let it be well-offered (sviṣṭa)—whether by one person or by many—let that be "svāhā," may it be well-offered!
Eating only sacrificial oblations, being non-emetisers, and finding the bliss of sexual union only when capable [of restraint], they have conquered their senses;

they do not shave their heads, they do not bathe, they are devoted to the Lord, devoted to the recitation of mantras, and devoted to the meaningful service of the Lord; they are free from desire, free from formal salutations, and free from embraces, yet they are marked with the signs of the Blessed One.

Those who desire to sacrifice to a deity should become intent upon the nectar remaining from the deities; then that sacrificial session (*satra*) is commenced with conventional powers (*sāmayika-śakti*) numbered according to the years [of the session], and with those [powers] being more numerous and more excellent—
some say it is not with fewer nor less excellent, but rather with more and more excellent ones.

Surānanda, having commenced the sacrificial session (*satra*), should dismiss the deities until the completion of the session; this is the rule for the sacrificial session. Through this sacrificial session, those who possess the nature of the Supreme Self become selves of the Lord;

those who possess the nature of the Lord become individual selves (*jīvātman*) that are divine; and the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādin*) become practitioners of the sacrificial session (*sātrika*).

If one should perish during the sacrificial session (*sattra*), the primary officiant (*mukhya*) or any one of the temporary officiants (*sāmayika*)—as previously described by virtue of being the primary or temporary officiant—is to be chosen. Having poured out the water-pitcher, they purify themselves; this is the *amṛtha* (the concluding bath). || 68 ||
When the sacrificial session (sattra) has concluded, all those prohibitions that were in force for the participants of the session cease to be prohibited.
Now we shall describe the procedure for the festival.
Worshipping the deities with a festive rite, he should have all the chambers decorated and painted.

He should cause the doors of the palace to be adorned by well-ornamented elephants, horses, and courtesans standing there; and in the second courtyard, he should station well-adorned drummers and others with musical instruments, bards and singers led by panegyrists, and Śūdras who perform the duties prescribed for them.

The patron, for whom the Brahmins had performed the rites for auspiciousness, who had undergone the tonsure, the anointing, and the ritual bath, and was himself well-adorned, [was surrounded] by Kshatriyas with arms raised holding weapons and by well-ornamented courtesans exultant in their youth.

A Brāhmaṇa who has bathed after his studies but has not yet married, having abandoned the life of a student (brahmacarya), is chosen as a priest (ṛtvij) for the sake of a festival, [with the words]: "I choose you as a priest for the festival. Being thus chosen, he should mutter the nine-syllable Great Mantra (mahāmanu): "O Lord, I am your servant" (*īśvarātman tava dāso 'ham*). For these [syllables] are indeed nine oceans; therefore, this is called the Nine-Ocean mantra.
If one should know this mantra— "We worship that God who is here"— or understand it as the first utterance of the Lord, and if one desires that four-syllabled name,
it becomes, as before, the ocean of nine syllables. This [mantra] consists of four quarters.
The mantra is the fourfold Dharma; therefore, he who utters it with his voice places the fourfold Dharma within his own self. [This includes] study, sacrifice, and giving.
And these four are the feet of Dharma; or rather, since it has four feet, it consists of exactly four sections (*varga*).

Or, since these are the four *yogas*, therefore, whoever utters this with speech places the four sections—that is, the *yogas*—within himself. This mantra is indeed the accomplisher of all; therefore, this...

This [mantra] has four fruits; it may be taught even to Cāṇḍālas, and it may be accepted even from a Cāṇḍāla. By neither the giving nor the receiving of this mantra do both the teacher and the disciple become [bound by conventional status].
Therefore, this mantra is of great fruit and free from bondage; the very desire to receive it constitutes its initiation (dīkṣā).

That recitation which is performed in silence is true recitation; that non-violence which is practiced by one who is pure or impure, and that austerity which is performed anywhere at all—having been chosen, he becomes one who has performed this recitation. The sacrificer says to the barber, "Shave him," meaning "shave his disciples.
If his body hairs were soft, and if his eyebrows and eyelashes were likewise soft...

Avoiding the crest-lock (*śikhā*), he should shave all the body hair; first the pubic hair, then the head hair, and then the nails. Thus, being shaven, he should perform the bathing and other rites just like the patron (*yajamāna*).
Then he should begin the special worship of all the deities, specifically that deity who is desired by him. The patron—
One should attend to the living [deities] as if they were one's own kin, with clothing, water, perfumes, flowers, and garlands as available,
and with mental honors as appropriate; specifically, one should perform special worship for Brahmins, married women, and maidens at every watch, or at least in the evening and morning.
In the morning, at midday, in the evening, and at midnight. || 72 ||
One should worship Vāmī with all the mantras previously mentioned; this alone is the distinction. || 73 ||

Since all are authorized, they are initiated; they drink and eat the remnants of the Lord’s meal, and they sport with women and with one another, either in regular order or out of order, according to their desire.
And the mantras for seizing the left-handed ones. || 75 ||
"I receive this purifying nectar, the medicine for existence, which severs the bonds of the bound soul and is the cause proclaimed by Bhairava"—thus begins [the mantra]. (76)
"I accept this mudrā, the remnants of the Lord's meal, which destroys the torment of the heart, generates joy, and is prepared from an abundance of food"—thus for the second [offering]. (77)
"I shall seize a divine woman, intoxicated and endowed with youth,
whose heart is ever full of bliss and who performs my ritual practice"—
thus [he seizes] either the wife of Kāma or the wife of Artha. (78)
Having taken handfuls of mental flowers, they cast them or cause them to be cast upon the image of the deity.
(79) For each act of worship, there should be both invocation and dismissal; however, some say this is not so, as in the case of a long sacrificial session (*sattra*). (80)
At the conclusion of the festival, one should satisfy the officiating priest with sacrificial fees.
Now we shall describe the procedure for the offering of the bali-oblation. || 82 ||
The offering of the bali-oblation is of two kinds. || 83 ||
Cutting and discarding. || 84 ||
Or there shall be excision by the king or by one who has the authority. || 85 ||
Those offenders who deserve to be executed by the sword must be put to death. || 86 ||
(72) There are indeed these three worlds; in them there are three wombs, each subsequent one being greater than the preceding, and each subsequent womb being greater [than the preceding].
Therefore, this human being, who is subject to death, does wrong to the deity, just as cattle [do wrong] when they are human.
Because they cause harm, these are to be slain; therefore, the two *bala* [breaths] are to be slain. || 87 ||
Or rather, because punishment is a foot of Dharma, for this reason the exponents of Brahman employ it for the conquest of the heavenly world.
Some say that those ascetics who restrain themselves through austerity alone, yet punish living beings with physical punishment, attain infinity. 89.
Violence is of two kinds. || 90 ||
Violence through exertion and incidental violence. || 91 ||
That which a living being performs today by means of the body for the sake of separation [from it] is [the cause]. 92.
The other than that is the second. || 93 ||

Or, for example, when one throws wood or other materials into the fire, the living beings contained within them are indeed harmed. Even though he does not desire to deprive them of their lives, he performs an action that results in their being deprived of life. While he is performing that very action, they become separated from their lives. Therefore, this [consequence] is incidental (*prāsaṅgikī*). This remains the case.
Whether walking, sitting, or lying down, by means of this second non-violence, one incurs neither sin nor fails to attain spiritual prosperity; such is the supreme bliss. 94.
For by offering a sacrifice to any other deity, or by causing injury in any other manner, one incurs sin. || 95 ||
"Indeed, by offering the bali-oblation and killing predatory animals with a weapon, one attains infinity"—so says Surānanda. (96)
Now we shall describe the procedure for the offering of the bali-oblation. || 97 ||

Having bathed, adorned himself, and worshipped the deity, he should leave a space of one man's length in front of the deity, or according to the specific requirement; having dug a pit there, he should fix a pillar— either made of metal or otherwise— into it,
reaching as deep as the ground above, using clods of earth, wood, or stones.
One should fill it with muddy earth so that the pillar shall not move, except by being uprooted. || 98 ||

Having brought a strong hempen rope and bound the sacrificial post with it, one should adorn the post at four places with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers, [reciting]: "For the sake of the victim animal’s attainment of the same world as the deity and for its departure, I adorn you; this is the fear of death from immortality."
"Should he flee, make him stand firm; I shall endow him with immortality, glory, and splendor;

make him steady"—thus, having adorned a pillar, [he says] "make him ascend the path of well-done deeds, which is full of love"—thus, having adorned a rope with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers, [he binds] the man with it.

Having tied [the victim] by the neck and cast everything into the water, one should perform the oblation here as in the *paśu-homa*. After the separation of life-breaths, the *ghāta-homa* (slaughter-oblation) is performed; this oblation may be performed or not performed. That king, depriving those deserving of punishment of their lives, partakes of immortality. Both bipeds and quadrupeds are considered "animals" (*paśu*).

When one anoints this person with a special fragrance used for the worship of the Puruṣa— on the head, on the neck, in the throat-pit where a sword-stroke would fall, and in the heart— it makes that person pure from the outside,
whether he be naked, wearing wet clothes, or wearing dry clothes; then, with a sword, one should deprive him of his vital breaths.
Because this one has fallen naked from the womb, therefore one should cut him while he is naked— thus says Surānanda.
Because this one emerges drenched in blood, therefore one should cut him while he is wet— thus says Unmādānanda.

"One who wears dry clothing attains knowledge; therefore, one should cut that which wears dry clothing. Thus says Jñānānanda. Another [teacher] says that a beast should be cut while naked, but one of the female sex should never have its sacrificial offering (bali) cut anywhere.
Some say that [the punishment] is scriptural and not physical. Amṛtānanda maintains that there is indeed a cutting of the flesh for one of the female sex;

even for a wicked pregnant woman, we shall state the specific rule regarding the pregnant: having cut her, and having torn open the belly with a sword or a cleaver, and having ascertained the state of the fetus and extracted the fetus—if that fetus should still be alive...

If the head were joined with the neck, one should revive it; but if it were severed from the neck, having cut off the entire [head], if it were not thus [joined], one should place it in a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), smear it with cow-dung, and scatter over it perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, and *dūrvā* grass— measuring an arrow-length, or a span, or even longer.

One should fill the ground with the dust of the sacrificial wood in order to cause him to go to the heavenly world, to cause him to ascend, and to drive him along the edge of a sword; thinking "I am filling [the pit]," one should fill it. Behind the pillar, having silently adorned him, one should bind his neck with another rope and fasten it to that sacrificial post.
He should bind it so that the stroke of the sword may not fall elsewhere;

having bound it, he touches the neck, thinking: "I touch it for the sake of turning back from the lower worlds, for the sake of sending [the deceased] to the heavenly world, for the sake of releasing him from the noose of Yama, and for the sake of liberating him from distress—[I touch it], O righteous one."

Having touched the rope with the mantra, "Thou art the noose of Varuṇa," [the following are assigned]: the first is the offering (bali), the second the pillar, the third the rope, the fourth the sacrificial wood, the fifth the binding rope, the sixth the sword, the seventh the vessel of blood, the eighth the fire, the ninth the lake, the earth, or "I" (the self)— provided that the one who cuts [the head] is someone else.
Thinking, "May this be the rule," a trustworthy person— whether a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Śūdra— and no one else,
having recited the mantra "The deity of the tenth stage," facing north or east, first joins [the disciple] with the sixth [syllable],
places a flower upon his head, and after a long time, that which is to be reached, that which is unattainable by those lacking yoga, and that which they go toward— [is attained].

"O virtuous one, it has been severed; go quickly!"—having thus sprinkled the instruments with water, the Agneya Dharmapāla is fit for cutting; otherwise, another [instrument] made of iron (lauha) and belonging to Agni is fit for cutting.
Measured by the thumbs, index fingers, middle fingers, ring fingers, and little fingers held crosswise, it is one hundred long finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length;

marked by the characteristics of Dharmapāla and measured by exactly ten finger-breadths [in width], this is known as the "Black Sword" (kālakhaḍga), and nothing longer than this is desired. || 100 || 1400 ||
The sword of the directions (dikkhaḍga) is likewise half as wide and that much longer. || 1 ||
Thirty, twenty-five, or twenty-four finger-breadths in length,
three finger-breadths wide, and half a finger-breadth thick— or even lower— this is the sky-sword,
known as Candrahāsa. || 2 ||
The limit of the desire of the sacrificer or the officiating priest is the completion of the pair.

When each finger is ten *tsaru* long, the sword is designated as *vijaya*; when nine, it is *asi*; when eight, *khaḍga*; when seven, *tīkṣṇadhara*; when six, *durāsada*; when five, *śrīgarbha*; when four, *viśasana*; and when three, *dharmapāla*. These are explained in their respective order. || 4 ||

Some say that he is explained by that very designation with which he is endowed—namely, the designation "Manohara" (Charming), "Manoharadīrgha" (Long-armed like a charming one), and "Manoharākṛti" (Of charming form). || 5 ||

Or, during the day, having performed the offering of the *bali*, he should say: "Chindhi chindhi baliṃ svāhā! Cause his vital breaths to depart for the heavenly world; do not cause him to suffer. Having heated the sword over the fire, he should strike three times from above, with each blow separated by three [steps], thinking: "The *rakṣas* are separated; the enemies are separated."
With the mantra "By her! Burnt away is the Rakṣas, burnt away are the enemies," and saying "I anoint you with the splendor of Vāyu and Agni," he pours [the water] and,
with those eight ritual names, [anoints] the sword in eight places.
Some say that they should place the perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and flowers on both sides; others say that if there are two blades with two edges, there should be four.
"The sword is the slayer, the scimitar, the sharp-edged, the difficult-to-approach."
Śrīgarbha, Vijaya, and likewise Dharmapāla.

This sword is indeed the very image of Time; therefore, when it is worshipped, Time itself becomes worshipped. Consciousness is distinct from the insentient, and the insentient is distinct from consciousness. All insentient things have presiding deities.
The deities are indeed the individual souls (jīvas); through various yogic attainments, they obtain lordship over their respective domains, just as [the deity of] water [presides over] the waters.
Varuṇa: "Holding that sword and that arrow, for the sake of his heavenly world, I sever him at the neck; I separate his body from his vital breaths with this sharp-edged blade, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having spoken thus once, the executioner, using both hands or a single hand, should cut [the victim] and bring the blood into a vessel.
Having placed red sandalwood from Kāśmīra, or water, camphor, milk, curd,

or a flower upon that skull, and having covered it with both hands, one should consecrate it by reciting "Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Cāmuṇḍāyai Vicce," then place it before the deity while reciting either the Kālī-gāyatrī or the specific gāyatrī of that deity.

Having touched it, one should say, "Enjoy this," or one should offer it; the offering consists of pouring water, lighting a lamp, or burning camphor with the hair of a four-legged animal—for they are fond of smoke—therefore, one should cause smoke to issue forth for them. Having first kindled blood in that light, the fire of space, for the sake of pacification:

Having offered oblations with "Svāhā" to the shaven-headed ones from the portions of forest produce, to the blood-shaven-headed ones and other deities from the remnants of their portions, to those individual souls who have been initiated for the sake of the Lord, and to those Lords for whose sake they were initiated, one should wear a blood-mark on the forehead. Whoever indeed wears this blood-mark truly brings the deity under his control.

Therefore, one should make a tilaka of that [substance] which is desired by oneself. Having placed that body in a pit and filled it with earth, one should make the ground appear as if unknown; whoever recites the mantra over it becomes one whose mantra is perfected (*siddhamanu*).
Or, one may discard that body to the north of the village, or in the evening, to Śmaśānabhairava.

Having offered one oblation of clarified butter with the mantra "svāhā," if there is only one fire, [he should proceed]; if there are three fires, he should place this very [offering] into those fires,
complete the remainder of the oblation, and having constructed a human-shaped pile of wood— whether for a human or for an animal—
he should burn it with one fire or with all the fires, following the smoke from that [fire].

One becomes worthy of being seen by the deities; indeed, by means of smoke, one goes to the heavenly world. By reciting the *Manu* [hymn] over the heat of a blazing fire in a particular spot, one becomes a perfected (*siddha*) sage.
If that fire should go out, one should re-establish the fire and burn it again in this manner during the ritual cycle.
As long as that [deity] remains present, there should be no cessation of worship nor dismissal;

these are the observances for the sacrificer: eating very little, abstaining from sexual intercourse, bathing after voiding urine or feces, sipping water (ācamana) upon waking from sleep, and bathing upon touching something impure—these observances apply even during the *sātrikā* [rite].

If a sacrificial session (*sattra*) has been performed according to this rite, or if, in the case of a sacrificial session where all the sacrificers are sages, one takes the bones from the remaining cool ashes—having again established the *śvetāgni* fire—one [should place] those bones in milk... with two white cloths, [their] fringes... *(Note: The text fragment provided appears to be incomplete or corrupted at the end; the translation reflects the legible portion.)*
Having crushed it and formed it into a ball, [one should mix it] with honey or with wheat flour or a ball of *māṣa* beans;
having enveloped the ball with a triple-layered thread and burned it with that fire—
if there should be remnants left over— one should again do so in the same manner when the ashes have cooled, once the remainder of the ashes has been removed.
The lay follower Śmaśānakānika should wear ashes on six parts of his body;
[this is] the procedure for the offering of the bali-oblation.

"One should enjoy that [meat] through the application of the hide"—thus says Ākāśabhairava. Or, as Unmattabhairava states: "In whatever manner, one should offer as a *bali* whatever predatory creatures one slays with a sword, whether they have committed an offense against oneself or not; or, in whatever manner, one should cut the *bali* with a sword before the deity. This is the procedure.
The Ritual for the Offering of the Sacrificial Victim (Balidānavidhi) || 6 ||
Now we shall explain the consecration of deities. || 7 ||

Having constructed a temple for the deity out of stone and plaster, and having commissioned a representation of the deity made of either stone or metal, one should have the Brahmins recite benedictions (*svasti*). Then, having offered oblations to the deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*), one should bathe the image with milk; as for the fashioning of its limbs, it may be crafted by artisans using iron tools and chisels.

"Therefore, I remove this defect from him; I nourish him with cool milk and purify him, adorning him with splendor"— with these words, one should wash the ornaments, weapons, vehicles, powers, and limbs of the deity,
and those of the Vāmī [deity] as well, first with the cleansed water and then with milk from the north.
"One should arrange [them]"—thus says Unmattabhairava; "in the place of milk"—thus says Ākāśabhairava.

One should establish them whether they are standing, seated, or mounted on a vehicle. When [the deity] is established, the vehicle should be to the right of the deity without any interval, or it may be in front of the deity. The Śakti is to the left of the deity, facing right; to her left is [the other].

The vehicle is indeed the face of the deity’s vehicle. If one desires a firm and stable installation, thinking, "I shall install and establish the image firmly for a long time," one should install it with lime or by some other means so that it does not waver; [one should also include] those charming features which are the marks of the respective meditations.

They are to be firmly established, not otherwise; they are mobile supports. Thus there is a distinction: "I establish this mobile one for a long time," saying this, he places it down during the settling (*nyāsa*); thus it becomes mobile.
Having honored [the deity] with special worship, or having carried forward the fires or a single fire and offered oblations, [he says]: "Svāhā to the earths! To the waters!"
“Svāhā to the splendors! Svāhā to the winds! Svāhā to the directions! Svāhā to the times! Svāhā to the spaces!
Svāhā to the firm foundation! Svāhā to the moving foundation!”—as many as there are distinct forms, so many [offerings] are there for each.

The consecration oblations take place; having completed the remainder of the oblation, at the conclusion of the worship, Pārānanda should dismiss the deity together with the maṇḍala.
