There are two kinds of images: those established by means of consecration and those from which the deity has been dismissed. Even those from which the deity has been dismissed are worthy of worship and salutation; thus they remain.

How much more so, then, should those [images] which have not yet had deities invoked into them be worshipped and venerated? Regarding the Śāligrāma stones and the like, some maintain that consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is not performed through the manifestation of distinct limbs; rather, the Śāligrāma stone is consecrated according to meditation (*adhyāna*), and thus the properties of the consecrated reside within the Śāligrāma stones and other earthen objects.

When images have been fashioned but not yet consecrated, the deities invoked therein remain present, so that those objects become worthy of salutation and worship; once the deities have been dismissed, they become unworthy of salutation and unworthy of worship, for some maintain that the capacity for invocation no longer exists there. Furthermore, the temple has three doors.
To the east, south, and north of them, there are the dwellings of the assembly members situated in front;
the inner sanctum for the deities measures one thousand cubits on all sides, with the outer courtyards being double that size,
then half of that, then half of that, and so on as appropriate, until the surrounding enclosure walls.

Some authorities maintain that [the trees] are to be cut down from their trunks. Now, regarding what has been done and what remains to be done: one should plant large trees—such as the *sāmla*, *karavīra*, *udumbara*, *śirīṣa*, *aṭarūṣaka*, *rājādana*, and others—around the temple of the deity, as far as possible.

He should honor tanks, ponds, and wells; he should cause delightful reservoirs to be constructed from which water has been drawn or replenished for the benefit of the poor; and he should provide medicine and other necessities for the sick.
He should appoint those who are capable of managing it there; likewise, he should appoint various givers for the sake of those seeking various things.

For the purpose of guarding and purifying this [temple], he should employ Śūdras through sweeping and other such tasks, and servants by providing them with food, clothing, and wages, all around this entire temple complex.

For the sake of success, they prepare a special firm wall; the specific details should be understood from the treatises on architecture (*vāstuśāstra*), such as its aesthetic appeal and so forth. They proceed with the examination of the ground, the offering of oblations (*bali*), the feeding of Brahmins, thousands of great fire-sacrifices (*homa*) ending with the word *svāhā* performed with their [the deities'] names, grand festivals, and blood-offerings.

"One should consecrate an image that is either fashioned or unfashioned, devoid of power, and without a vehicle," says Unmattabhairava; "without weapons," says Jñānānanda; "only a Brāhmaṇa should consecrate it through the rite of consecration, not a Kṣatriya or others," say some; or one may consecrate it in this manner.

In some way or another he attains infinity; for, apart from the loss of his limbs, the divine image does not become worldly. Thus, when that worldly state has arisen, Unmādānanda, having dug a pit in the earth measuring two men's height, placed him therein, filled it with dust, and [covered] that earth—
They restore what is unfit for use by re-consecrating it in a temple; they establish a second image and make a dilapidated hall as good as new,
and they proceed with the Vāstu-homa sacrifice.
Thus ends the first daily lesson in the Uttarādhyāya of the Pārānandasūtra.

Now, we shall explain the sequence of ritual practice for the sake of attaining the grace of the deity. || 9 ||
One should perform [this] for a year, a half-year, a season, a month, a fortnight, by day, or by night. || 10 ||

Having had a Brāhmaṇa recite the *puṇyāha* formula and having accepted the rules of initiation (*dīkṣā-dharma*), one should perform the practice— excluding the ritual bath— according to the fortnight, as "worship once [per day]"; whether it be at midday for the right-hand path (*dakṣī*) or at midnight for the left-hand path (*vāmī*), or in the morning for the right-hand path or in the evening for the left-hand path, the latter of these two is superior.

He who ordains this is the Year; he beholds the deity, he beholds the deity. Having become thus, one should offer oblations at midday—one thousand oblations, or for each of the thousand names, one hundred oblations, with the names individually ending in "svāhā," [offering] to ten Brahmins.

Having honored [the guest] with the madhuparka, one should cause him to sacrifice with whatever [substance] is available. Having cut off [portions] according to the rules for the *avadāna* (cutting-off), [he sacrifices] with the *caru*, with the oblations (*bali*), or with blood; or, as an alternative to the non-cutting-off method, with clarified butter, milk, or curd, according to the stated options regarding the time.
He who ordains this very [course] sees the deity; he sees the deity. || 13 ||
Having become thus, at the prescribed time, one should cause the offerings (bali) to be cut by those who delight in the supreme.
He who ordains the seasons, he beholds the deity; he beholds the deity. || 15 ||
Or a learned man may give the blood from his own limbs; some say that a Brāhmaṇa should not give it, while Unmattabhairava says that even a Brāhmaṇa may give it. || 16 ||

A Brāhmaṇa should offer blood from his head or heart; a Kṣatriya from his arms or throat; a Vaiśya from his thighs or belly; and a Śūdra from his forehead. Or, according to the ritual for offering oblations (*bali*), he should cleanse the image of the deity with the blood from his own limbs, or having drawn out blood, he should present it as an offering (*naivedya*).
He should sip water twice, then take hold of the axe with his right hand, saying: "Thou art the axe; thou art the protector of the gods;

thou art the cutter of the woods; thou art the drinker of blood; thou art the doer of what is dear to the gods; thou art the drinker of dharma. Just as the milk of a calf is left over [for its mother], so the gods take that which is the milk; this blood is thy leftover."

Having taken up the sacrificial knife with the words, "O divine weapon, do not harm me," and having taken a blade of grass or *dūrvā* with his left hand, he places it beneath the skin with the mantra, "Thou art nectar, thou art Soma, thou art the nourisher of the gods;
O herb, protect me! Then, uttering "Huṃ Phaṭ," he lets the blood flow into a vessel.
Having slightly mixed this with water and sprinkled it repeatedly with the Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī mantras, one should employ it; such is the rite of the offering of blood from one's own limbs. || 17 ||
He touches the woman, saying: "Thou art a desirable woman; thou art the beloved of the gods; thou art prosperity; thou art the kindling-wood of men for the youth.

Having firmly embraced her and kissed her mouth, he should anoint his erect penis with fresh butter and rub it against her vulva, or if she should first emit [fluid] or be overflowing with menstrual blood.

Then, at that very spot, he should also remove his own lute. Having sipped water and become pure, and having worshipped with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers, he should take [the ghee] from that [vessel] with a ladle into the ghee contained in the vessel, fill it with that ghee, and having kindled the fire with the syllable *ram* before the image of the deity on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), [he should offer it], saying: "Thou art the oblation (*bali*)."
One should pour [the remainder] into the fire for the deities. || 18 ||
Having dismissed the deities, one should cease [the ritual]. || 19 ||
Having worshipped the deity with flowers, one should honor them by name with a thousand, a hundred, or ten [verses].
Do not [speak] thus. || 21 ||
Whatever fragrance belongs to which [substance], one should smear with that fragrance using its *pratīka* (opening verse) from the *Gāyatrī*; the remainder is as previously stated. || 22 ||
The same applies to the fortnight. || 23 ||
One should remember her in the morning, those who are her devotees; the rest has been stated [previously]. During the day, whoever... || 24 ||
The marking and the covering with armor should be performed according to the number prescribed in the scriptures.
To him who [performs] the *nakta* [vow], indeed... || 26 ||
The ritual bath performed upon the completion and relinquishment of the observance. || 27 ||

Through its performance, [merit accrues] to Brāhmaṇa women whose husbands are living and whose offspring are living, to learned Brāhmaṇas and their husbands, and to young girls; for it is through the desire of those girls that they attain the state of maidenhood during the year of the mirror.
One should bestow garments, ornaments, water-jars, sandals, umbrellas, mirrors, soft beds, houses, gardens, ponds, wells, tanks, and food. || 28 ||
At the conclusion of the performance of the Vāmānuṣṭhāna, [the same applies] for the Kālikeya and likewise for the courtesans.
Giving to those mentioned according to possibility, as far as possible. || 30 ||

To the students (brahmacārins) at the end of the Saura [mantra]; to the householders (gṛhasthas) at the end of the Vaiṣṇava; and to the householders at the end of the Śaiva—some say also to the forest-dwellers (vanasthas) at the end of the Vaiṣṇava. || 31 ||

Some say that one should give food preceded by the word "annam" (food) to householders at the end of the *gāṇapatya* [section], to renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) at the end of the *śaiva*, and to those who have completed their studies but are unmarried (*snātakas*) at the end of the *śākta*. One who performs the ritual must not fail to give food;
for among all these, the one who has completed his studies but is unmarried is considered foremost. Therefore, in the absence of each of the others, [food should be given] at the very end to them.

One should give to him: that which shaves one who has not yet been shaved; that which provides sacramental rites for one whose body has not yet been consecrated; that which gives clothing to one who is unclothed; that which gives ointment to one who has bathed;
that which gives shoes to one who is barefoot; and food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty.

He gives it away and thus makes his own practice complete. Or rather, in whatever way and for whomever there may be afflictions, he should cut them away for others. In that he cuts away the afflictions of others, he himself becomes one whose afflictions are severed; therefore, [he should give] to those who seek such things as far as possible.

One should give various goods to the student (*brahmacārin*), household goods, clothing, ornaments, and food to the householder, and forest goods to the other; "the goods for the student have been mentioned"—to this some reply: they are the sweet forest products suitable for a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*).

Soft forest edibles, the skins of wild animals, and fear of wild beasts—for having killed these, food and clothing are given to the renunciants; this is the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) for all. 32.
Having become thus, one should perform the bath at the time prescribed for speaking. || 33 ||
He who ordains the year sees the deity; he sees the deity. || 34 ||
He marks his own limbs with the symbols of his chosen deity using either clay or ash, and having become thus, he speaks as described.
He who indeed ordains the two courses (of the sun). || 36 ||
Having become thus, he recited the reading of the thousand divine names as previously described. (37)
He who ordains the season in this manner... || 38 ||

The recitation (*japa*) may correspond in number to the syllables of the mantra, or to the age of the deity in years; or, just as the image is to be consecrated (*pratiṣṭhāpyā*), it corresponds to the age of the deity in years, and its measurement is in *vitastis* according to that same number.
Or, the recitation is performed by measuring the length [of the cord] in this manner, or it consists of the desired number of repetitions corresponding to that [age].
He recites [the mantra] for thousands of years, numbering as many hundreds of thousands as there are years in his own lifespan.

At the conclusion of this, there are these seven ancillaries: consecration (abhiṣeka), sprinkling (mārjana), anointing with fragrant paste (gandhānulepa), flowers (puṣpa), fire-oblation (homa), feeding of Brahmins (brāhmaṇabhojana), and libation (tarpaṇa); these constitute its parts.
There are preliminary rites. Regarding this, some say that one should perform all of them with the Gāyatrī verse.
He himself should perform a small portion of the rite regarding the seven limbs, while the remainder is performed by the Brāhmaṇas.
If one so desires, then by means of the recited mantra, one may personally turn back all things. || 41 ||
If one is personally unable to perform the *gāyatrī* [japa], one should accomplish all [the rites] with the root mantra of that deity:
the ablution (*abhiṣeka*) is one-tenth of the japa; the sprinkling (*mārjana*) is one-tenth of that; the anointing with fragrant unguents (*gandhānulepana*) is one-tenth of that;
the flowers are one-tenth of that; the fire-oblation (*homa*) is one-tenth of that; and the feeding of Brahmins (*brāhmaṇabhojana*) is one-tenth of that.
The libation (tarpaṇa) is performed with one-tenth of that amount. || 43 ||
Or all [these] occur by means of a tenth part of the recitation. || 44 ||
Having uttered the mantra "I consecrate you," the sprinkling with water is performed upon the face. 45.
Having recited the mantra, one performs the sprinkling (*mārjana*) with the words "I sprinkle" (*mārjayāmi*), using *kuśa* or *dūrvā* grasses at the various parts of the body.
Having recited the mantra over the fragrance with a ladle or a finger, one should apply it to the face, saying, "I anoint with fragrance."
Having recited the mantra, one performs the offering of flowers with the words "I honor [you] with a flower" at the representative image. 48.
Having recited the mantra, one should offer the oblation with "svāhā. || 49 ||

When the Brahmins were seated, he recited the mantra over the well-prepared food in the vessels before them; then, according to the rule for the *avaddna* offering, he made an oblation with the *sruk* ladle while saying "vaṣaṭ" upon the palm of the Brahmins' right hands, and silently offered water with the *sruva* ladle upon the palms of their left hands. Then those Brahmins [placed it] into their respective *kamaṇḍalus*.

They pour water into that which is already full of water; in this way, one should honor those who have bestowed wealth upon the recipients with food, perfumes, flowers, garlands, and garments. || 50 ||

They satisfy [the ancestors] with milk or with water from a sacred ford (tīrtha); having uttered the mantra, they cause the water to flow forth, saying, "I satisfy [them] through the divine ford. || 51 ||
One should complete all the ancillary rites with one hundred recitations counted by all the [prescribed] numbers;
some say, however, that this should be done with one thousand.
The state of being a tenth part continues as long as unity has not been attained;
once unity is reached, then, according to some, the repetition ceases.
The four limbs are the fire-oblation (homa), the libation (tarpaṇa), the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), and the feeding of Brahmins; thus says Digbhairava. || 54 ||
Kālabhairava states that the three limbs begin with the fire-oblation (homa). || 55 ||
Ākāśabhairava says: "By means of cleansing and satiation, [one attains] two limbs. (56)
One should perform ten breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), or a number equal to the years of one's age. || 57 ||
He who performs it in this manner for a year beholds the deity; he beholds the deity. || 58 ||
One should perform meditation. || 59 ||
He who performs this installation in this manner is a god. || 60 ||
One should give gifts to the Brāhmaṇas according to the sacred tradition. || 61 ||
He who ordains the season in this manner... || 62 ||
Now we shall speak of Kālikā from the left side. (63)

Having applied *kālpi* vermilion or one of the red sandalwoods to his forehead, he should bring a woman and engage in sexual union with her. When his semen has been emitted, he should withdraw the penis from the vulva, pour the semen into a vessel containing water,
scatter fragrant flowers over it, and then mix it with flour, *japayā*, and red sandalwood paste.
Covering [the vessel] with his hand, he should pour out [the water], saying: "What you are, that am I; what I am, that are you.

Having spread *kuśa* grass upon water or upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), he should offer libations to the Self of the Lord, who is gratified by the *svayaṃbhū* flower, and to the one who dwells in the cremation ground, who is worshipped by the individual soul as the Supreme Soul and is beloved by those devoted to the Supreme Self. || 64 ||
He who performs it in this manner... || 65 ||
Actions performed do not go to waste; they either bring about the grace of the deities or bestow heaven. || 66 ||

One with disheveled hair and naked, dead by an arrow in battle; or one dead by any of the following—discus, mace, sword, trident, axe, noose, or goad—in battle; or one whose head is severed or whose head is not severed; or one who has died in combat; or one who is handsome and young.

Some say that a corpse which has remained for five days following the commencement of battle is not yet considered stale (*aparyuṣita*). Others say it remains fresh as long as blood continues to flow from it.
[One should place it] with its head facing west or east, its feet facing south or north, or with its face upward, [touching it] with the hand.

Having touched the deceased, he consecrates him with the mantra: "O deceased one, go forth (preto 'si) from this world by means of knowledge, power, vigor, valor, prosperity, and truth. Having mounted [the vehicle], while muttering the *Manu* or reciting a hymn (*stotra*), [he proceeds] except in the case of battle; likewise on a four-legged animal facing north, or near the flames of the funeral pyre.

Before the collection of bones has occurred, or when the fire has been extinguished and the human presence has ceased, that which remains small is called an "empty abode" (*śūnyālaya*). Whether it be such a place, or one crowded with the fear of tigers and the like, he who dwells there or hears the howls of jackals is known as a "son of Kālī. Thus he attains renown.

Possessing knowledge like Bṛhaspati, wealthy like Kubera, powerful like Vāyu, and as difficult to conquer as Death, he becomes like Maheśvara; O Lord of Yogins, he who eats what is drinkable, edible, or even the leavings of another, becomes the master of all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 67 ||
He who praises with hymns crosses over terrible sins. || 68 ||

Having brought a young woman—whether she be a wife for wealth, a wife for pleasure, or a wife for dharma—who is in her menses, [the practitioner should consider] that first day on which the menstrual flow occurs as the "rising" (*udaya*); for one who knows the nature of the rising, she remains in her menses only until the end of that first day.
At the conclusion of that first day, he should mix water, *dūrvā* grass, fragrant flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) into a vessel.

Having consecrated it with the Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī mantras, he sprinkles her with water drawn from that [vessel], saying: "Just as you are Bhaga, shining with passion (*rajas*), so may I be [endowed] with knowledge, with the thunderbolt-like slaying of enemies, and with strength.
Having sprinkled with the nectar of the *kṛṣya* [milk] that [image] which was shining with prowess, and having adorned it with a golden cord,

a golden crescent moon on its neck, bracelets on its two hands, earrings on its two ears, and with fragrance, flowers in their respective places, and a flower garland, [he placed it] upon an excellent covering.

Having laid her on the couch supine, naked, with her head toward the east, and having placed her right foot in his right hand and her left foot in his left hand, he should smear her vulva with flowers and fragrant oil,
scatter flowers over it, and then, looking at her vulva in this manner, stand up facing the east.

Naked, with his topknot tied, having shaved his hair, beard, body hair, and nails— except for the hair of the eyebrows and the eyelashes— and marked with drops of blood or red sandalwood paste, adorned with garlands and unguents,
he should recite the Kālīgāyatrī mantra ten times, or one hundred times, or one thousand times, or even once.

As he desires, so should he recite [the mantra]. If his virility has been aroused, he should take that semen while in a waterless or watery place; even if the penis has not yet become erect, he should pour that semen along with the water onto a moist mound, or into her vulva, saying, "May pleasure and desire be satisfied. He should satisfy her with garments and other gifts—he who performs it in this manner.
He becomes as beautiful as Madana and attains the state from which there is no return. || 69 ||
Having brought a young woman endowed with beauty, having bathed her, honored her with garments and other offerings, sprinkled her with the *Sāvitrī* mantra,
touched her while reciting "Bhago 'si," and having touched the *bhaga* (vulva) with both hands holding *pavitra* grass,
one should mutter the root-mantra consisting of one hundred and eight names; then one should engage in sexual union— he is the Lord of all Vidyās.
It is accomplished. || 70 ||
Naked, with hair loose and the topknot released,
having shaved his head— or else having shaved the hair of his beard, armpits, and nails— he enters the house;
having entered that place abundant in fragrance and pleasant according to the season, he [places] those women in the eastern and other directions.
Having established them, he should place one to the north and one to the south; some say he should place ten.

In the *aparājita* direction (the northeast), he should touch [the Brahmin] with his right hand, saying, "I choose you as my officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). He should reply, "I am chosen. Having honored him with the *madhuparka*, and those...
With garments, food, and drinks, and with courtesans, he should satisfy them through the union of his own genitals with their vulvas, and with laughter and jesting;

or, if lacking such power, having entered that maṇḍala and sat down facing north, he should mutter the Gāyatrī ten times and the Kālikā-mantra, and then say to him: "Make him hear this Gāyatrī three times in a whisper and three times aloud."

He should respond, "I shall cause [it] to be heard," and act according to the command; for him, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consists of golden earrings, a ring, or a garland. Having done this, he becomes a sky-walker (khecara). || 71 ||
If there should be no union with a woman, one should extract the semen by whatever means possible;

at the time of extraction, the practitioner should mutter the *kālībīja* mantra and cause it to be heard as "the Śrāvaka of the cremation ground" (*śmaśānakālika*). Having muttered this, he becomes a true poet. Once that semen has been extracted, he should pour it onto a moist patch of ground to the north; for him, there shall be food [as abundant] as a lotus-pond.
And [they give] a sacrificial fee, water, a pair of garments, or a pair of sandals, or an umbrella. || 72 ||

Delighting a naked young woman with the method of the plough (sīrata), having recited "Mahākālī" three times and heard it three times from a disciple, one becomes a sky-walker (khecara) of immeasurable strength, firmness, and prowess. || 73 ||

One who desires to be liberated from sin should, during sexual union accomplished according to the prescribed method, recite the Gāyatrī mantra three times; or, having approached the Śrāvaka [disciple] with the words "O Blessed One, O Auspicious One," he should cause him to hear it three times. Having gone to a crossroads, he should offer at that crossroads cooked rice accompanied by honey, milk, and sugar in vessels.
Saying, "I shall take away the strength of others," (p.

One should fill six vessels with lac-dye, wine, and milk, having consecrated them for the purpose. Then, having brought a young, healthy courtesan, having refined her with ointments and massages,

Saying, "Invoke Rati," he should place a red flower on her head; saying, "For Kāma, invoke Kāma," he places that same flower on his own head. Regarding the phrase "the state of being the locus of the *bhaga*": having touched the breasts and then grasped the *bhaga*, thinking, "I am churning you, who are offered for the sake of the semen and for the means of cleansing the womb with blood and semen," one should insert the *liṅga* into the *bhaga* and bring about the flow of the essence of sexual union (*suratosava*).
Alternatively, if it should quickly flow out, what is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in that case? [The text continues: while withdrawing it...

Holding the nozzle of the applicator with the thumb over the penis while gripping it with the index finger, one should take that nectar from the vulva and fill a vessel containing water with it for the fourth [application]. With that same water and semen, one should perform the fifth.

He fills the sixth [vessel] with the water used for washing his feet. He should pour out the first [libation], saying: "I satiate Kālī, the supreme devotee. He pours out the third, saying: "I satiate Kālī, who is the Jīvā of the Abhajanā."

"Delighted by the nectar of the *bhaga* and *liṅga*, I satisfy Kālā"—this is the fourth [offering], the festival of semen (*śukrotsava*). "I satisfy Kālā"—this is the fifth. "Satisfied by the water used for washing the *bhaga* and *liṅga*, I satisfy Kālā"—this is the sixth.
If he, being liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), sequentially receives all these without remainder or with remainder, it is through truth.

One should consume [the substance] with the formula: "I seize you, O immortal one, for immortality through splendor. However, if this occurs in a dream-vision, its success is declared to be only half. Therefore, some say that those who have achieved half-success should desire them.
Some say that one remains consecrated (*dīkṣita*) for twenty-four days. If they were to consecrate him together, they would all honor him slightly, very slightly.
There are exactly six cups; like a mother, Kālikā becomes his benefactress. || 76 ||

Having somehow accomplished sexual union and meditating on Kālī who is attached to him, while muttering the mantra with rapid breath, he—though naked and with disheveled hair—soon becomes a lord of yogis. || 77 ||

Having gone to a cremation ground, [one should offer] upon whichever corpse of a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra is blazing; or, in the absence of such, having visualized Kālī there and cut off an offering, one should pour out the remaining blood in the direction [of the corpse], saying: "O Blessed One, I give this to the Bhūtas, Pretas, and Piśācas, headed by Mahārudra, who dwell in the cremation ground. If...
If a human is severed in the north, then [the victim] is one who moves upon the earth; if severed in the south, then [the victim] is one who does not move upon the earth.
Or indeed, if [severed] in the west, [the victim] is one who moves through the sky; or indeed, if in the east, [the victim] is one who moves through the air.
When that *bali* offering is blazing intensely, having brought there a young woman endowed with health, and having summoned Rati and Kāma—

Having performed the churning of the portions (*bhagamathanam*) and placed the *liṅga* upon the *uttārikā*, one should pour the semen—which has flowed into curd mixed with ghee—into it while reciting "asīti. Then, having looked at the sun, one should satisfy the person with garments, food, and wealth, [reciting]: "I take refuge in Kālī; I take refuge in the excellent sword; I take refuge in Muṇḍā and Abhayā."
I take refuge in the circles adorned with garlands and earrings; I take refuge in Kurukullā; I take refuge in the lion of Kurukullā; I take refuge in the Kālikeyas.

"I take refuge in the Supreme Self, the Lord-Self who bestows grace upon the individual soul; I take refuge in the one who increases [prosperity], who dwells in the cremation ground; I take refuge in the trident, I take refuge in the skull-bowl, I take refuge in Pārvatī, I take refuge in the bull, I take refuge in Pārvatī and the bull, and I take refuge in the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas."

Then he should cause it to be recited and dismiss those [women] with this very [mantra]; by this, one purifies an unconsecrated woman; therefore, this is the mantra for the purification of women. A devotee should himself recite it and place a thousand *arka* flowers to the left or to the right of the fire—naked, unadorned, and with disheveled hair—dedicating them to her with that curd.

"Mixing [the flowers] together, I offer them into the fire; may she be pleased by this"—this is the dedication (*uddeśa*). Therefore, having recited the mantra for each flower, one should cast it into that fire; thus he becomes a wanderer at will (*svairacara*). || 78 ||

Having removed the hair, beard, body hair, and nails that have fallen inside the house, and having taken one of these with a cloth-broom, a broom of *kuśa* grass, or a broom of *kāśa* grass, or covering them with the hand,
one should recite the *yopāśodhana* and the *māyābīja* mantras; then, by sprinkling her with those waters, [the purification is accomplished].

This purification by the *yopā* applies everywhere. Having united with her, one should pour the *śukra* (semen) into the water-filled cup; some say [it may be] with sediment or without sediment. Having placed the broom (*samārjanī*) there, at midday, having once uttered the seed-syllable of Kālī—*kālikāyai sarvādyāyai sarvādṛṣṭaśūnyāyai svāhā*—[one should offer] with the cup.
Having offered [this], one becomes accomplished as a master of all [sciences]. || 79 ||
Having laid a courtesan face upwards as previously described and having united with her, he should discharge his semen right there into her womb.
Then, rising while his semen is still falling, he should perform ritual purification (ācamana) and, sitting down, gaze repeatedly at his own semen-filled womb;
by reciting the *Manu-sahasra* here, he becomes free from dejection and, at the end, attains the abode of Kālī.

He who meditates upon that Kālī—who brings delight to her devotees who are intent on the bliss of sexual union, regardless of how or where they engage in nocturnal amorous play—he becomes Śiva. || 81 ||
Those who execute wicked men condemned to death at the point of the sword attain, moment by moment, the fulfillment of their desires. || 82 ||

One who has self-control, eats sixteen mouthfuls of sacrificial food (haviṣya), performs one hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajāpa), and is solely devoted to the feet of Kālī— whether eating as he pleases by day or by night— attains inconceivable sovereignty if he accomplishes union after performing one hundred recitations.
He who recites it a thousand times at midnight becomes surrounded by a hundred young women. || 84 ||
By this, the perverse ritual practices of the lords have been explained. (85)
Some say that these are indeed the Kālikeyas. 86.
Some say that those [limbs] of hers are auspicious, with the exception of the drinking [organ]. 87.
What is the cause for the propitiation of the deities? || 88 ||
Exertion toward that. || 89 ||

Some [recommend] the private recitation of the Veda. || 95 ||

Because the deity is independent, [the Lord] is obtained through him alone whom He chooses; and because of the scriptural statement, "The Vedas all flow toward that goal," some say it is by His will. || 96 ||

Or rather, just as this individual soul (jīva) independently chooses for itself another action—whether it be one that yields sin or merit—because he is independent, so too does the Lord (īśvara) [choose] the individual soul. || 97 ||
Thus ends the second daily lesson in the Uttarādhyāya of the Pārānandasūtra.
(p. 85) The third chapter in the Pārānandasūtra.
We shall now describe the characteristics of the grace of the deity. || 98 ||
Just as there are indeed many individual souls (*jīva*), so too are there many Lords (*īśvara*) to be reckoned;
yet when an individual soul is initiated, it chooses one single Lord as its own and becomes disciplined for the sake of beholding Him.
In this way, through initiation by means of the *bhānāmaya* [sheath], the Lord becomes initiated—that is, the Lord is initiated whenever an individual soul is initiated.

The Lord accepts as His own that soul which has been initiated for its own sake and has performed its prescribed duties, and He bestows grace upon it; for the Lord knows everything— both the soul that has been initiated and the specific practice it performs— since the Lord is omniscient, and thus this soul is not [independent] in this manner.
One understands the Lord as one's own self even though He is initiated; for just as this person becomes initiated, so too does He become initiated through devotion.
That which one does not know, He knows that very thing. || 99 ||

When that Lord has been initiated, certain signs arise in this living soul (jīva); by these arisen signs, he should recognize: "He was initiated for my sake. We shall now set forth those which arise. || 100 || 1500 ||
Regarding the deity whom one worships, some hold that the form of that deity consists of milk and curds counted according to the number of years; however,
Kālabhairava maintains that for all [deities], the form consists of milk and curds for twelve years.

Regarding the phrase "sixteen years old": Ākāśabhairava is one whose beautiful form can be compared to the beauty of ten million Cupids, who possesses a marvelous fragrance, whose body hair and facial hair have not yet emerged,
whose hair and nails have not grown long, and whose pair of eyebrows and the hair of his eyelashes have not yet developed.

The state of being free from defects caused by improper actions, possessing strength equal to ten million Vāyus, freedom from disease, being devoid of sweat and impurities, inconceivable agency, and being served by humans, Gandharvas, or gods— so say some. And as for the color, it is black mixed with white for Vaiṣṇavas, and white for Śaivas.

Some maintain that [the light] of the Śākta, Saura, and Gāṇapa schools is white, mixed, and red respectively, being as white as a stream of cow’s milk, as pure as meat, and like the color of blood; however, others do not accept this. Within a radius of two *gavyūtis* around it, all living beings possess knowledge of all languages, and their speech becomes slow and deep.
It is pleasant to hear, not harsh, and audible equally whether one is near, far away, or in between.

Some do not accept this. Some teachers of Brahman declare that living beings who have abandoned their enmity for a hundred *krośas* all around become friendly toward one another; others say it is for a distance of only one *krośa* all around.
Tigers and the like, horses and the like, and heroes—

each manifesting their own chosen lord, weapon, and a single vital point (marmāṣṭama) of this [deity]— establish themselves in the directions, appearing in the sky above as its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); by this, that which was grasped through a cause becomes indeed relinquished.

Furthermore, there is likewise the quality of moving with great speed: two human *gandharvas* serve as attendants, one holds the parasol, and another holds the lion throne; there is also the power of traveling everywhere, even entering the realms of insects and animals.
The earth all around is level, free of thorns, pure, with pure water, and likewise possessed of sandy shores.

To the north, the ground was favorable; the breeze was gentle, fragrant, and very cool. To the north was a reservoir of water, two arms’ length in width and as long as the span of two outstretched arms. That water was pure and deep; it flowed like a stream, rising from the west and subsiding in the east.

His desire becomes unimpeded; he knows all the Vedas and Smṛtis, and he knows every single object of knowledge along with its origin, its development, and its dissolution; therefore, he becomes omniscient.
His activity regarding food and excretion occurs spontaneously, and hunger does not afflict him.

Through thirst and sleep, the dissolution of the ignorant occurs at the end. His semen produces progeny; therefore, some say it becomes devoid of vigor. For those who have attained discipleship among teachers, and likewise for enemies, there would be servitude, as well as for those who are despondent and intoxicated.

Humility arises. [He is called] Nārāyaṇa because his strength is immeasurable; his body is indestructible and impenetrable by weapons or missiles. It is the state of being devoid of even the slightest fault and untouched by merit or sin.

There is the state of being awake as a single condition and the state of being dependent solely upon the Lord. Those [beings] that arise at dawn on the day remain throughout the night, and the bodily organs of one who is attached [to them] exist at all times. Excluding these two final cases, all other characteristics follow His will without distinction of place or time; therefore, by this [it is established].
It should be understood that he has become initiated as a lord within me. || 1 ||

Having understood this, one should kindle the fire and offer oblations: in the center, saying "Svāhā to [Name], the name of one's chosen deity, whose essence is the Lord"; and around it, saying "Svāhā to [Name] and others," or "Svāhā to the weapon of [Name]"; and around it again, saying "Svāhā to the ornaments of [Name] and others," or "Svāhā to [Name] and others."
With "Svāhā to [Name]’s [Name] Śakti," he offers oblations all around; with "Svāhā to [Name]’s [Name] Vāhana," he offers all around;
with "Svāhā to the ornaments, weapons, and vehicles of [Name]’s [Name] Śakti," he offers to the south; and with "Svāhā to the ornaments of [Name]’s [Name] Vāhana," he offers to its left.

"To such-and-such a devotee, who has attained a divine, sādhaka, or infinite body, [I offer] svāhā"—thus he should offer to each one individually, or to those beginning with such-and-such; some say that after this, "na" (not) should be repeated for each. He should offer oblations of milk, ghee, curd, sesame seeds, oil, fuel-sticks, leaves, flowers, or fruits, whether he has bathed or not, during the night when the sun has risen.
Having divided [the day] into six parts or five: these are Brahmā, Śakti, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, and Dantin;

their times of direct manifestation (*sākṣātkāra*) are to be known respectively as evening (*pradoṣa*) and morning (*aprātaḥ*). The *anuvatsara* belongs to Brahmā, the *parivatsara* to Śakti, the *saṃvatsara* to Viṣṇu, the *idāvatsara* to Sūrya, and the *ilāvatsara* to Dantin.
[The *sādhyāyana*] belongs to the elephants; or all [the seasons] belong to all [deities], according to some.
Spring belongs to Śakti, summer to Sūrya, the rainy season to Brahmā, autumn to Viṣṇu, winter to the elephants, and the cool season to Śiva;
spring belongs to all [deities], according to some. Or all [seasons] belong to all [deities]. The seventh [lunar day] belongs to Brahmā, the ninth...

The tenth [tithi] belongs to Śakti, the eleventh to Viṣṇu, the twelfth to Śiva, and the sixth or fourth to Gaṇeśa. By whatever characteristics manifest in him, this atom (aṇu) becomes great through its qualities;
just as these Lords, who are the Supreme Self, are of intermediate dimension and yet great compared to space and the other elements.

These [elements] become great because they are not insentient (*ajaḍatvāt*). These [elements], such as space and the rest, although possessing the dimension of "great," remain inferior to that which is non-insentient; therefore, this individual soul (*jīva*), though minute, is the Lord (*īśa*) and the Seer (*draṣṭṛ*). What follows from this? Even prior to the direct realization of the Lord, what [consequence] arises from it? On this point, the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: the individual souls are independent.

Regarding the performance of actions, the experience of the unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by those actions is dependent upon the Lord; therefore, through His direct perception, they proceed to experience suffering as commanded by the Lord, yet they remain free from pain by His grace. This is the resolution on this point that the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādinaḥ*) maintain.
Thus ends the third daily lesson in the second chapter of the *Pārānandasūtra*.
