Now we shall explain the sequence for the direct realization of the Lord.
The food, possessing the characteristic of being manifest, is offered while facing north.
Then, at the prescribed time, a circle of absolute darkness rises in front of him from the north as he cries out;
thereupon he should recite the armor (*kavaca*) of that deity, and then a solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*), brilliant like the sun, appears.
Then he should recite the *Sahasranāmastotra* mantra while contemplating it, and the form of the Lord (*Īśvara*) becomes clearly manifest to the devotee.

Then, with devotion, one should recite the nine-syllable mantra (*navārṇa-manu*). Whether or not one has the capacity for the *āvāhana* (invocation), the weapons and ornaments appear on the left according to their respective places; thus everything becomes manifest. When it has become manifest, one should prostrate. Upon prostration, that deity asks, "What is your welfare? Then, whatever one says, [it is granted].

"Since all that is wholesome has been taught by the Teacher, I have attained similarity with you. Then that deity says, "It is true, it is true, just as you have said; nevertheless, I shall grant you a certain boon," and she offers him a weapon in the form of a missile. Having bowed down, he should receive it from her with his palms joined in reverence (*añjali*).

"May you appear before me at every season, or in every fortnight, for a moment or for two moments, whenever we desire it, or come at that very time"—thus one should choose a boon. And she grants exactly as desired; the method of disappearance is just as previously described. || 5 ||
Then, having cast off the vital breaths (*vāsūn*), he wanders at will and attains his desired world;

thus Parā also becomes manifest, says Unmattabhairava. First, Īśvara manifests as its concealer, and afterwards, along with other Īśvaras, that Supreme Self (*parātmā*) is the Lord, even though His signs are unmanifested.
Some say that he perceives both himself and others.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Uttarādhyāya of the Śrīpārānandasūtra.
(p. 88) The Fifth Chapter of the Pārānandasūtra.
Now we shall explain the sequence of expiations (*prāyaścitta*) by means of which unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) [is produced] when one has committed forbidden acts.
That which, when performed, brings about the destruction of suffering is called *prāyaścitta* (expiation).
Regarding expiations such as fasting (*upavāsa*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), bathing (*snāna*), and so forth:
[if one asks], "What is the expiation for one who should punish those not deserving of punishment?"—the answer is: "One should fast for three days; this is it."
Expiation is prescribed for the performance of what is prohibited; expiation is not prescribed for the performance of what is not prohibited.

Since there is no sin in performing what is not prohibited, there is spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) in performing what is enjoined; therefore, because expiation is itself enjoined, there is likewise spiritual prosperity resulting from it.
Thus says Unmattabhairava. Therefore, we shall now declare the sequence of expiatory rites.

Whether knowing or not knowing, whether involuntarily or voluntarily, whether by concealment or without concealment, and whether with relish or without relish— among these, if one should commit a sin knowingly, involuntarily, by concealment, and with relish, the expiation there is fourfold; and as each preceding factor is successively diminished, the expiation is proportionately less.

If King Pārānanda were to suppress other doctrines and systems because he was not a sovereign emperor (*asamrāṭ*), then he ought to establish his own doctrine and its systems; he should arrange matters such that the *āstika* (theistic) systems are superior to his own, and the *nāstika* (non-theistic) systems are inferior even to those. If he were to act in this manner, what would be the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for him?

One should fast for one day for sins committed in three ways: physical, vocal, and mental. Among these, regarding physical sin, if one should strike with the feet those worthy of honor such as cows or Brahmins, the expiation for that is to remain standing during the day when the sun has risen, and sitting in the open air during the spring or autumn when the sky is cloudless.

In a place more than five *krośas* away [from a town], water that flows naturally constitutes a sacred bathing-place (*tīrtha*); having gone there on foot and bathed therein, one becomes pure. This sinner is purified by three means: by the king's punishment, by experiencing suffering beginning with this life and ending in the next, and by expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). If one should act contrary to the established doctrine, what [remedy] would there be?

Regarding "expiation" (*prāyaścitti*): one should perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*) again if one should contemplate anything contrary to the doctrine, or if there is [error] regarding the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth; therein, expiation consists in performing the initiation consisting of contemplation (*bhāvanāmayī*) once more.
In a re-initiation, there is nothing else for the teacher; everything else is the same as in the rules for initiation.

For those [actions] which are impossible to perform, there is no need for initiation because they are not performed; however, through the excellence of initiation, one who is initiated becomes superior. Therefore, one should salute him. If, after saluting him, one should happen to eat before [the teacher], what is the expiation for that?
Having bathed, one should perform a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*); thereafter, one eats clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*). Whatever one eats, that indeed purifies the downward breath (*apāna*).
When he practices breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he shakes off the very dullness born of lethargy; when he consumes clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), he makes himself resplendent;
or rather, he should bow down before him like a staff and, having prostrated, say to him:
"Whatever I have failed to salute out of negligence, cut that away from me—grant me prosperity and serenity."

"Place [the mantra] in me. When there is a deficiency in a limb of the body, that specific limb alone undergoes repetition until, from the commencement of the removal of impermanence, the deficiency at the start becomes complete.
If one who has been initiated should teach the mantra to a disciple who is uninitiated, there must be initiation again.
For one who has been initiated, there is initiation again after entering another stage of life; for one who has gone to another teacher, there is initiation again.
That alone which constitutes an expiation (prāyaścitta) is truly efficacious, for it eradicates both types of consequences arising from sin; thus, just as sin is rendered fruitless through expiation,
so too can merit be rendered fruitless by some misdeed— but never that which is born of the nature of the Lord.
(89) This unseen merit, which prevents the two [types of suffering], cannot be warded off by anyone;
it yields infinite fruit from being performed even once. Therefore, the wise person should accumulate it. || 10 ||

Now follows the secondary rule for the daily worship: when a king punishes those who deserve punishment, he performs that very daily worship; therefore, just as one performs an expiation after omitting the daily worship, so too, by failing to punish those deserving of punishment and by punishing those undeserving of it, the king [incurs a debt] for one day.
One should fast for two or three days.

Now, the alternative procedure for the daily worship: having invoked with "Bhūḥ," [one worships] in the Pratīka [image], saying: "To [Name], who is the Īśvara-self, together with weapons, together with ornaments, together with vehicles, together with the ornaments of the vehicles, together with the seat of her own vehicle, together with Śakti, together with the weapons of Śakti, and together with the ornaments of Śakti."

"To the one with her power (śakti), vehicle, ornaments, seat, and retinue, to the deity [Name], together with her own devotees, obeisance! Bhuvaḥ!"—with these words he offers a handful of flowers; or else, having praised her with "Obeisance to [Name]! Svaḥ!", he concludes with "Mahaḥ!"
One should perform the dismissal with this mantra. He who acts in this manner obtains the fruit of the threefold worship;

therefore, even as a substitute for the threefold worship, he who worships the deity with a handful of flowers by means of this mantra is a true worshiper through his special worship of the deity—even if it be with a single flower or a portion of a single flower.
Thus it is accomplished; this is the expiation. 12.

He who should desire, "May I attain youth through the grace of the deity," [should offer] to his own chosen deity [goats] that are well-formed, more than eight years old, and whose age has not yet exceeded that specific year.

For the Brahmins, having shaved all the hair on their bodies with a barber's razor—except for the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) and the hair of the eyebrows, eyelashes, and body—he should have them shaven; or rather, he may do so as long as they believe that by shaving, this person is lifting himself up from sins. Having had them perform an oil massage and a dry rubbing, [he should proceed].
Having bathed with warm water, [he wears] the first loincloth, the second around the waist, the third at the region of the navel, and another large one as the fourth.

Likewise, ten sets of four garments, or [the application of] black collyrium from stone for the third and fourth [eyes], are explained as ornaments; as well as a parasol, sandals, water-pots, flower garlands,
saffron, red sandalwood, pure mercury, or copper and stone which destroy many diseases.

When one gives great medicine, milk, curd, ghee, prepared food, or water; or when one provides a comfortable bed, or even a beautiful young woman who is normally enjoyed repeatedly for the sake of a single enjoyment—such as a courtesan—one thereby causes oneself to prosper through the grace of the deity. One should offer salutations to them.

If one who is capable gives with faith to faithful householders, or if he should desire to give to someone other than those [householders], then for him there is this alternative rule: "to that person, that object.
In this case, there is no deliberation regarding whether the recipient is a worthy vessel or not; for a twice-born man is the worthy vessel for the act of teaching.

Between the giving of the sacrificial fee and [the receiving of] gifts, the learned Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with both knowledge and conduct is the worthy recipient; he alone is the true sacrificer through his faith.

And the capacity of one possessed of courage is especially [the desire to give] when a benefactor who was previously seen is present; some say that such a person is a constant worthy recipient (pātra). 15.

In whatever measure there may be an offense of speech—whether greater or lesser—in that same measure are the recitations of the *brahmapada* the expiation for all offenses of speech; for all offenses of mind, the sacrifices are the expiation; and likewise, for all offenses of mind, the breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) are the expiation.
(90) Expiation consists of giving gifts to worthy recipients in various ways for offenses such as theft of grain and the like, or it is the acceptance of royal punishment; such is expiation. || 16 ||
Visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*), performing twenty-one fasts as a universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*),

fasting, abstaining from food, or subsisting on water— having performed these, one gains the knowledge that "by this being done, no fruit shall arise [from the sin]"; this is the shaving (*muṇḍana*) of the hair of the aged.
Except for the hair of the eyebrows, eyelashes, and the tuft on the crown, there shall be the shaving of the head and beard;
for the elderly, bathing, sipping water (ācamana), and marking the body are required both before and after the mere performance of penance. || 17 ||
On the sixth day from the day on which the performance of the expiation takes place, the performance of the tonsure and other rites occurs; thus it happens later. || 18 ||
Thus has the sequence of expiations been explained. || 19 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Uttarādhyāya of the Pārānandasūtra.
(p. 91) The sixth chapter in the Pārānandasūtra.
Now we shall explain the method of exposition. || 20 ||
In the Kṛta Yuga at the beginning of creation, various doctrines and various ritual practices were expounded by the seers;
they explained them and imparted them to their respective disciples,
and those disciples followed those mental dispositions and modes of conduct— concerning this, I say:
The Blessed One Parānanda, pleased by their various meditations and the practices they had performed,

desired to instruct them in the doctrine according to its true meaning; as he was descending, thinking "I have descended," the sages Vasiṣṭha and others rushed toward me as I sat upon a lotus seat on the favorable bank of the Gaṅgā.

Having prostrated, they said to me, "Instruct us; explain [the path]. I replied, "According to my view, those who have not been initiated are not to be instructed; there is neither renunciation nor non-violence [for them], and so forth. They asked, "Violence is heard of in the sacrifice; why is it not practiced by those initiated according to your doctrine? Do they not incur sin? To this I replied:
It is appropriate that what has been stated should not be subjected to mere reasoning or logic; rather, it must be determined with the conviction that "this is the truth.

This is to be applied as a suggested meaning (dhvanyartha), joined together as a discourse for one who does not seek further inquiry. Such discourse is of three kinds, and of these, I shall speak only of the first; therefore, you should listen with faith.
"Listen to me; if not, then go as you please. Having been addressed thus, they said, "There is no doubt regarding your word; we shall examine what has been heard from you.
When asked, I then replied, "Not until one is joined with the initiation of Pārānandī."

The injury to living beings in a sacrifice and the consigning of living beings to the lords [of initiation] occur prior to the initiation of supreme bliss (*pārānandī dīkṣā*); thus, injury is to be performed in the sacrifice, for thereafter there is the bliss of knowledge for those who are sinless.
They asked: "What is that initiation (dīkṣā) by which, having been initiated, we shall become qualified for hearing [the scripture]? The initiation previously explained was then explained to them:
initiation consists in adhering to at least one of those observances (niyamas) in whatever way possible.
It is accomplished. || 22 ||
The same applies to the initiation with material offerings (upadīkṣā) and the subsequent initiation (uttaradīkṣā). || 23 ||
The same applies to the rules for constant performance and occasional rites. || 24 ||
But the primary [view] is as previously stated. || 25 ||

Thus it was explained to them; they said, "We shall perform the primary [rite] itself. To those who had been initiated for twenty-four days, having given each the specific mantras according to their desire, and having taught them the respective doctrines and duties, he also instructed them in the constant performance of the rites.

Considering themselves to have achieved their purpose, they bowed to me and departed for their respective homes as they pleased; having gone there, they propagated this very teaching according to their respective authority. || 26 ||

Agastya and others, as well as Nārada and others, said, "We shall become practitioners of the Vāmācāra path. To them, I spoke of the dual practice consisting of liquor (*madya*) and the *mudrā* (the consort), or sexual union (*maithuna*).
Some authorities maintain that there are two types of this practice, namely *mudrā* and *maithuna*. || 27 ||
They also [are] as before. || 28 ||

Two sages named Deva and Devadeva approached me and said, "We shall become practitioners of the Northern Way (Uttarācāra). I likewise imparted the Northern Way to them. Having attained the Northern Way and being freed from their distress, they departed as they pleased; they too became as before.

(92) "The capable one, the learned one, and the seeker—these three indeed were the sages who came together. First they were consecrated for Dakṣa, then for Vāmin, and then for Uttara; they were also [consecrated] in the same manner as before. (30)

Vasiṣṭha initiated Sudarśana, who was the ruler of Ayodhyā, as a Śākta named Pārānanda; then, knowing that king to be non-violent, all the kings from every direction, having prepared for battle, challenged him. That king, having prostrated before Vasiṣṭha, said: "By me..."
Vasiṣṭha, having taken him aside and asked whether war should be waged by one who practices non-violence or not, rushed toward me; having prostrated before me, he addressed this question:
"This King Sudarśana, the lord of Ayodhyā, has become my disciple; Śākta has become my disciple, and Pārānanda has been born."

Having learned this, other enemies of his, thinking, "This man is non-violent; therefore he will not fight from now on," stood all around this country, blocking him while remaining prepared for battle. Knowing this, he asked me, "He has been brought into your presence; please instruct him. || 31 ||
I said to him, "Bring him here. He approached, having prostrated himself, and I instructed him:

"Other than that which is righteous from battle, there is no other [duty] for you, O King; therefore, fight, cut off their heads, and attain victory. Having been thus instructed, he, Vasiṣṭha, and those two both departed.
The two became [such]. || 32 ||
And he obtained victory. || 33 ||

Certain followers of Pārānanda, performers of the Agnihotra sacrifice, began a ritual by bringing living beings with the intent to kill them; while they were being bound to stakes and slaughtered, Nārada arrived there while wandering about and said to them, "What is this that you are doing? They replied, "It is a sacrificial session (satra). He said, "This is no sacrificial session; this is a non-sacrifice."

Those Pārānandas, who were intent on killing living beings, said, "This is true, this is true; for that very reason we do not see the deity. May your lordship tell us how we might see [the deity] through this sacrifice performed by the Lord.
Thus questioned by them, Nārada said, "Pay close attention to the sacrificial procedure of Pārānanda."

In sacrifices such as the *homa* and others ending with the subsequent rites, those who perform animal sacrifices for the purpose of slaughter, making images of as many animals as are required and performing their actions while meditating, "We are performing divine duties by resorting to these [images]," do not attain those [divine results]; they do not reach the divine worlds, but are subject to falling. || 36 ||
Violence is indeed the destroyer of life-span and the destroyer of the wealth of merit.
If one were to perform thousands of heaps of meritorious deeds by resorting to violence, [it would not equal the merit of a single act of non-violence].
We are not able to grant him happiness by any means whatsoever.
One should desire that diseases such as consumption (yakṣman) and others, by relying upon [the patient], become effectors of happiness.
Otherwise, through improper conduct, they would not grant you happiness. || 37 ||
Just as water mixed with poison can never quench thirst anywhere.
Likewise, merit joined with violence is not able to bestow happiness. || 38 ||
For any violence committed against those who are innocent, whether it be prescribed or prohibited;
Since it brings suffering in every way later on, one should therefore avoid it entirely. || 39 ||
Relying upon a single act of non-violence, one may [overcome] even mountains of evil.
By means of non-violence, that man makes all beings pure and free from sin.
Thus,

for those men who anywhere perform the cutting, the slaughter, the buying, or likewise the selling of a human body— which is otherwise not to be killed and not to be punished— [they incur the following].
Benefit, formative activity, enjoyment, cutting, and approval.
Indeed, those who are experts in violence would even go so far as to perform dismemberment of the limbs.
The cutting, slaughter, buying, selling, processing, or consumption of the limbs of innocent creatures who have been harmed by humans and who were previously characterized by a state of tenderness;
or the assistance, the approval, or even the engagement in any one of these aforementioned actions.
For he too would become a partaker of suffering, such as that arising from violence and the like. || 42 ||
Whether it be consecration or slaughter, purchase or sale,
as well as assistance, enjoyment, and likewise the consent to mutilation.
Violence is of seven kinds; these secondary forms are equal to actual injury.
Therefore, one who has been favored by the Lord should avoid the eightfold injury.
In those scriptures where the injury of innocent living beings is prescribed,
one should fashion an image of the specific creature mentioned there out of flour.
Then, the wise and pure person should touch a living being made of flour.
Having first discarded the animal sacrifice and then the flour-based offering,
whatever rite the wise man should perform, he should arrange the ritual procedure in that very manner.

Or, on a square mound made of flour, using a bamboo twig as a writing stylus, the patron, the *hotṛ*, the *adhvaryu*, the *udgātṛ*, the *brahmā*, or whoever else one might designate, should draw the figure of that person. If the patron is a Brāhmaṇa, [the lines] should be drawn with a twig of *pālāśa* wood; if a Kṣatriya, with an *audumbara* twig; if a Vaiśya, with a *vailva* twig; for all, however, a bamboo twig may be used.

Therefore, having caused a living being to be seized by means of a bamboo branch upon which everything has been inscribed, and having released that living being to the north of the *śāmitra* shed, one should lead the inscribed object to the *śāmitra* and place it there with its head toward the east or the west and its feet toward the north; then, whatever [mark] from the line on the limb—
Whichever limb he extracts, having mixed it with the milk thus drawn and stirred it with water, he should cook it and sacrifice with those [limbs]. || 45 ||
"With the ghee of a cow, the milk of a cow, and the curd of a cow—for all animals"—thus [says] Digbhairava.
"By means of a buffalo for all animals," says Kālabhairava. (47)
Whatever form [of the deity] may have been painted or fashioned, [the ritual applies] to one of that same class; thus says Ākāśabhairava. (48)
For all sacrificial animals, [the offering] consists of wheat flour. || 49 ||
Water with red sandalwood and water with lac juice [are used] for all types of blood. || 50 ||
(94) Blood is red sandalwood water mixed with sour substances; thus says Digbhairava. || 51 ||
Lakṣārasa water mixed with jambīra juice is "blood," according to Kālabhairava. || 52 ||
Red sandalwood water, lac juice water, and blood mixed with curd—this is Ākāśabhairava. || 53 ||
Vasiṣṭha says that water alone is blood. || 54 ||
Or, from whatever he may desire this, he should place a small portion of that into it; by means of that, he should sacrifice to him.

Avoiding violence and discerning what is appropriate, the wise man should perform all actions, perceiving in some cases the contemplation of the departure of the vital breath and in others the performance of rites with flour-based offerings. || 56 ||

By those who practice non-violence (*ahiṃsaka*), all forms of violence must be eliminated by Pārānanda, except for unavoidable violence, violence resulting from punishment, and violence against those who commit heinous crimes; for while violence resulting from punishment bestows prosperity, others likewise [attain it] in three ways, according to some, as distinct from Pārānandas.
Vasiṣṭha: 57.
One should touch him with that animal-skin, or else one should touch him with that sacrificial grass (barhis) which has been touched by it. || 58 ||
Furthermore, some teachers who discourse on Brahman say that living beings are not to be sacrificed by those seeking the supreme bliss,
with the exception of horses, humans, oxen, camels, elephants, birds that fly, and wild animals; among these, they proceed only with those made of flour,
for other living beings are excluded from sacrifice because they share a single common nature, such as being conveyed, drunk, or slaughtered.
The extraction of the marrow and so forth is the same. 59.

Now, some who perceive the truth, the Pārānandas, who eliminate the sacrificial duties toward living beings everywhere and instead revive those beings, perform their rites using only flour-based offerings; in that case, the procedure from the preliminary consecration (*upākaraṇa*) up to the end of the constituent sacrifice (*aṅgayāga*) is the same, with the exception of drinking, moving, and the ritual quieting (*saṃjñapana*).
Mudga-bean flour [is beneficial] for creatures that consume grass. || 61 ||
The flour of *guḍūcī* is for those who eat fruits. || 62 ||
The paste of black gram is for meat-eaters.
Sesame paste [is the offering] for aquatic creatures. || 64 ||
Rice is [the food] of those who move on the earth. || 65 ||
Chickpea flour is for the sky-walkers. || 66 ||
Or one may perform any one of these for all [the deities]. || 67 ||
Wheat flour is for all [of these]. || 68 ||

Those who possess sacrificial fires, having immolated either living animals or animal-shaped effigies made of flour, and having released the living animals, bring those flour-made animal-shaped effigies to the *śāmitra* fire on the north side; having established them there, they extract their omenta and offer the portions of the limbs, O exponents of the Veda.
Those who sacrifice with these [verses] attain the splendor of Brahman; he who sacrifices attains infinity.
Having been thus instructed, they acted accordingly and beheld their own chosen deity.
Honored by them, Nārada ascended to heaven. || 71 ||
95) There was once a king named Khaḍgaprasiddha Pārānanda; considering that "this is the sovereign dharma," he attained freedom from rebirth simply by punishing those deserving of punishment.
The initiated Śākta departed without performing any other religious duties.
The son of the Brahmarṣi Ṛṣyaśṛṅga was named Ṛṣabha.

Having been initiated and having studied the Vedas after sixteen years, he abandoned the life of a religious student; becoming a Pārānanda, he did not engage in teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or accepting gifts, and being rejected by his father, he left his home.

Pārānandavruva performed the Pārānanda Dharma; then, when questioned by someone, that Śākta said, "I am Pārānanda. Soon thereafter, purified by faith and liberated while living, that Kālika Śākta moved about in the presence of the deity.
There was a certain Brāhmaṇa named Dīrghatamas; he had three sons, Gautama, Pragautama, and Avagautama. Their father was blind, while their mother was Surūpā;
she was unchaste, constantly seeking out new men, and bringing them in perpetually, one after another.

The man took pleasure [in her], and by the stamping of his feet, her blind husband discovered him; overcome with great anger, he cursed her. She, enraged because her sexual pleasure had been interrupted, said to him, "Kill this Gautama who has thwarted my pleasure. He replied, "Do not kill me! He then subjected him to an investigation. This one...
"This is my father, this is my mother; what wrong could I possibly do? he reflected.

He realized, "My mother has greater authority over me than my uninitiated self," and so he killed his father; yet he was not tainted by sin. Thereafter, he was initiated by a sage with the food of a hermit.
Having seen this, Prabarhin did the same after being initiated; he was joined with evil therein, but then, through the initiation of Pārānandī Śaibyā, he became cleansed of that evil.
The descendant of Bhṛgu, known as Paraśurāma, was the son of Jamadagni.
Having seen a certain wealthy man, his mother became enamored of him; knowing this, Jamadagni said to Paraśurāma, "Kill this mother of yours with my own marrow. She replied, "Do not harm me!"
He reflected upon this: "This is my father, this is my mother; whom among them should I kill?
He then realized that once he was initiated, he would become superior to them. He killed his mother with a sharp-edged blade, yet he was not tainted by sin; Śiva made him Pārānanda, the son of Kālī.
Having seen this, the uninitiated Prahāda caused his mother to be slain by the command of his father;
thus defiled by that sin, he subsequently became cleansed of his evil through the initiation of Kālīkeyī, the daughter of Parāśara.
Nāciketa was the son of Brahmarṣyāyaṇa, initiated into the mantra of his own chosen deity.

He who initiates one is an *ācārya*; he who teaches is an *upādhyāya*; and he who initiates a disciple into the meaning of the mantra of the deity to be worshipped and instructs him in that mantra is a *guru*. Regarding this, they cite the following verse:
The father is the best teacher; the preceptor (upādhyāya) is superior to him;
the guru is superior to the preceptor; and among all living beings, there is none higher than the guru.
He became intent on giving all his household gold to his teacher; however, his parents became opposed to this. Knowing this, Nāciketa cut off their heads with a sword.
Upon learning of this, the teacher was pleased and restored them to life.

Having seen that the sacrificial seat (*prastara*) which had been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) became smeared with sin due to the syllable *ca*, he [the Lord] then became one whose impurities were shaken off by the Vaiṣṇava initiation (*dīkṣā*) known as Pārānandī. || 78 ||
Vali, the son of Virocana and a devotee of Vishnu, became intent on giving everything to Vishnu; his preceptor, who was intoxicated by pride, became an obstacle for him.
Seeing that the preceptor—who was liberated while living—did not incur sin because he had offered [the gift] for the sake of his own deity, [Vali proceeded].

At dawn, Prayūṣa, who was already liberated while living (jīvanmukta), performed this for his own guru; he became anointed by that initiation of Pārānandī, and through Saurī, he once again became cleansed of all sin. || 79 ||
With the remnants of the Lord of Svarādhyā, one whose mind is fixed on another should sacrifice to the Self from the Truth; some say that one should sacrifice to the Self from the Lord of the Truth.
The knowers of Brahman, the Brahman-sages known as the Pārānandas, declare that one should not sacrifice with reference to oneself unless one possesses devotion toward Him [the Lord]. 80.
O Pārānanda, there was a king named Yamaparākrama belonging to the Kālikeya clan;

while he was establishing the Kālikeya dharmas, that liberated-while-living (jīvanmukta) king’s courtiers and city-dwellers were for the most part Kālikeyas, their limbs smeared with red sandalwood paste and adorned with shimmering golden garlands.
Wearing a garland of red flowers and bearing sharp weapons, the peaceful king Pārānanda summoned Varuṇa.
Summoned, Varuṇa arrived and he said to him, "Bring the wine of Varuṇa for the worship of Kālikā.
Seeing that it had been brought by him, he said to him, "Give me some of this best [wine]. To him, Varuṇa replied.

"Examine the *surā*," he said. It fell from his hand; from that vessel, *ikṣu* (sugarcane) spirits appeared. Varuṇa took the essence from them and gave it to the king. He declared, "It is excellent! Therefore, sugarcane spirit is given in place of *surā* when *surā* is unavailable.
He began to worship the deity; his sacrificial materials were smeared with excellent sandalwood and honored with red flowers.
As he was touching the *kuśa* grass that had been slightly moistened with red sandalwood, a man driven by the wind brushed against him.
That man, afflicted with leprosy, threw it away; as he cast it, he fell down, and having been cured of his leprosy, he immediately attained a divine body and ascended to heaven.

It is known that by understanding the greatness of one who bears the anointing of red sandalwood, what man could possibly describe the majesty of such a person? Therefore, a learned and capable man should wear this ointment in a temple of the deity,
whether it be one dedicated by a king or as prescribed, when the four castes have been summoned for a special worship.

Having completed the *cakra* crowded with courtesans, liquor, and food, one should recite the peace-mantra (*śānti*): "Whatever obstacles he has, whatever evils he has, and whatever ill-performed rites he has—let them be cast down by Bhairava and roll upon the ground;
and those who are faithful toward him, let them be free from affliction and, being virtuous, may they sport through the grace of Bhairava."

In the world of men and likewise in the world of the gods, those wise ones who, being tranquil, recite this peace-mantra three or four times according to their number, dwell in peace. Immortality, which is attained by yogis, is obtained by those virtuous people devoted to [the deity] who recite this peace-mantra; thus it is stated prior to the worship of Peace.
Or else, whatever may be deficient in the worship, one completes it with this [mantra];
or one may perform the worship using other practices that are not contrary to the *Pārānanda*; or one may follow what is stated in this very sūtra;
or one may follow what is stated in the *Āhnika*; or one may follow what is stated in the *Prakaraṇa*; or one may follow what is stated in a single sūtra.
O Pārānanda, by whatever is offered with devotion through the path that is not opposed to Pārānanda, one attains perfection. Offering to the deity from the left is superior;
on the left, offering to the deity from the right is superior.
Some say that everything from the left to the right is otherwise the same; this mandala-worship is concise:
it consists of the invocation of the deity, the deity’s power (śakti), and the vehicle of the deity’s power, such as Lakṣmī-Garuḍa, Viṣṇu-Garuḍa, and Lakṣmī—this is the mandala of Viṣṇu.

97) *Kurukullāsiṃha* and *Kālikāsiṃha*: "Kurukullā" is a name for Kālikā, and "Pārvatīvṛṣabha" and "Śivavṛṣabha" are names for Śiva; likewise, "Pārvatī" is a name for Śiva. Furthermore, "Sūryāśva" and "Saṃjñā" are names for Sūrya.
Bhairavī belongs to Bhairava, and Bhairava belongs to Bhairavī; the mouse of nourishment belongs to the elephant, and the elephant belongs to the mouse of nourishment.
The Brahmin swan belongs to Brahmā, and Brahmā belongs to the Brahmin swan. One who worships such [deities] as their own respective [forms], that very thing is attained by him. || 81 ||
He who always dwells making, touching, and seeing the supreme bliss through its gradations becomes powerful everywhere. We shall describe this incompletely: among animals, humans are superior;

among them, the Brahmins; among them, the learned; among them, the ascetics; among them, the perfected ones (siddhas); higher than them are the deities; and higher than them are the liberated ones (muktas).

Thus, the father is superior to the mother, the preceptor to the father, the mantra to the preceptor, and the deity to the mantra; from the insentient comes the sentient, the Lord from the insentient [such as the Śāligrāma], from that the Supreme Self, and from that the individual souls; from the individual souls come the Lords, and from the Lords comes the Supreme Self. There is nothing higher or more excellent than that which is denoted by the syllable Om.

Just as the learned do not press [the Soma] for the sake of the Lord as if He were independent in every respect, but rather press it for the sake of the Supreme Self alone— of this we shall cite further examples— just as a wise man indeed honors a learned man, an unlearned man, one who is hungry, and one who has arrived as a guest in every way.

He is equal toward both in removing hunger; indeed, food functions identically for both. He offers sweet food to this one [the knower] for the sake of destroying hunger, and to that other, the ignorant one, he offers inferior food.
Thus it is in all cases, such as speaking, censuring, praising, saluting, bowing, offering a seat, and giving gifts.

The gradation among these states has been explained: just as one feels compassion toward a mind that is suffering and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward one that is happy; joy (*muditā*) toward one who performs actions born of virtuous unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); and equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward one who performs actions born of non-virtuous unseen merit—or else, in the final case, restraint: one who is capable of exercising gradation but unable to do so cultivates equanimity. Or alternatively, [the gradation applies] to whoever...

One who, knowing thus, contemplates, speaks, and acts according to this gradation; who restrains, favors, gives, sacrifices, and remains equanimous—he is fit for immortality; he attains his desired goal and becomes established in perfection. || 82 ||
Thus ends the sixth daily lesson in the Uttarādhyāya of the Pārānandasūtra.
(p. 98) The seventh daily lesson in the Pārānandasūtra.
Now we shall describe the sequence of the duties of a king (*rājadharma*).
A Kṣatriya possesses a majesty consisting of strength, prowess, health, beauty, intelligence, wealth, and so forth, obtained through the grace of the deity;
such that all weapons become futile against him in his body, and he remains ever-victorious over all.

For one whose every weapon or missile is unfailing in all circumstances—whose entire army is useful for victory in battle, and thereafter useful for protection or for splendor—he is a king liberated while living; he is the best among men. One born of such a lineage is base [if he acts otherwise].

One who performs human duties through the combined strength of reasoning, application, power, wealth, forts, and so forth, is superior; one devoid of these is the lowest of the low. For such a king, there are four principles: punishment (*daṇḍa*), generosity (*dāna*), self-restraint (*dama*), and compassion (*dayā*). Among these, punishment is preeminent, for by its application—like a great medicine against what is blameworthy—it maintains the stability of the subjects.

One may remove diseases; through an abundance of teachers, one removes ignorance; through giving, one removes poverty; by establishing progeny, one removes the suffering in the hearts of the virtuous; and by punishing the wicked, one removes [evil]. Furthermore, a brother, a son, a worthy guest, a mother, a father, a teacher (*upādhyāya*), an instructor (*ācārya*), a preceptor (*guru*), a supreme preceptor (*paramaguru*), those of divine origin such as *gandharvas* and others, a father-in-law, and a maternal uncle [are likewise to be honored].

Whether it be a paternal uncle or anyone else who is an object of affection, if he should deserve punishment according to the facts, he must indeed be punished by the king; for there is no one whatsoever who has deviated from his own duty (*dharma*) whom the king may not punish.
Punishment may consist of decapitation, confiscation of all property, flogging with a whip, fasting until unconsciousness, or subsisting on water alone.

The sixteen-fold fetter-bond (*nigaḍabandha*) consists of dishonor and the performance of the prescribed penance; these punishments are equal to the *pārānanda* decree. However, according to the *pārānanda* doctrine, there is neither the destruction of limbs or senses nor a lifelong fetter-bond. I shall now describe the procedure for decapitation: having brought the man condemned to death, he should be bathed.

In a clean and level place before Kālikā, having bound the neck of a victim prepared for sacrifice— such as one intent on taking life— to a pillar with a rope or similar means, and having worshipped the deity Siṃha Kurukullā, Kurukullā-Siṃha, the sword, and the *bali* offering with red sandalwood and flowers,
[one should worship] the pillar, the rope, and the ground with what remains.
If the executioner himself performs the worship, some say he should first [worship] his own self. Thereafter, he stands before [the victim] and recites:
"O Kālikā, by the cutting [of this head] in your presence, may this person go to the heavenly world, free from passion and free from sin;
and may I likewise go there, free from passion and free from sin. May the two lions be satisfied with his blood."
"May other dogs than these, as well as his own skin, come for peace, O sages and ancestors; may they rejoice.

May the flesh-eating ancestors who eat his flesh, and the gods, depart rejoicing with his leavings. Through policy, through justice, and through discipline, being satisfied by the punishment of one deserving of punishment, grant desires to the sacrificer"—having thus offered worship.

Uttering "Hūṃ Phaṭ," having severed the head and taken it with its blood into a vessel, he places it before the deity; then, into another vessel of water, he pours his own *sruk* ladle filled with that blood, offering the first ladle with the mantra: "To Kālikā, who delights in drinking blood, Svāhā! and thus pours out the first ladle.

"To the lion, who delights in drinking blood, I offer this blood; may he, being pleased by it, grant desires to the sacrificer—Svāhā! This is the second [offering]. "To Kurukullā, I bring this blood; may she, being pleased by it, bestow desires upon the sacrificer—Svāhā! This is the third [offering]. Kurukullā is the lioness who destroys enemies.

"Engaged for him, I bring this blood; may he, being satisfied by it, grant desires to the sacrificer—Svāhā! This is the fourth [offering]. Then, with the fifth ladle, she pours out the blood filled [with the formula]: "Those gods who thirst for blood—the seers, the ancestors, humans, those known and unknown, the animals, and the piśācas."

(99) "I offer this to those living beings who are devoted to the Dharma; may they grant desires to the sacrificer, svāhā! Having thus lit the lamp on the fifth [finger], he approaches the sword with the mantra: "Thou art the sword (asir asi)."

You alone are the protector of Dharma, the sharp-edged, unassailable sword whose essence is glory; you are victory and the destroyer, the benefactor of the world. You bestow this-worldly [happiness] upon those who should not be slain, and the happiness of the next world upon those who deserve to be slain.
Toward those who should not be slain, you are peaceful with a peaceful edge; toward those who deserve to be slain, you are fierce with a sharp edge.
"Be pleased with the blood of the victim; salutations to you! Do not harm me;
being satisfied with the blood, grant victory, happiness, health, and constant fearlessness to the sacrificer.
Having thus performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), they worship with three handfuls of flowers as prescribed and conclude the rite of worship. This same procedure applies to every victim.
The ritual for the slaying:
"We worship the three-eyed one, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
Like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from death, not from immortality."
They prescribe that very blood-mark (rudhiratilaka) first on the forehead, the pit of the throat, the head, the roots of the arms, and the heart;
thus, one who possesses the mark is not joined with untimely death, but through death in battle or the like, he is joined with a divine state.
Therefore, this mantra is for all marks (tilakas). What are those "all" marks? [They are] the turmeric-mark (hāridra), the ash-mark (bhasma), and so forth.

Whether they be Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas, Sauras, Śāktas, Brāhmaṇas, or Gāṇapas— those who use red sandalwood or those who use clay— all these [regard] the acceptance of Bali as their food; some say it should be taken from those who perform that rite,
some say it should be cast into the forest, some say into fire, some say into water, and some say into a pit in the earth.

Some say [the ritual] involves a deposit (*nikṣepa*). Now, if the king should obtain many men to be executed—whether they be male or female—he should have their heads cut off at the edge of the *kālikā* (the dark fortnight), according to some; others say they should be bound and blinded.
This very *kālikā* is known as the recipient of the sacrificial offering (*balihāriṇī*) among all sovereign deities, because all Śākta practitioners belong to her.

Sauras, Śaivas, Gāṇapas, Brāhmas, Vaiṣṇavas, or Kāpālikas—having captured those condemned to death, the kings would offer their heads as a blood-sacrifice; so they say. Even women, when condemned to death, likewise recite this verse:
In former times, Rāmacandra slew Tāṭakā, who caused suffering to the people;

therefore, wise men have declared that wicked women are to be punished or even executed. One who is eager to offer a sacrifice to the devotees of Kālikā should give [the victim], and they should slay them according to the ritual procedure for the offering.

When a king causes those deserving of death to be executed, he makes himself high; for the heavenly world is indeed high. When he does not harm those deserving of death, he makes himself low; for hell is indeed low. When he honors the virtuous with wealth, humility, and what is pleasing to them, he makes himself exceedingly high.
Furthermore, they cite this verse concerning the world of Īśvara, which is exceedingly high:
"That king who punishes those deserving of punishment and properly executes those deserving of death has performed sacrifices completed with the most excellent sacrificial fees."
He who, according to the scriptures and following the prescribed method, causes a profusion of blood to fall upon the ground from the neck of one condemned to death with a sword—
he has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices.
By him all the Vedas have been studied, and every meritorious deed has been performed;
by him all gifts have been bestowed, who has carried out the execution of one condemned to death.
By thus offering the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to those condemned to death, he conquers heaven.
He who is merciless toward those deserving of execution, yet always overflowing with compassion for others,
is declared to be the true vessel of mercy for all the gods.
He who is compassionate toward those deserving of death is merciless toward his own self;
for he leads his own bewildered self to the place of hell. He who would not carry out the execution of one deserving death is a slayer of his own self and indeed a slayer of a Brahmin.
If a king does not desire the execution of those who are present and condemned to death,
they know that he is the abode of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin;
yet, if he abandons the lawful execution of those condemned and performs all other righteous deeds, [he is purified].
One should know that those [punishments] have become futile; such is not the execution of the condemned. This is the occasional duty (naimittika-dharma) proclaimed for kings;
having obtained the seven-limbed kingdom, one should not carry out the execution of the condemned here.
Later, he grieves for himself while dwelling in hell,
just as a man who, having acquired wealth, does not pursue virtue, and later,
having become destitute, truly laments for his own self.

Therefore, a wise man should not give to prosperous Brāhmaṇas those who deserve to be killed, nor land-dwelling animals such as horses; some say he may give the price for them instead, but a lord of the earth should not give away land, except for tanks, gardens, and uncultivated plots.

At some time, in some place, for someone, one should engrave upon a copper plate the genealogy of the donor and recipient as well as a description of the boundaries of the land, and bestow it upon the recipient; one should not take back what has been given, whether by oneself or by another.
For taking it unjustly, there shall be the punishment of a reproach, the punishment of fasting, the punishment of fetters, or the punishment of death.

Expiations and punishments should be applied according to the law. Some say that those who kill a person, those who violate the king’s command, and thieves who act with prior intent are to be punished with the death penalty; others say they should be punished with fetters. Thus, punishments—whether individually or collectively—should be applied to those deserving of punishment by one who exercises his own sovereign authority according to the law.

Having ascertained the direction, place, time, space, offense, strength, age, wealth, conduct, health, and learning of those subject to punishment, he shall inflict punishment upon them according to justice. Those who are diseased, the incapacitated, and so forth— all such persons are exempt from punishment, whether by number or by death.

Having established the kings there according to their respective ranks, the wise one should then command that they be released in successive order; for every ten, there shall be one leader, and he shall command them.
Without his command, those followers of livelihood do not engage in business during their working hours, except in the event of the death of their masters. All [this]...
His command is to be honored and carried out without hesitation. He who is the lord of these ten is a lord of a hundred; everything regarding him should be understood accordingly.
By this, the lord of a thousand is explained; there may be human lords of a hundred thousand, except for those who perform superhuman deeds.
The fines for them shall be double those [of the previous category], the fines for them shall be triple, and the fines for them shall be quadruple;
thus is the punishment for offenses explained. Their three punishments are: the lash of a whip.

One who issues an order after a short lapse of time regarding the abandonment of nourishment, execution, the discharge [of waste], the taking [of food or water], or the processing [of grain]— such persons and others like them are to be punished with a whip-lash; likewise, one who orders the discharge of feces and urine,
the taking of food and water, sexual intercourse, sleep, or the processing [of grain] by those living on bribes when they have been appointed by their master.
Except for the king’s own command, except for disobeying the orders of one appointed by the king—

provided it does not result in the death of the king— and except for one who repeatedly disobeys an order or one who knowingly disobeys an order, those such as these, as well as a murderer of a man, are to be punished with the second [type of] punishment.

One who transgresses a great command of a master, or one appointed by a master, or the master himself—such cases are included under the third [category]. Furthermore, a king’s command should not be in vain; that command which aims at the destruction of others’ dharma, learning, wealth, health, or life, provided it does not conflict with his own interests, is of this nature.
Having issued commands to those subordinate rulers in turn— according to region, time, and troop-strength—
he should cause them to rotate, such that for a year or a half-year, he might direct everyone thus: "In such-and-such a region, let this one be the head of such-and-such a troop."

One should cause [the mind] to waver; one should lead from a previously experienced state to a subsequent state, but not to a state never before experienced, nor even to a lower one—even if it be skillful. Having attained the most excellent state after five or ten years, one might be displaced from that state; yet, having fallen from it for as long as life lasts, one has not actually attained anything at all.

One should maintain [the dependents] with half of that amount, or provide wealth sufficient for as long as one lives, or give enough to suffice for the dependents at that time; this should be done justly in all positions. One should gradually lead [the subordinate] to become capable in all matters. The extraction of wealth by those who live on bribes involves all positions being occupied by two [parties].
Limited are the women, food, drink, vehicles, and garments according to the divisions of time; limited are the objects of enjoyment;
and when the king gains an advantage over those engaged in battle, then they are to be slain. || 83 ||
Or whoever masters this knowledge of two chapters, consisting of the daily rituals of the fourteen sciences, attains the bliss of the beyond and reaches immortality. || 84 ||
Whoever explains even a single Sūtra or half a Sūtra by means of speech—for him the Brahmayajña is completed; for him the Brahmayajña is completed. || 85 ||
Thus ends the seventh daily lesson in the Uttarādhyāya of the Pārānanda-sūtra.
And thus the Pārānandasūtra is completed;
and this Pārānandamīmāṃsā is also completed.
Thus, Oṃ.
